name: Imbalance-Aware Adaptation in Stream-Based Active Learning
description: This topic concerns mechanisms for handling class imbalance in active learning for data streams by adaptively reweighting ensemble classifiers. A damped class imbalance ratio (DCIR) is used as a streaming-aware indicator of how underrepresented each class is, based on its observed frequency over time. When a newly labeled instance is identified as belonging to a minority class via DCIR, a reinforcement-based update adjusts the dynamic classifier weights: classifiers are multiplicatively rewarded if they correctly predict the minority instance and penalized otherwise. These updates occur online after each queried label, allowing the active learner’s ensemble to quickly adapt its focus toward poorly represented classes in the evolving stream. The approach tightly couples label acquisition in a streaming setting with imbalance-aware model adaptation, improving performance on minority classes under limited annotation budgets.

name: Histopathology Datasets for Deep Active Learning Evaluation
description: This topic covers specialized histopathology datasets designed for evaluating deep active learning methods in medical image analysis. The ADI dataset focuses on human adipocyte cell histopathology and provides 150 samples with a predefined 50/100 split to simulate realistic labeled–unlabeled partitions for active querying. The DCC dataset comprises diverse tissues and species, with 176 samples and a 100/76 split, enabling assessment of how well deep active learning strategies generalize across heterogeneous histopathological domains. Together, these datasets serve as benchmarks for studying query strategies and performance under limited annotation budgets in challenging medical imaging settings.

name: Cold-Start Strategies for 3D Medical Segmentation
description: This topic focuses on deep active learning methods designed to address the cold-start problem in 3D medical image segmentation, where no or very few labeled samples are initially available. Methods such as ProxyRank use tailored self-supervised pretext tasks (e.g., threshold-based proxy segmentation in CT) to learn meaningful representations and generate proxy labels that guide the selection of the first samples to annotate. These representation-driven rankings aim to outperform random sampling when constructing the initial labeled set. Benchmark studies comparing ALPS, CALR, TypiClust, and ProxyRank on multiple MSD datasets reveal that while TypiClust tends to perform best overall, no method consistently surpasses random selection across all datasets. This highlights the instability and dataset dependence of current cold-start active learning strategies in medical image analysis and motivates further research into more robust initialization techniques.

name: Deep Active Learning for Critical-Domain Information Extraction
description: This topic covers the use of deep active learning to extract structured information from critical-domain text such as disaster-related tweets and clinical reports. Models based on RNNs/GRUs are combined with active learning strategies that query the most informative tweets or sentences for annotation, focusing particularly on those likely to contain key entities like infrastructure damage and locations. Active learning is also applied to clinical EEG documentation and other specialized reports to identify salient findings while minimizing expert labeling effort. Across these applications, active learning-guided pretraining and selective annotation enable rapid, high-precision information extraction in high-stakes domains like disaster response and medicine under constrained labeling budgets.

name: Generative Deep Active Learning for Aortic Stenosis
description: This topic covers the use of generative deep active learning to predict calcification levels in aortic stenosis from CT images. A bidirectional GAN combined with physics-based labeling is used to synthesize and automatically label informative samples, directly targeting regions of the feature space that improve the classifier under a limited annotation budget. By actively generating and selecting high-value samples instead of passively relying on random generation, the approach improves annotation efficiency by up to an order of magnitude. The DAL context is crucial because expert grading of calcification severity is time-consuming and requires specialized clinical expertise, making label-efficient strategies particularly impactful for this medical imaging task.

name: Dataset Splits and External Test Sets in Deep Active Learning for Medical Imaging
description: This topic covers how train–validation–test splits are designed for deep active learning experiments in medical image analysis. Datasets such as NCT-CRC-HE-100K are partitioned to define the labeled data pool used for active learning cycles and model tuning, typically via fixed ratios (e.g., 9:1 for training and validation). An independent dataset like CRC-VAL-HE-7K, collected from non-overlapping patients but sharing the same acquisition protocol and classes, is reserved purely as an external test set to assess generalization of AL-based models to unseen subjects. The discussion also highlights that partitioning and reporting units (images, slices, volumes) differ across datasets and modalities, which has implications for how active learning performance is measured and compared. Overall, these protocols aim to fairly evaluate both in-distribution performance and robustness of DAL systems across different patient cohorts.

name: Committee-Based Uncertainty and Normalized Entropy Selection
description: This topic covers committee-based acquisition strategies where empirical class probabilities are derived from model vote distributions and then used for uncertainty-driven querying. For each unlabeled pixel, an ensemble (committee) of models produces class predictions, and an empirical class probability pBAG is computed as the relative voting frequency per class, yielding a discrete probability distribution over classes. A normalized entropy query-by-bagging (nEQB) heuristic then measures uncertainty by the Shannon entropy of this empirical distribution, normalized by the logarithm of the number of distinct predicted classes to avoid bias toward regions with many overlapping classes. The most informative samples are selected by maximizing this normalized entropy, making the approach particularly suitable for multiclass settings and ensemble-based deep active learning pipelines.

name: AVIRIS Indian Pines Hyperspectral Benchmark for Active Learning
description: The AVIRIS Indian Pines scene is a classical hyperspectral benchmark widely used in studies of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification. It consists of a 220-band hyperspectral image of an agricultural/rural area in Indiana, with spatial dimensions of 145×145 pixels and 16 land-cover classes mainly corresponding to different crops. A ground survey provides 10,366 labeled pixels as ground-truth class labels, enabling evaluation of label-efficient learning methods. Its high-dimensional spectral data and structured land-cover classes make it a standard testbed for validating the accuracy and behavior of active learning methods in hyperspectral image classification under limited annotation budgets.

name: Auxiliary Uncertainty Networks for Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers the use of auxiliary neural modules to enhance uncertainty estimation and acquisition quality in deep active learning. Mixture Density Networks (MDNs) are integrated into detection architectures by replacing standard classification and localization heads with MDN heads that output full predictive distributions, including variances for both class labels and bounding boxes; these variances are then used as selection criteria in active learning loops. Such MDN-based approaches can match the empirical performance of MC dropout and ensembles while being more efficient in inference time and model size. More generally, model-aspect DAL methods attach auxiliary networks, such as loss prediction networks, that are trained jointly with the backbone to predict future classification errors or losses, and these predictions directly guide sample acquisition. These designs explicitly tailor the model to produce acquisition-relevant signals, going beyond raw softmax scores to richer, DAL-specific uncertainty measures.

name: Active Learning for Radiographic Landmark Detection
description: This topic covers the use of deep active learning for anatomical landmark detection in medical radiographs, where precise keypoint localization is required. In cephalometric analysis on lateral head X-rays, models must predict 2D coordinates of orthodontically relevant landmarks, but annotations are costly because they require expert radiologists or orthodontists. Similarly, hand radiograph landmark detection supports bone age assessment and deformity analysis, with datasets comprising hundreds of images and multiple joint keypoints per image. Deep active learning is applied to these settings to select the most informative radiographs for expert labeling, thereby reducing manual annotation effort while maintaining accurate landmark localization performance.

name: Optimal Experimental Design Criteria in Active Learning
description: This topic covers the use of classical optimal experimental design criteria, such as G-, I-, and V-optimality, as acquisition strategies in active learning. G-optimality selects points that minimize the maximum prediction variance over a region of interest, thereby controlling worst-case predictive uncertainty in the input space. In contrast, I- and V-optimality integrate or average the prediction variance over the region, aiming to improve overall predictive accuracy rather than focusing solely on extreme cases. Within deep and stream-based active learning, these criteria guide the selection of new samples to label so as to improve the predictive model under limited annotation budgets, with different trade-offs between robustness to worst-case uncertainty and global performance. The choice among these criteria affects sensitivity to anomalous observations and the spatial distribution of queried instances.

local_topics.title: G-, I-, and V-optimality via prediction variance

name: A-, D-, and E-optimal Design Criteria for Active Learning
description: This topic covers classical optimal experimental design criteria (A-, D-, and E-optimality) used to guide query selection by minimizing parameter uncertainty. A-optimality minimizes the sum of variances of the regression coefficients, or equivalently the trace of the inverse information (moment) matrix, focusing on improving the average precision of parameter estimates. D-optimality maximizes the determinant of the information matrix, which corresponds to minimizing the volume of the confidence ellipsoid around the parameters and encourages globally informative designs in a joint, multivariate sense. E-optimality minimizes the largest eigenvalue of the parameter covariance, shrinking the longest axis of the confidence ellipsoid and improving the worst-estimated linear combination of parameters. In an active learning context (including data streams), these criteria determine where to place or request new design points so as to most efficiently reduce model uncertainty under limited labeling budgets.

name: Context-Aware Selection in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that explicitly exploit contextual information when selecting queries. One line of work formulates active learning as a reinforcement learning problem, where a BiLSTM-based selector models dependencies among candidate samples and uses contextual diversity as a reward to favor both informative and contextually varied instances. Another direction looks ahead to active learning with foundation and visual models, framing the selection of in-context examples or prompts as an active learning problem. In this view, active learning strategies are used to choose optimal prompts for in-context learning, extending sample selection ideas from traditional supervised settings to prompt-based usage of large models.

name: DAL for Complex Tasks and Challenging Data Distributions
description: This topic concerns how deep active learning must be adapted to complex tasks and non-ideal data distributions. For structured, multi-step problems such as Visual Question Answering, existing DAL methods show limitations, suggesting the need for task-specific acquisition strategies and better feature representations that align with the task structure. The topic also highlights realistic data issues—including out-of-distribution samples, rare classes, severe class imbalance, redundancy, and extremely large unlabeled pools—that can dramatically alter DAL performance. Recent work explicitly targets these properties, designing DAL mechanisms to prioritize rare classes, mitigate redundancy, and remain robust under OOD and imbalanced conditions, pointing toward more distribution-aware and task-tailored DAL frameworks.

name: Sliding-Window Strategies in Stream-Based Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on sliding-window mechanisms for stream-based active learning, where only a temporally limited subset of recent data is retained for model updates. A forgetting strategy discards labeled instances that will fall outside a future training window once their labels arrive, preventing the learner from training on soon-to-be outdated observations and keeping the model aligned with the most relevant segment of a non-stationary data stream. A kNN-based approach maintains a moving reference set updated either in FIFO fashion or by preferentially retaining actively selected examples, thereby adapting to concept drift. Its query strategy combines a margin-like distance criterion, which targets instances near conflicting class neighborhoods, with a diversity criterion, which selects samples far from the current reference set via distance thresholds. These ideas are directly applicable when designing deep active learning systems for evolving data streams, where both temporal relevance and diversity must be managed under limited labeling budgets.

name: Bayesian Stream-Based Active Learning for Novel Class Discovery
description: This topic covers Bayesian online active learning methods for data streams that can both refine known classes and discover previously unknown classes. The models use nonparametric Bayesian clustering, such as Dirichlet process mixture models and Pitman–Yor process priors, to allow a flexible and potentially unbounded number of clusters/classes. Query selection is typically committee-based and disagreement-driven: labels are requested when sampled hypotheses disagree on the current instance, or when they jointly indicate assignment to a novel class index. This balances exploration (unknown-class discovery) with exploitation (improving decision boundaries among known classes) under a selective labeling budget in streaming settings. The result is an integrated framework for active querying and incremental class discovery without fixing the class set in advance.

local_topics.title: Bayesian committee framework for unknown-class discovery

name: Batch Selection and Redundancy in VHR Active Learning
description: This topic concerns active learning in very high resolution (VHR) remote sensing imagery where labels are obtained via on-screen photointerpretation. Due to strong spatial correlation, selecting many neighboring pixels with similar appearance leads to highly redundant training sets that slow learning and contribute little new information. To counter this, active learning is typically run with many iterations and relatively small query batches, which makes it feasible to use more complex selection heuristics. Diversity-promoting strategies, especially those enforcing spectral diversity among queried samples, are emphasized to reduce redundancy and better explore the feature space. The computational cost of these diversity-based acquisition functions increases rapidly with batch size, further reinforcing the small-batch regime in VHR active learning workflows.

local_topics.title: Photointerpretation and redundancy in VHR imagery

name: Breaking Ties Uncertainty Sampling in Active Learning
description: The Breaking Ties (BT) strategy is an uncertainty-based query method for pool-based active learning that selects samples where the classifier is most ambiguous between the top predicted classes. It typically measures uncertainty as the smallest difference between the two highest posterior class probabilities p(y|x), so samples with nearly tied top probabilities are prioritized. These points tend to lie close to the decision boundary and are thus expected to be highly informative when labeled. BT can be implemented with any probabilistic classifier, including probabilistic neural networks and maximum likelihood models, as long as they output calibrated class likelihoods. By relying on a single probabilistic model rather than an ensemble, BT offers computational efficiency while still exploiting posterior information for query decisions in deep or non-deep active learning setups.

local_topics.title: BT method using single probabilistic model

name: Superpixel-Based Annotation and Labeling in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on superpixel-based annotation strategies that reduce labeling cost in deep active learning for medical images. Dominant labeling assigns the majority class label within each superpixel and propagates it to all pixels in the region, trading exact boundary delineation for substantially improved annotation efficiency. Combined with class-balanced sampling, superpixels containing minority classes are preferentially queried, improving class balance in the labeled set under a fixed annotation budget. Building on this idea, adaptive merging of similar neighboring superpixels and splitting of complex ones yields region units that better align with anatomical structures, enhancing both label consistency and uncertainty estimation. These superpixel-centric methods outperform precise patch-level labeling under equal click budgets and improve the effectiveness of region-level query strategies in DAL.

local_topics.title: Adaptive merging and splitting of superpixels

name: Historical Trends and Survey Gaps in Deep Active Learning for NLP
description: This topic examines the historical development of active learning in natural language processing and its evolution toward deep active learning in the neural era. Foundational AL work and early NLP-focused surveys from the 1990s and 2000s, such as Settles (2009) and Olsson (2009), are now outdated relative to modern neural architectures and large-scale datasets. Bibliometric analysis of ACL Anthology publications shows a peak in AL work around 2009–2010, a subsequent decline during the rise of neural models, and a recent resurgence of interest specifically in deep active learning. Together, these observations motivate the need for contemporary, comprehensive surveys that explicitly address DAL methods, setups, and challenges in modern NLP.

name: Bandit-Based Label Budget Allocation in Active Learning
description: This topic covers the use of multi-armed bandit algorithms to allocate a limited labeling budget across multiple models or tasks in active learning, particularly for data streams. Querying a label is modeled as pulling an arm, with each model (or arm) having an unknown difficulty that must be estimated online. Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) principles are used to balance exploration and exploitation, combining estimated performance and uncertainty to decide which model to query next. Extensions such as trace-based UCB and norm-thresholding provide refined uncertainty measures for guiding budget allocation, aiming to learn all models uniformly well under shared annotation constraints. This bandit-based perspective makes the budgeting and selection mechanism explicit, aligning acquisition decisions with formal exploration–exploitation guarantees.

name: Modeling Label Dependencies in Deep Active Learning for Chest X-Rays
description: This topic focuses on explicitly modeling inter-label relationships in multi-label chest X-ray classification within deep active learning pipelines. Methods represent each disease label as a node in a graph, with edges encoding co-occurrence and dependency patterns, and use graph neural networks to propagate information between labels. Building on this, graph multiset transformers over label graphs are introduced to capture richer and higher-order interactions than standard message-passing GNNs. These structure-aware models aim to improve multi-label prediction quality under limited annotation budgets, thereby supporting more effective active learning on medical imaging data.

local_topics.title: Graph multiset transformers for label relations

name: Deep Active Learning for Question Answering and Dialogue
description: This topic covers the application of deep active learning to question answering (QA), dialogue systems, and multimodal visual question answering (VQA). DAL methods selectively query the most informative or uncertain question–answer pairs, dialogue turns, or image–question combinations to optimize annotation effort. Conversational datasets such as CMDC and JabberWacky chatlogs, as well as multimodal resources like Visual Genome and VQA, serve as pools from which to actively sample. The focus is on improving QA accuracy, dialogue quality metrics (e.g., BLEU-like scores), and VQA correctness under constrained labeling budgets by targeting ambiguous or high-uncertainty interactions for labeling or refinement.

name: Impact of Pretraining and Feature Quality on Deep Active Learning
description: This topic analyzes how backbone pretraining and resulting feature quality affect deep active learning performance, especially under dataset bias and spurious correlations. Using ResNet18 with and without ImageNet-1K pretraining, the studies show that pretrained models provide richer, more semantic feature representations that shift attention from backgrounds to objects, thereby improving DAL query selection. On simple datasets like MNIST, pretraining mainly raises overall accuracy while largely preserving the relative ranking of DAL strategies, with some methods such as LPL benefiting more from stronger features. On the spurious-correlation Waterbird dataset, non-pretrained backbones cause DAL methods (e.g., Entropy, EntropyD, CEAL, KMeans) to select biased samples that can even worsen mismatch and worst-group accuracy as the budget grows, whereas pretraining mitigates this by aligning predictions with object semantics. Budgeted accuracy curves across methods and datasets quantify how pretraining influences label efficiency, robustness to group imbalance, and the comparative behavior of uncertainty- and diversity-based DAL strategies.

name: Model Mismatch Between Query and Successor Models in Active Learning
description: This topic concerns the problem of query–successor model mismatch, where the model used to select instances for labeling differs from the final deployment model. Such mismatches commonly arise when a lightweight model is used during active querying for efficiency, while a heavier or updated model (often a deep model) is later trained on the collected labeled pool. Differences in inductive biases between these models can undermine or even negate the expected performance gains from active learning, since the queried samples may not be optimal for the successor model. Empirical studies show that this issue can substantially affect the long-term utility of AL-collected datasets, motivating methods that explicitly account for or mitigate query–successor mismatch when designing active learning strategies.

name: Confidence Intervals in Active Learning Evaluation
description: This topic concerns the use of confidence intervals to report classification accuracy in active learning experiments. In studies comparing query strategies such as random sampling (RS), margin-based sampling (MS), and MCLU/MCLU-ABE/MCLU-ABD, accuracy curves are accompanied by confidence intervals across runs or sampling realizations. These intervals capture the statistical variability of performance estimates under different labeling budgets, enabling more rigorous and reliable comparisons between strategies. By indicating whether observed performance differences are statistically meaningful, confidence interval reporting helps prevent over-interpretation of small gains and supports sound empirical evaluation practices in deep active learning.

name: Confidence-Interval Evaluation of Active Learning Strategies
description: This topic addresses the use of statistical confidence intervals to evaluate and compare active learning sampling strategies such as RS, nEQB, MS, and BT. Instead of relying on single accuracy values, performance is reported with uncertainty bounds derived from repeated runs or resampling, capturing variability in overall accuracy for each strategy. Incorporating confidence intervals enables more robust and statistically grounded comparisons, helping to determine whether observed differences between active learning methods are meaningful rather than due to random variation. Such evaluation practices are directly applicable to deep active learning experiments, where stochastic training and data selection can produce high variance in outcomes.

name: Pavia ROSIS Hyperspectral Benchmark for Active Learning
description: This topic covers the ROSIS hyperspectral image over Pavia, Italy, which is widely used as a benchmark dataset for supervised classification and active learning in remote sensing. The dataset provides very-high-resolution imagery with 102 spectral bands and five main land-cover classes, offering rich spectral–spatial information and extensive labeled pixels for controlled annotation-budget studies. Visualizations of mean spectral profiles and data manifolds show that the main classes are spectrally separable and well modeled by common linear and nonlinear classifiers, which informs the design and evaluation of active learning strategies. Together with AVIRIS Indian Pines and Zurich QuickBird images, Pavia ROSIS forms part of a multi-sensor evaluation suite enabling comparison of active learning algorithms across different spectral and spatial resolutions under standardized experimental conditions.

name: Deep Active Learning for Spinal Cord Compression Grading
description: This topic covers the application of deep active learning, combined with semi-supervised learning, to grade metastatic epidural spinal cord compression on spine MRI. A deep classification framework is trained with only a small fraction of labeled images (e.g., 10% plus an additional actively selected 5%), aiming to reduce annotation costs while preserving high diagnostic performance. The active learning component selectively queries the most informative MRI samples for expert labeling, which is critical in this high-stakes, labor-intensive medical imaging setting. Experimental results show that this strategy effectively improves performance for automated severity grading of spinal cord compression, demonstrating the practical value of DAL in clinical decision support.

name: Fundus Image Datasets for Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers retinal fundus image datasets and setups commonly used in deep active learning for medical image analysis. Patch-based configurations, such as those built on the e-ophtha dataset with tens of thousands of patches split into training, validation, and test subsets, enable lesion or structure detection with fine-grained supervision and flexible sampling of informative regions. Vessel segmentation tasks on fundus images, exemplified by the Fed-Fundus dataset, provide benchmarks for delineating retinal vasculature, which is crucial for diagnosing ophthalmic and systemic diseases. The federated nature of some fundus datasets supports privacy-preserving and distributed deep active learning workflows, where acquisition and labeling decisions must respect data locality and confidentiality constraints.

name: Superpixel-Based Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that operate at the superpixel (region) level to guide annotation in medical image segmentation. Instead of querying individual pixels, methods aggregate model evidence within superpixels and prioritize regions with high uncertainty or disagreement across multiple views or models, as in ensemble or multi-view settings. Edge-focused criteria, such as entropy and divergence around boundaries in OCT images, are used to capture uncertain class transitions and refine segmentation along object borders. Other approaches introduce regional consistency, comparing each superpixel’s dominant class to the model’s prediction and combining this with entropy and diversity metrics to find the most informative foreground and background regions. By selecting superpixels with high uncertainty, disagreement, or low regional consistency, these methods reduce annotation cost while focusing labeling effort on the most informative parts of the image.

name: Performance-Prediction-Based Slice Selection in DAL
description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that use learned quality predictors to guide slice selection in 3D medical image segmentation. A dedicated quality assessment module is trained to predict task-specific performance metrics, typically the per-slice Intersection-over-Union (IoU), and these predicted scores act as surrogates for true evaluation. The predicted IoU values are then used as acquisition signals to prioritize slices for annotation, either by targeting low-scoring slices where the current segmentation is likely poor or by selecting key slices expected to strongly improve the model. In interactive segmentation setups, experts are prompted to correct slices with low predicted IoU using scribbles, bounding boxes, or clicks, tightly coupling performance estimation with human-in-the-loop refinement. This yields a DAL framework where query selection is driven by explicit predictions of segmentation quality under a limited annotation budget.

name: Active Learning with Foundation Models and PEFT
description: This topic focuses on how deep active learning must adapt to foundation models and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) regimes. Instead of training large models from scratch, modern workflows rely on supervised or self-supervised pre-trained models that are adapted using PEFT or prompt tuning, where only a small subset of parameters is updated. In this setting, active learning is reframed as co-designed with low-parameter adaptation mechanisms, aiming to jointly minimize the number of labeled samples and the number of tunable parameters. The literature highlights the need to reassess classical AL strategies and to develop acquisition methods specifically suited to PEFT and prompt tuning. A concrete example is prompt-based AL for liver tumor segmentation, where a pre-trained segmentation model is adapted to in-house data using a prompt updater and a mixed uncertainty–diversity selection strategy, achieving near fully supervised performance with about 5% of samples and 6% of parameters tuned.

name: Deep Active Learning for Text Classification
description: This topic focuses on deep active learning methods tailored to text classification, where both the predictive model and the acquisition strategy are built on deep neural architectures. One line of work applies CNN-based sentence and document classifiers and selects unlabeled instances expected to induce the largest updates in word embeddings, explicitly targeting samples that most reshape task-specific representations. Another approach uses an RNN as a learned acquisition function that directly predicts which text instances are most informative to query. These strategies reduce the number of labeled examples and training time compared to fully supervised deep learning, while outperforming traditional, hand-crafted active learning baselines on sentence- and document-level tasks.

name: Online Active Learning with Expert Advice
description: This topic covers online active learning algorithms built on expert-advice forecasters for data streams. A learner aggregates predictions from a pool of experts (e.g., EWAF and GF), updates expert weights based on incurred loss, and analyzes performance via cumulative regret relative to the best expert. The forecasters are extended to an active setting by introducing a query variable that decides whether to request the current label, defining each expert’s cumulative loss only over queried instances to respect a label budget. Active variants (AEWAF and AGF) maintain predictions close to their fully supervised counterparts by using confidence-based querying rules that bound the difference between the active and fully supervised predictions. These confidence conditions are implemented via thresholds on pairwise expert disagreement or deviation from the aggregated prediction, with robust variants designed to handle noisy or unreliable experts.

name: Regret-Based Evaluation in Stream Active Learning
description: This topic covers the use of regret and related error measures as evaluation metrics for active learning and bandit-style algorithms on data streams. Instead of focusing solely on final classification accuracy, per-round and cumulative regret quantify how far the learner’s loss is from that of the best expert or strategy at each iteration. Evaluating regret (or prediction error) as a function of the number of trials or labeling budget emphasizes learning speed and efficiency over time, which is crucial in streaming and bandit formulations of active learning. Such metrics align naturally with online decision-making settings, highlighting how rapidly an active learner approaches optimal performance under budgeted interaction.

name: Deep Active Learning for Pulmonary Embolism Detection in CT
description: This topic covers the use of deep active learning to detect pulmonary embolism (PE) candidates in chest CT scans. The task is formulated as a classification problem on PE candidate regions extracted from volumetric CT data, using an in-house dataset of 6,255 candidate samples split into 3,840 and 2,415 instances. Deep active learning is employed to selectively query labels for the most informative or uncertain candidate regions, thereby reducing the annotation burden associated with large 3D CT volumes. This approach aims to improve automated identification of lesion- or thrombus-like structures in support of clinical PE diagnosis workflows.

name: Active Learning Experimental Setup for Remote Sensing Imagery
description: This topic covers how hyperspectral and very high resolution (VHR) remote sensing datasets are configured for pool-based active learning experiments under low-label regimes. The labeled dataset is split into an initial, very small seed set (typically 5 labeled pixels per class) and a large unlabeled candidate pool U, with an additional held-out test set used to assess generalization. Preprocessing steps include removing noisy spectral channels and excluding classes with too few labeled pixels, resulting in a multi-class classification task with carefully controlled labeled and unlabeled pools. The setup explicitly allocates tens of thousands of pixels between X and U to simulate realistic annotation budgets and data scarcity, while also dealing with strong class overlaps and high intra-class variability. Model-specific constraints, such as the need for Linear Discriminant Analysis to have more training samples than feature dimensions, can require increasing the initial labeled set size, illustrating how classifier properties interact with active learning design.

name: Multiclass Uncertainty Criteria for Active Learning
description: This topic covers the Multiclass Level Uncertainty (MCLU) criterion, which generalizes margin-based uncertainty sampling from binary to multiclass classification settings. MCLU leverages all per-class decision values of a classifier (e.g., SVM) to define uncertainty as the difference between the highest decision value and the highest value among the remaining classes, selecting points with the smallest gap for labeling. Compared to standard margin sampling, MCLU better captures ambiguous regions where more than two classes overlap by producing maximal uncertainty in highly mixed multiclass areas rather than only along pairwise decision boundaries. As an acquisition function, it refines uncertainty-based selection for pool-based active learning in complex multiclass scenarios and can be adapted to deep models that output per-class scores or logits.

name: Stable–Dynamic Ensembles for Stream Active Learning
description: This topic covers stable–dynamic ensemble designs used in active learning for data streams with concept drift. A pairwise strategy maintains a stable classifier trained on all labeled data seen so far and a dynamic classifier trained only on the most recent labeled batch, combining their predictions via a weighted output and replacing the stable model when the dynamic one consistently performs better; this favors rapid adaptation to abrupt drift but risks forgetting older patterns and struggles with gradual drifts. To better cope with mixed drift types, the reactive component is extended from a single dynamic model to an ensemble of dynamic classifiers, each trained on recent windows at different temporal scales, while the stable classifier continues to learn from all labeled instances. A more general stable–dynamic ensemble fixes the stable classifier’s weight (e.g., ω_s = 0.5) and uses multiple dynamic classifiers specialized on recent behavior, achieving a balance between long-term trend modeling and short-term responsiveness. These designs serve as base learners within stream-based active learning systems, allowing queried labels from evolving streams to update both persistent and reactive components in a drift-aware manner.

local_topics.title: Ensemble reactive models for mixed drifts

name: Deep Active Learning for Blood Cell Imaging
description: This topic covers deep active learning applications in microscopy-based blood cell analysis, including both detection and fine-grained classification tasks. Red blood cell detection in small, in-house microscopy datasets illustrates scenarios with very limited labeled samples, where DAL is used to prioritize informative regions or instances for annotation to improve object localization performance. Peripheral blood cell type classification with datasets like BloodMNIST provides a standardized benchmark for evaluating DAL strategies on fine-grained, multi-class cellular recognition under constrained labeling budgets. Across these tasks, DAL methods are assessed on their ability to achieve high diagnostic accuracy while minimizing the number of labeled microscopy images required, reflecting real-world constraints in hematological imaging.

local_topics.title: Red blood cell detection in microscopy

name: Multiview Entropy and Adaptive View Weighting in Active Learning
description: This topic covers multiview entropy as an uncertainty-based acquisition function in active learning, where predictions from classifiers trained on different views are fused into a multiview class probability distribution. The Shannon entropy of this fused distribution, HMV(xi), quantifies disagreement across views, and high-entropy samples are prioritized for querying. A key component is a view–class weighting matrix that encodes how discriminative each view is for each class, used to compute the fused probabilities. This matrix is iteratively updated using the true labels of newly queried samples and then normalized, so that more reliable view–class combinations gain higher influence over time. The result is a dynamic acquisition strategy that jointly exploits multiview uncertainty and adaptive reliability estimation to guide sample selection.

local_topics.title: View-class weighting matrix for prediction fusion

name: Determinantal Point Processes for Diverse Query Selection
description: This topic covers the use of determinantal point processes (DPPs) in deep active learning to explicitly promote diversity in queried batches. DPPs define a probability distribution over subsets via a pairwise similarity (kernel) matrix, favoring sets whose elements are mutually dissimilar by maximizing the determinant of this matrix. In DAL, DPPs can be applied directly to uncertainty scores or feature/gradient embeddings (as in Active-DPP and as a post-processing step in BADGE) to remove redundancy in the selected samples. This yields globally diverse, non-overlapping query batches that better cover the data space and decision boundaries than purely uncertainty-driven selection. However, the computational cost of constructing and sampling from DPPs is substantial, and practical studies report that cheaper clustering-based approaches such as k-Means++ can achieve similar effectiveness in some applications, including medical image analysis, while being more scalable.

name: Deep Active Learning for Colorectal Histopathology
description: This topic covers the use of colorectal (and combined lung/colon) histopathology image datasets as benchmarks for deep active learning under limited annotation budgets. The NCT-CRC-HE-100K dataset, with 100,000 image patches across nine tissue classes, is used for multi-class colorectal cancer diagnosis where only a very small fraction (0–5%) of images is labeled, matching DAL settings that prioritize query efficiency. Related work also includes the LC25000 lung–colon dataset, where 1–2% labeled data is used for cancer classification, highlighting severe label scarcity. These setups are employed to evaluate AL strategies for improving diagnostic performance while minimizing labeling cost in medical image analysis.

local_topics.title: Histopathology colorectal and pulmonary cancer classification

name: Deep Active Learning for Cardiac MRI Segmentation Benchmarks
description: This topic covers how deep active learning is applied to cardiac MRI segmentation using standard benchmark datasets such as HVSMR 2016 and ACDC. In these settings, individual 2D slices or subsets of slices from 3D volumes serve as the query units under limited annotation budgets, with strategies like labeling every 5, 10, 20, 40, or 80 slices to reduce manual effort. The protocols emphasize whole-heart or multi-structure segmentation (e.g., LV, MYO, RV) while carefully handling anisotropic resolution, often training models on 2D slices but evaluating performance on reconstructed 3D volumes. These dataset-specific design choices define realistic DAL scenarios in medical image analysis, where spatial redundancy and volumetric consistency must be balanced against the cost of expert annotations.

name: Chunk-Based Ensembles for Stream Active Learning
description: This topic covers window- or chunk-based ensemble frameworks for active learning on data streams. The incoming stream is partitioned into successive chunks, and separate base models are trained on each chunk, forming an ensemble that reflects different temporal segments of the data. At any time step, the ensemble—composed of the current and several recent chunk models—predicts labels for the unlabeled instances in the current chunk and guides which instances should be queried for labeling. Weighting and weight-update rules adapt the influence of past models to concept drift, enabling reuse of historical knowledge even when raw past data are unavailable. This structure provides a DAL-relevant mechanism to make informed, budget-aware annotation decisions under evolving data distributions in streaming settings.

name: Angle-Based Diversity for Batch Active Learning
description: This topic covers MAO (Most Ambiguous and Orthogonal / maximum angle-based outlier) and related angle-based diversity criteria for batch-mode active learning in remote sensing classification. Starting from a margin-based uncertainty set, MAO iteratively selects samples that are both highly ambiguous and as orthogonal as possible to already chosen points in feature or kernel space, thus explicitly enforcing diversity within each batch. Orthogonality or dissimilarity is quantified via angular distance or kernel similarity between feature vectors, preferring candidates that are least similar to the current batch. The framework is modular and allows user-defined diversity measures such as MAO, cSV, and ABD, enabling tailoring of the diversity notion to specific data characteristics while remaining grounded in an active learning selection loop.

name: Density-based Representativeness in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on density-based active learning strategies that aim to select representative samples by modeling the data distribution, particularly in deep representations of medical images. It highlights that traditional density estimators such as kernel density estimation and Gaussian Mixture Models become unreliable and inefficient in high-dimensional feature spaces common in deep models. These limitations reduce the effectiveness of representativeness-based acquisition functions in modern deep active learning pipelines. To address this, the topic proposes the use of advanced generative density estimators, especially normalizing flows, which are better suited to high-dimensional distributions. Integrating such high-capacity density models into density-based active learning could yield more accurate representativeness measures and improve sample selection for complex medical image datasets.

name: TypiClust: Density-Based Typicality for Cold-Start Deep Active Learning
description: TypiClust is a deep active learning strategy that prioritizes querying "typical" samples based on data density in a learned feature space, particularly targeting the cold-start phase with very limited annotation budgets. It uses a self-supervised encoder to project unlabeled samples into a high-dimensional representation space, then defines a density- or typicity-score via k-nearest neighbor distances. To ensure coverage and reduce redundancy, TypiClust performs clustering (e.g., k-Means) and selects high-density, prototypical points from each cluster, yielding a diverse yet representative initial labeled set. This approach contrasts with purely uncertainty-based selection by emphasizing representativeness and coverage of the data manifold rather than model predictive uncertainty. As a result, TypiClust aims to improve label efficiency early in the active learning process, where uncertainty estimates are often unreliable.

name: Deep Active Learning for Diabetic Retinopathy
description: This topic covers deep active learning applied to diabetic retinopathy detection from retinal fundus images, focusing on efficient annotation of large medical image datasets. Studies on the EyePacs dataset explore image-level classification with different scales, ranging from a very large corpus of nearly 90k images with an initial labeled pool of 1,000 and query batches of 5,000, to a smaller 4,460-image setup using a 10% initial label ratio and observing about an 11% performance gain through selective sampling. Comparisons with other exudate-related tasks, such as the smaller GlaS colon histopathology dataset with patch-level labels and tiny initial pools, highlight how dataset size, label granularity, and modality drive active learning design choices (e.g., initial pool size and batch size). Work on the APTOS-2019 diabetic retinopathy dataset similarly emphasizes selecting the most informative retinal images for labeling to improve diagnostic accuracy while keeping annotation costs constrained.

name: Label-Efficiency Curves in Remote Sensing Active Learning
description: This topic covers experimental protocols that evaluate active learning methods for remote sensing image classification via learning curves over the labeling budget. Labeled pixels are incrementally added to the training set, and overall classification accuracy is plotted as a function of the number of labeled pixels, capturing how efficiently different heuristics convert additional annotations into performance gains. The number of labeled pixels directly represents annotation effort, enabling analysis of marginal returns and saturation effects as the budget increases. A large, independently sampled pixel-based test set is reserved to measure generalization on unseen data, decoupled from the active selection process. Such budgeted evaluation is central to assessing the effectiveness of active learning strategies in pixel-wise remote sensing scenarios.

name: Graph-Structured Representations for Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that explicitly model sample relationships using graph-based feature representations. Medical images are embedded as nodes in a graph, where edges encode pairwise L2 distances in learned feature space to capture manifold or structural similarity. Graph neural networks (e.g., GCNs) are used to augment feature representations before selection, enabling more expressive, structure-aware embeddings. Query strategies then combine representativeness, measured over these graph-augmented features, with diversity, often enforced via farthest-first traversal in the graph space. By exploiting the underlying data structure, these methods aim to select more informative and diverse subsets under limited labeling budgets in medical image analysis.

name: Deep Active Learning for Machine Translation
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods for building neural machine translation systems under limited annotation budgets. Active learning is used to select source sentences or sentence pairs whose human translations are expected to most improve translation quality, particularly in low-resource language pairs where parallel data is scarce. Acquisition strategies include semantic similarity-based selection to ensure representativeness, and decoder probability-based or related uncertainty criteria to identify informative, difficult-to-translate sentences. These methods are evaluated on benchmarks such as OPUS, UNPC, IWSLT, and WMT across various language pairs, with improvements typically measured by BLEU under constrained human translation budgets. Overall, the focus is on optimizing which sentences to translate so as to achieve better MT performance than non-active, random, or heuristic selection given the same labeling cost.

name: Domain-Specific Deep Active Learning for Medical Imaging
description: This topic concerns the need to design and adapt deep active learning methods specifically for medical image analysis, rather than relying on generic AL strategies. Medical images exhibit complex modalities, clinically important but often small or subtle structures, and typically imbalanced or scarce labeled datasets, all of which affect uncertainty estimation and sample selection. Consequently, AL algorithms must be tailored to these characteristics to be clinically effective. At the same time, many proposed AL methods perform well only within narrowly defined domains (e.g., particular organs, modalities, or tasks) and often fail to generalize to other clinical settings, raising concerns about robustness and transferability across diverse medical imaging problems.

name: Distance-Based Representativeness in Medical Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on designing and using distance, diversity, and density metrics to capture representativeness in deep active learning for medical images. In pool-based selection, representative samples should be well spread across the underlying data distribution to avoid redundancy and preserve its structure, which requires robust sample-wise and distribution-wise distance measures. Discrepancy-based active learning, in particular, depends critically on how distances between probability distributions are defined, motivating improved metrics tailored to the specific characteristics of medical images rather than reusing those from natural-image domains. Because discrepancy- and representativeness-based methods are still underused in medical image analysis, developing such specialized distribution-distance metrics could substantially enhance the effectiveness of deep active learning in this application area.

name: Deep Active Learning for Sentiment and Fake News Detection
description: This topic covers the use of deep active learning to build sentiment and news veracity classifiers under limited annotation budgets. DAL is applied to labeled datasets such as KDnugget’s Fake News, various Harvard Dataverse collections, the Liar dataset, and the GitHub fake_real_news_dataset, where instances are annotated for truthfulness, stance, or sentiment. Active learning strategies prioritize querying ambiguous or controversial news items and statements, focusing human fact-checking effort where model uncertainty is highest. By iteratively selecting the most informative articles for labeling, DAL improves the robustness and data efficiency of misinformation and sentiment detection systems in settings where manual verification is expensive.

name: Expected Improvement and Model Change Querying
description: This topic covers active learning strategies that score candidates by their expected impact on future model performance, rather than by uncertainty alone. Expected loss/error reduction methods estimate how much the test error or predictive variance would decrease if an instance were labeled and used for training, often requiring a model of label or parameter uncertainty to evaluate hypothetical updates. Closely related are expected model change strategies, which prioritize points whose (unknown) labels are predicted to induce the largest change in model parameters or predictions, for example via estimated gradient updates. In deep active learning and streaming settings, these ideas are instantiated with approximations that make repeated retraining or gradient estimation tractable, while still directly targeting performance improvement. Together, these approaches form a principled family of acquisition functions that explicitly link each query to anticipated gains in generalization.

name: Training Regime Effects in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic examines how training hyperparameters, particularly the number of epochs per iteration and the query batch size, influence the performance of deep active learning pipelines. Ablation studies on CIFAR10 show that increasing the number of training epochs in each AL cycle generally improves area under the budget curve (AUBC) for both simple (Random) and informative (Entropy, Badge, WAAL) acquisition strategies, with uncertainty-based methods like Entropy benefiting most. However, these gains display clear diminishing returns, and excessive training can harm generalization despite higher computational cost. Varying query batch size (from 500 to 10,000) further reveals how the interaction between batch size and training duration affects label-efficiency and overall DAL effectiveness, underlining the need for carefully tuned training regimes in DAL experiments.

name: Human-in-the-Loop Interaction in Active Learning
description: This topic views active learning explicitly as a human-in-the-loop framework where models iteratively solicit targeted supervision from human annotators. It emphasizes how query strategies and acquisition decisions must be coupled with effective human–computer interaction mechanisms, including interfaces, feedback modalities, and interaction protocols that support annotators. In streaming or online active learning for data streams, the interaction design becomes time-critical, as humans must respond to real-time queries for the most informative instances. The discussion also highlights that different labeling scenarios and annotator configurations (e.g., multiple experts, varying expertise, or task constraints) can shape how queries are presented and how labels are acquired over time, directly influencing the efficiency and effectiveness of deep active learning under budget constraints.

name: Concept Drift Detection in Stream-based Active Learning
description: This topic examines how concept drift detectors are integrated into stream-based active learning under label scarcity. It contrasts error-based drift detectors, such as DDM and ADWIN, which traditionally require continuous labeled feedback, with distribution-based and multiple-hypothesis testing approaches that can operate in an unsupervised manner—highlighting their suitability when query budgets are tight. The cluster focuses on reusing the sparse labels acquired by an online active learner to drive error-based drift detection, enabling performance monitoring without assuming full supervision. Within this framework, ADWIN-triggered adaptation is applied to ensembles, where the worst-performing classifier is replaced upon drift detection, allowing the active learner to continually track evolving concepts in non-stationary data streams. Overall, the topic emphasizes the fusion of query selection and incremental model adaptation to handle drift efficiently with limited annotation budgets.

local_topics.title: Error-based drift detection with sparse labels

name: Drift-Aware Budget Control in Stream-Based Active Learning
description: This topic addresses how stream-based active learning systems dynamically allocate labeling budget in the presence of concept drift. Drift detectors such as ADWIN trigger temporary increases in querying activity by either lowering uncertainty thresholds or raising the labeling rate, so that more informative samples are labeled when the underlying data distribution changes. Budget control is often modeled as a piecewise constant function over time, with phases of high, low, and nominal labeling rates tied to drift warnings, confirmed drifts, and post-drift stabilization. These strategies are designed so that the long-term average budget respects a predefined annotation rate, while still concentrating label requests during critical adaptation periods. The explicit coupling between drift signals and budget scheduling is a core design element for effective online deep active learning on non-stationary data streams.

name: WI-DL Hybrid Deep Active Learning
description: This topic centers on WI-DL (Weighted Incremental Dictionary Learning) as a deep active learning framework that combines unsupervised feature learning with supervised fine-tuning under limited annotation budgets. Within a Deep Belief Network setting, WI-DL first performs unsupervised pretraining on both labeled and unlabeled data to learn representations, then applies supervised fine-tuning only on labeled samples to improve task performance efficiently in AL cycles. Its query strategy is stage-wise and hybrid: during unsupervised learning it prioritizes data representativeness, while during supervised refinement it emphasizes uncertainty, integrating both criteria via weighted incremental dictionary learning. Applied to hyperspectral image classification, WI-DL selects samples that are simultaneously representative of the high-dimensional data distribution and highly uncertain for the current model, illustrating hybrid acquisition in a complex imaging domain. Overall, it exemplifies how deep active learning can jointly exploit unlabeled data, hybrid selection criteria, and staged training to address label scarcity.

name: Deep Active Learning for Text Classification and Sentiment Analysis
description: This topic concerns the use of deep active learning for generic text classification, including sentiment polarity, subjectivity detection, and topical categorization. Deep models iteratively query the most informative sentences or documents for labeling, guided by uncertainty or diversity-based criteria, to efficiently improve classifier performance. A variety of benchmark corpora, such as Subj, MR, JHU sentiment datasets, and numerous review and news datasets (e.g., CR, AGN, AMZP, AMZF, YRF), are used to evaluate and compare query strategies in natural language processing. These benchmarks allow systematic assessment of how different deep active learning strategies reduce manual annotation while maintaining or improving accuracy on text understanding tasks.

name: Posterior-Probability Uncertainty Heuristics in Active Learning
description: This topic concerns active learning strategies that use estimated posterior class probabilities p(y|x) to rank unlabeled samples. By measuring classifier confidence and how candidate labels would change global or per-class posterior distributions, these methods target points that are highly uncertain or expected to induce large model updates. Heuristics such as KL-max and Breaking Ties instantiate this idea by operationalizing different ways of exploiting the posterior over classes. Posterior-based strategies are computationally efficient but can struggle to form diverse, informative batches, and they require additional approximation steps when the base model does not natively provide calibrated posteriors. They are particularly recommended when the initial labeled set is very small, since direct use of prediction uncertainty can still guide effective early querying under severe label scarcity.

name: KL-Divergence-Based Acquisition in Active Learning
description: This topic covers active learning criteria that use Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence to quantify the expected change in a model’s predictive distribution when querying a label. KL-max heuristics select instances whose inclusion in the labeled set maximizes the KL divergence between posterior class distributions before and after labeling, often aggregating this effect over the remaining unlabeled pool. Variants extend this idea to ensembles of probabilistic models, where disagreement in posterior class probabilities across models is captured via KL-related measures. In streaming settings with Bayesian or probabilistic models, KL-divergence is also used to regularize updates of the weight posterior, balancing adaptation to newly labeled data against staying close to the previous posterior. These KL-based criteria provide model- and task-agnostic acquisition functions that can be instantiated with deep probabilistic models in pool- and stream-based Deep Active Learning.

name: Repeated Runs and Statistical Reporting in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers experimental protocols in deep active learning that account for stochasticity by repeating each active learning heuristic multiple times with different random initializations or initial labeled pools. Performance is reported using aggregated statistics, typically the mean and standard deviation of accuracy or related metrics across runs. Such reporting practices assess robustness to initialization, quantify variability due to randomness in sampling and training, and provide statistically reliable performance curves over annotation budgets. These procedures enable more rigorous and fair comparison of deep active learning strategies across datasets and budget settings.

name: Contextual Bandit Formulations for Stream-based Active Learning
description: This topic frames stream-based active learning as a contextual bandit problem, where the decision to request a label is modeled as an action whose reward reflects its utility. Linear contextual bandits are tightly connected to active linear regression, since the learner sequentially selects feature vectors (arms) to estimate an unknown parameter vector under noise, mirroring informative sample selection for regression. In more applied settings, query selection is cast as maximizing cumulative reward, with positive rewards for label requests that prevent misclassifications and negative rewards for unnecessary queries. Ensembles of experts decide whether to query based on prediction certainty thresholds, and are adaptively weighted according to their past reward and agreement, yielding a learned querying policy. These formulations provide a principled, policy-learning view of acquisition strategies that can be combined with deep models in deep active learning for data streams.

name: SVM-based margin and clustering strategies in active learning
description: This topic covers SVM-based active learning methods that combine margin-based informativeness with clustering and adaptive selection criteria. Multi-class SVMs are used together with nonlinear clustering of unlabeled candidates to query cluster representatives, reducing redundancy while maintaining diversity. The hMCS-i approach further extends margin-based cluster sampling by hierarchically partitioning both candidate points and bounded support vectors, restricting selection to clusters without bounded SVs to avoid repeatedly sampling near the same decision boundary regions. These designs explicitly control overlap between iterations and target highly informative margin regions. In addition, criterion-switching strategies dynamically choose among multiple SVM-based selection criteria to better handle class imbalance in pool-based and streaming scenarios, guided by unsupervised evaluation scores influenced by recently queried labels.

name: Deep Active Learning for Chest X-ray Classification
description: This topic covers the use of deep active learning for disease detection and diagnosis in chest X-ray imaging. Large public datasets such as RSNA Pneumonia and CheXpert provide extensive pools of labeled and unlabeled radiographs for pneumonia and pleural effusion detection, respectively, enabling pool-based active selection of the most informative cases for expert annotation. Smaller benchmark datasets like PneumoniaMNIST support controlled evaluation of DAL strategies for binary pneumonia vs normal classification, where the goal is to reach high diagnostic performance with substantially fewer labeled images. Across these tasks, deep active learning exploits uncertainty and informativeness in the model’s predictions to prioritize labeling of challenging or ambiguous X-rays, thus improving efficiency in clinically relevant annotation budgets.

name: Deep Active Learning for Whole-Slide Pathology with MIL
description: This topic focuses on applying deep active learning to pathological whole-slide images (WSIs) modeled under a multiple-instance learning (MIL) framework. Due to the enormous size of WSIs, they are decomposed into many patches, and annotation costs for patch- or cell-level labels are prohibitive, motivating active selection of the most informative slides or patches. In the weakly supervised MIL setting, each slide is treated as a bag of instances (patches) with only slide-level labels, and models must learn to localize task-relevant regions (e.g., cancerous tissue) from these coarse labels. Deep active learning strategies operate on this bag–instance structure to query the most informative WSIs or patches, aiming to filter out large numbers of irrelevant patches and improve performance under limited labeling budgets. The interplay between weak supervision, extreme class imbalance at the instance level, and query selection defines the specific challenges of DAL for WSI classification.

name: Evaluation Protocols for Stream-based Active Learning
description: This topic covers how active learning methods for data streams are evaluated, with an emphasis on choosing protocols that match stream properties such as stationarity and concept drift. In stationary settings, a fixed holdout test set is commonly used to repeatedly assess performance as more labeled examples are acquired, enabling clear tracking of improvements due to the active sampling strategy. For non-stationary or drifting streams, prequential (online) evaluation is preferred, often combined with forgetting mechanisms such as sliding windows or fading factors so that performance estimates reflect current rather than historical behavior. The choice between holdout and prequential evaluation is thus closely tied to whether the active learning algorithm is designed to handle drift. In parallel, some works focus purely on theoretical analysis—studying sample or label complexity and regret bounds—without relying on empirical protocols, contributing formal guarantees that complement empirical evaluation of stream-based active learning.

name: Query-While-Learning for Streaming Decision Trees
description: This topic covers query-while-learning strategies for decision tree classifiers in data stream settings, where labeling decisions are made online for each incoming instance. The methods use entropy-based intervals derived from evidential likelihood to quantify predictive uncertainty and decide whether a new instance should be queried. A complementary approach orders attributes by information gain ratio and defines dominant attributes that guide the label request: if no dominant attribute is present for an instance, a label is queried to reduce uncertainty. These strategies adapt active learning specifically to tree-based models under streaming constraints, optimizing when to request labels while the model is being incrementally updated.

name: Standardized and Reproducible Deep Active Learning Evaluation
description: This topic addresses the need for robust, reproducible, and standardized evaluation protocols in Deep Active Learning. It emphasizes the design of shared experimental platforms that fix key configurations (datasets, architectures, training schemes) and provide a strong, unified random sampling baseline to fairly compare query strategies. The works call for careful scrutiny of how different DeepAL methods behave under varying conditions, including multiple runs with different random seeds and consistent hyperparameter settings, to avoid conclusions driven by experimental artifacts. By promoting transparent reporting of full experimental details and common benchmarking infrastructures, this line of research aims to resolve current inconsistencies in reported DeepAL performance and enable more reliable method comparison.

name: Labeling Budgets and Performance in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers how deep active learning experiments structure and analyze incremental labeling budgets. Studies increase the labeled set in fixed-size batches (e.g., N+5, N+20 samples) or in small percentage steps (e.g., 10–30% or 30–50% of data with 2.5% increments) to simulate progressive annotation. Performance is reported across multiple active learning rounds and budget levels using metrics such as ACC, AUC, and DSC, often with mean ± standard deviation across runs. Results are shown for multiple query strategies (e.g., Random, Confidence, Entropy, Margin, BADGE), enabling comparison of how efficiently each method converts additional annotation effort into performance gains. Budget–performance curves are used to study saturation effects and to quantify the trade-off between labeling cost and model quality in deep active learning.

name: Deep Active Learning for Brain MRI Segmentation
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods for brain MRI segmentation, focusing on both tumor and anatomical structures. The studies operate under extremely low initial annotation budgets (e.g., 0.5–1% of BraTS 2019 volumes, 6% of MALC cases, or 200 labeled slices from BraTS 2018) and iteratively expand the labeled set through active querying. Different sampling units are explored, including full 3D volumes and 2D slices, to balance annotation cost against model performance. The core Deep Active Learning aspects involve designing query strategies to select the most informative MRI slices or volumes under strict labeling budgets and evaluating how these strategies accelerate segmentation accuracy compared to random sampling.

name: Deep Active Learning for EM-Based Neural Tissue Segmentation
description: This topic covers electron microscopy (EM) datasets of mouse neural tissue that serve as benchmarks for deep active learning in dense segmentation tasks. The datasets include volumetric EM data for neuron boundary delineation, targeted synapse detection, and mitochondria (organelle-level) segmentation. They are structured with distinct training and testing splits and sometimes varied annotation strategies, such as labeling every 4, 16, or 64 slices, to emulate different labeling budgets. These resources enable systematic evaluation of deep active learning strategies for high-resolution, small-structure segmentation in connectomics and related neural circuit reconstruction applications.

name: Active Learning with Weak and Partial Box Annotations
description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that start from weak supervision for object detection and selectively acquire more expensive bounding-box annotations. Models are initially trained using only image-level labels, avoiding dense spatial annotation. Acquisition criteria then identify either images whose predicted boxes exhibit informative patterns (such as 'box-in-box' configurations) or specific objects within images that show high prediction disagreement. Only these selected images or object proposals receive precise box-level labels, thereby concentrating annotation effort where it most improves the detector. The focus is on integrating uncertainty- and disagreement-based selection with weak supervision to reduce overall bounding-box labeling cost.

name: Active Learning Robustness to Noise and Redundancy
description: This topic concerns how noisy and redundant data affect the behavior of active learning sampling strategies. Redundant samples can unnecessarily slow model training and bias estimated class statistics, ultimately degrading classification performance even when labels are cheap to obtain. In the presence of label or input noise, misclassification-based sampling can become unreliable, as it tends to select mislabeled or boundary-misplaced instances that misguide model updates. These effects highlight the need for active learning strategies that explicitly handle annotation noise and filter redundancy, to avoid overfitting and performance deterioration in supervised and streaming settings.

name: Deep Active Learning for Lung CT Analysis
description: This topic concerns the application of deep active learning to lung disease analysis from CT images, covering both classification and tumor segmentation tasks. In classification, a large MICCAI CT Lung Tianchi dataset is used with only 5% of the data initially labeled, demonstrating label-efficiency gains of about 7% by selectively querying informative CT scans. For segmentation, a smaller MICCAI lung CT dataset with 3D volumes is annotated using weak labels such as scribbles, bounding boxes, and extreme points to further reduce annotation cost. Together, these setups highlight how deep active learning can leverage small labeled budgets and weak supervision to improve performance in computationally intensive medical image analysis scenarios.

name: Deep Active Learning for COVID-19 Chest Imaging
description: This topic covers the use of deep active learning for COVID-19 diagnosis from thoracic medical images, including CT and chest X-ray data. Studies on lung CT volumes (e.g., CC-CCII and other large CT collections) frame COVID-19 detection as a classification task and use pool-based active learning to select informative 3D scans while keeping only a fraction of volumes labeled, often around 10% of the dataset. Similar DAL setups are applied to large-scale chest CT datasets with explicit train/validation/test splits, focusing on maximizing diagnostic performance under strict annotation budgets. Other work targets chest X-ray datasets such as COVID-QU-Ex, using active acquisition strategies to choose subsets of 2D images to label, thereby reducing radiologist workload while maintaining high COVID-19 detection accuracy.

name: Taxonomies and Comparison Dimensions for Active Learning Methods
description: This topic covers how surveys systematically categorize and compare active learning (including deep active learning) algorithms along multiple methodological dimensions. Active learners are organized by algorithmic family, specific heuristic or acquisition function, and literature references, as well as practical aspects such as batch vs. sequential selection, reliance on uncertainty estimates, use of classifier diversity, and the number of models trained. Beyond uncertainty-based criteria, methods are further classified by whether they exploit data representativeness, integrate semi-supervised or self-supervised learning within the active loop, adopt region-based querying, or employ generative models. Such structured taxonomies provide a unified framework for analyzing diverse deep active learning strategies and clarifying which auxiliary paradigms and selection criteria they incorporate.

name: Generalization and Distribution Shift in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic concerns how reliably deep active learning strategies generalize when there are changes in data distribution, task, dataset, or model architecture. It emphasizes robustness to distribution shift between training and testing, particularly in sensitive domains such as medical imaging, where data from new scanners, institutions, or populations may differ from the labeled pool. The discussion includes whether specific acquisition functions (e.g., gradient-embedding-based methods) are tightly coupled to particular network backbones or can transfer across architectures and domains. Evaluations typically consider performance on unseen domains, stability of active learning gains across diverse experimental setups, and the extent to which selected samples and learned representations remain informative under shift. These aspects are framed as key open challenges for designing practically reliable and broadly applicable deep active learning methods.

name: Stream-Based Active Learning for Fraud Detection
description: This topic focuses on stream-based active learning for financial fraud detection, where transactional data arrive continuously and must be classified in real time. Online active learning methods selectively query labels for the most informative or suspicious transactions, balancing expert labeling costs against the need for timely, accurate decisions. The models must update rapidly to adapt to evolving fraud strategies and changing customer behavior, embodying continuous concept drift in the data stream. The DAL-specific aspects include streaming acquisition of instances, cost-aware querying for human annotation, and continuous model refinement under non-stationary conditions typical of fraud detection environments.
