name: Transductive Experimental Design in Bandit-Based Active Learning
description: This topic covers transductive experimental design in multi-armed bandit formulations of active learning, where queries are chosen from a set X to optimize predictions or decisions over a separate, fixed target set Z. Rather than aiming for global generalization, the learner exploits unlabeled points in Z to guide which arms in X to pull so as to improve performance specifically on Z. In the transductive best-arm identification setting, methods seek to infer the best arm or preference structure over Z using strategically selected pulls from X. Recent work also extends this to online and streaming scenarios, explicitly balancing time complexity (how many unlabeled instances are scanned) against label complexity (how many labels are queried) to determine when to stop and confidently declare the best arm. This framework directly connects bandit algorithms, label-efficiency, and task-focused generalization in active learning for data streams.

name: Active Distillation in Stream-based Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on integrating knowledge distillation with deep active learning, particularly in streaming scenarios. A smaller student model is trained to mimic a larger pre-trained teacher while actively selecting data instances from a stream, rather than passively consuming all teacher-labeled samples. A central concern is confirmation bias: the student can overfit to the teacher’s erroneous predictions instead of correcting them. To mitigate this, one line of work targets samples where the teacher is likely to make mistakes, encouraging learning from teacher–student discrepancies. Another line uses confidence thresholds—estimated in a warm-up phase—to selectively query only high-confidence instances in online object detection, combining active learning with self-supervision to reduce reliance on human annotators while still controlling teacher-induced bias.

name: Budget-Aware Trade-offs in Deep Active Learning Strategies
description: This topic examines how the effectiveness of deep active learning strategies depends on the available annotation budget, particularly in difficult and imbalanced medical image classification tasks. Under low-budget conditions, representativeness- and diversity-based methods such as Core-Set and its variants outperform purely uncertainty-based sampling, emphasizing the importance of coverage and redundancy reduction when only a few labels can be acquired. As the labeling budget increases, uncertainty-based methods improve substantially and can become more suitable, while Core-Set remains competitive across budgets. These findings underscore that the optimal choice of acquisition strategy in deep active learning is budget-dependent, with diversity-focused approaches favored in data-scarce regimes and uncertainty-driven methods gaining advantage as more annotations become available.

name: Standardized Experimental Reporting for Deep Active Learning in Medical Imaging

The tables catalog datasets, imaging modalities, and regions of interest alongside clinical and technical tasks, linking each active learning method to its specific medical context. They formalize key DAL-specific experimental factors such as the sampling unit (e.g., image, slice), initial labeled pool size, and annotation budget per acquisition round. By also recording dataset sizes and train/validation/test splits, these schemas make it possible to compare how different budget constraints and pool configurations influence active learning performance across tasks like reconstruction and segmentation. Overall, the standardized descriptors support reproducibility and cross-study comparison of DAL pipelines in medical imaging.

name: Fully Supervised Upper Bound in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers the use of a fully supervised learning setup as an upper-bound baseline in deep active learning experiments. All training samples are labeled from the outset, and the resulting performance (e.g., a single accuracy or error value) serves as a reference against which budget-constrained active learning strategies are compared. In DAL studies, this baseline helps quantify the performance gap or potential gains of methods such as BADGE and Core-Set relative to an ideal, fully labeled regime. It provides essential context for interpreting how close active learning approaches can get to the fully supervised performance under limited annotation budgets.

name: Deep Active Learning for Gland and Lymph Node Segmentation
description: This topic covers medical image segmentation tasks on gland-related structures, especially lymph nodes and breast lesions, used as benchmarks for deep active learning methods. The tasks involve delineating small anatomical structures from surrounding tissue in ultrasound and related imaging modalities, reflecting realistic low-data, high-annotation-cost scenarios. An in-house ultrasound lymph node dataset with a very limited number of fully annotated images exemplifies experimental setups where DAL must maximize performance under strict labeling budgets. Breast ultrasound segmentation with superpixel-based processing illustrates region-level querying, where acquisition functions select informative superpixels rather than individual pixels or entire images to reduce annotation effort. Together, these setups highlight how DAL is applied to structure-aware, fine-grained medical segmentation problems under constrained supervision.

name: Deep Active Learning for Medical Image Segmentation
description: This topic focuses on applying deep active learning to medical image segmentation, a core task in clinical workflows where precise delineation of anatomical structures and lesions supports diagnosis and treatment planning. In this context, deep active learning is used to reduce the heavy annotation cost of pixel- or voxel-wise labels by selectively querying the most informative regions or cases for expert labeling. Specific segmentation tasks, such as fungal lesion segmentation and left atrial segmentation in cardiac imaging, serve as representative benchmarks to evaluate query strategies and annotation efficiency. These applications demonstrate how active learning-driven segmentation can integrate into real-world clinical pipelines by improving model performance under limited labeling budgets. Overall, the topic connects the central clinical role of imaging with DAL techniques tailored to dense, structure-level prediction problems.

name: Margin-Based Uncertainty in Streaming Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on margin-based uncertainty measures as acquisition functions in deep and traditional active learning for data streams. One approach defines uncertainty as the distance of an instance to the classifier’s decision boundary or hyperplane (e.g., absolute perceptron margin), which makes points near the boundary more likely to be queried in streaming settings. Another widely used measure is the best-versus-second-best margin, which computes the difference between the two highest posterior class probabilities and is particularly effective in multi-class problems. These uncertainty scores are sometimes combined with similarity measures (e.g., Manhattan distance) to encourage diversity among selected instances, though such combinations may require computing uncertainty and similarity for all unlabeled samples, limiting their applicability in strict single-pass streaming scenarios. Overall, the topic highlights how different operationalizations of “distance to the decision boundary” govern label selection behavior under budget constraints in stream-based active learning.

name: Deep Active Learning for Palmprint Recognition
description: This topic covers a deep active learning framework tailored to palmprint recognition, where the active selection problem is recast as a binary classification task distinguishing labeled from unlabeled samples. The method is inspired by domain adaptation: it seeks a labeled core-set whose distribution matches that of the full (unlabeled) dataset so that the two sets become hard to distinguish, effectively minimizing distribution shift. Instead of relying on explicit generative modeling in a high-dimensional space, the strategy iteratively selects samples that are clearly distinguishable from either the labeled or unlabeled pools, then adds them to the labeled set. This process corrects distributional mismatches created by earlier core-set methods that ignored data density and jointly adapts deep feature representations and query selection to improve palmprint recognition performance.

name: Probabilistic Margin-Based Querying for Data Streams
description: This topic covers stream-based active learning strategies that model the label-query decision as a Bernoulli random variable whose parameter encodes instance informativeness. Classical b-sampling and related rules define the query probability as a function of the current margin, so that points near the decision boundary receive higher labeling probability, turning uncertainty sampling into a smooth, probabilistic acquisition function. Variants include rational forms such as P_t = b / (b + |p_t|) and logistic/exponential forms like P_t = e^{−γ|p_t|}, which control how sharply the querying rate decays as model confidence increases, thereby tuning the trade-off between exploration and label budget. Further extensions introduce randomized querying mechanisms (including exponential mechanisms) that adjust Bernoulli parameters based on distance to a sampling region and privacy parameters, injecting controlled randomness while still favoring near-boundary instances in a data stream. These probabilistic query schemes are directly applicable in deep active learning pipelines by plugging them into streaming or online deep models to manage annotation effort over time.

name: Verification Latency in Streaming Active Learning
description: This topic covers verification latency (label delay) in streaming and online active learning, where there is a temporal gap between querying an instance and receiving its label from the oracle. Latency regimes range from null (immediate labels), through intermediate (finite delay), to extreme (labels never arrive, approaching unsupervised learning), each imposing different constraints on how query strategies and model updates can be designed. During the delay, the learner continues to process and query new instances, risking redundant requests in regions where multiple unlabeled, high-utility samples accumulate and forcing policy updates to rely on outdated information under concept drift. Methods therefore need mechanisms such as spatial awareness of pending queries, buffer management, and explicit handling of delayed supervision to distribute queries effectively across the input space and time. The discussion also emphasizes realistic sources of delayed labels (e.g., medical outcomes, physical inspections) and the compounding effects of imperfect oracles, making verification latency a central practical concern for stream-based active learning systems.

description: This cluster highlights the substantial time and expert labor required for fine-grained annotation of medical images, especially for tasks such as detailed segmentation and pathology slide analysis. Because annotations must be precise and clinically reliable, they demand intensive involvement of highly trained medical professionals, whose time is scarce. This high annotation cost is a primary motivation for deep active learning in medical imaging, where methods are designed to minimize the number of labeled samples needed while maintaining performance. In the DAL context, these constraints directly shape query strategies, budget allocation, and evaluation criteria, as algorithms aim to alleviate the annotation bottleneck in real-world clinical workflows.

name: Stopping Criteria in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers methods for deciding when to stop querying additional labels in (deep) active learning so as to balance annotation cost against achievable performance. Stopping criteria leverage a variety of metrics, including development-set performance, cross-validation estimates adapted to non-uniform AL sampling, uncertainty or confidence scores, model disagreement, estimated error, prediction stability, and simple budget limits. Beyond single-threshold rules, more robust approaches cascade multiple conditions or track trends over several AL iterations, e.g., flattening performance gains or stabilized prediction outputs. In Deep Active Learning, many systems still rely on predefined heuristics such as maximum iteration count, minimum labeled sample size, or target accuracy thresholds, which risk premature stopping or unnecessary over-labeling. The literature also connects AL stopping decisions to broader questions of performance prediction and early stopping in low-resource, incremental training scenarios.

name: Norm-Thresholding for Stream-Based Active Regression
description: This topic covers norm-thresholding criteria for online active learning in linear regression over data streams. The core idea is to select only those streaming instances whose norm or leverage score exceeds a threshold, thereby prioritizing samples that most reduce prediction variance. The threshold is calibrated to match a target labeling rate α, so that only a desired fraction of incoming points are queried, enabling explicit control of the annotation budget in a streaming setting. By connecting selection to A-optimal design, the method yields near design-optimal labeled sets using either scaled norms or leverage scores computed from the current labeled design matrix. These strategies exemplify theory-driven acquisition rules for stream-based active regression that can inform analogous designs in deep active learning contexts.

name: Clustering-Based Deep Active Learning with Self-Supervised Features
description: This topic covers clustering-based deep active learning methods that operate on self-supervised feature embeddings, primarily in medical image analysis. Off-the-shelf self-supervised models are used to extract rich representations from unlabeled medical images, on which K-Means or K-Means++ clustering is performed. Cluster centers in this feature space are selected as representative and informative samples for annotation, effectively approximating diversity-based selection without requiring label information. Silhouette-based model selection is employed to automatically determine the optimal number of clusters, improving cluster quality and the robustness of the acquisition process. These methods have been shown to reduce annotation effort while maintaining strong performance in tasks such as lung and lesion segmentation.

name: Active Learning Evaluation in Remote Sensing Scenarios
description: This topic covers the evaluation of active learning heuristics across multiple remote sensing classification scenarios, emphasizing robustness and generalization beyond a single dataset. Studies assess performance on diverse spatial and spectral conditions, including both multispectral and hyperspectral imagery. The experimental setups compare how different active learning strategies behave, highlighting their advantages and drawbacks when faced with varying spectral resolutions and high-dimensional feature spaces. These multi-scenario benchmarks are particularly relevant for designing and testing deep active learning methods for remote sensing, where scalability and adaptability to complex spectral data are critical.

name: Selective Sampling in Online Active Learning for Data Streams
description: This cluster focuses on stream-based online active learning methods that use probabilistic, margin-based selective sampling under an explicit labeling budget. Core algorithms compute a prediction margin and then draw a Bernoulli random variable with parameter b / (b + |margin|) to decide whether to query the label, making low-margin (uncertain) instances much more likely to be labeled while keeping the total labeling cost within a budget over a time horizon. Variants differ mainly in the underlying online learner, including perceptron and passive-aggressive update rules, where the latter adjusts the step size based on the incurred loss to more aggressively correct low-confidence or misclassified examples. Another variant aggregates predictions from multiple experts and applies the same Bernoulli-based querying mechanism to the combined margin, formalizing expert-advice–driven querying. These strategies are evaluated in application settings such as real-time spam filtering, comparing different margin-based querying rules (fixed threshold, Bernoulli b-sampling, logistic margin) and model-update regimes for streaming data.

name: Incremental vs Full Retraining in Deep Active Learning
description: Deep active learning often proceeds in multiple cycles or within continuous data streams, forcing a design choice between incremental training and complete retraining. Incremental training updates a model with newly labeled data while retaining prior parameters, greatly reducing computational cost but risking parameter drift and catastrophic forgetting if not carefully controlled. In streaming and online active learning, such incremental schemes—possibly augmented with regularization methods like elastic weight consolidation—are especially attractive because data and queries arrive continuously. By contrast, complete retraining from scratch on all accumulated labeled data can yield better adaptation under substantial distribution or concept drift, or when architectural changes are needed, but is far more expensive and can reduce overall efficiency of online active learning. Balancing these strategies is therefore a key practical question for scalable and adaptive deep active learning systems.

name: Model-Agnostic Online Active Learning for Data Streams
description: This topic focuses on model-agnostic active learning strategies designed for streaming scenarios, including both classification and regression tasks. The emphasis is on methods that do not rely on specific model internals, enabling reuse across diverse linear and nonlinear learners in online and single-pass settings. In data streams, such approaches must work under strict memory and computation constraints, often processing each instance at most once while deciding whether to query its label. The cluster also contrasts single-model and ensemble-based strategies: ensembles are highlighted for stationary and drifting classification streams where diverse uncertainty estimates and robustness to drift are beneficial, whereas single-model approaches are more common in regression, evolving streams, and object detection due to complexity and resource trade-offs.

name: Batch Size and Scalability in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic examines how the query batch size in deep active learning influences performance and scalability. Empirical studies show that for common uncertainty-based methods such as Entropy, performance metrics like AUBC are often weakly sensitive to batch size, allowing practitioners to use larger batches to reduce the number of AL cycles without substantial quality loss. At the same time, other work explores scaling AL to very large datasets with large query sizes (e.g., 10k–500k samples), leveraging distributed training, multiple model instances, and checkpoint reuse to search the pool efficiently. These results highlight that carefully selected subsets via AL can outperform training on the full dataset, and that batch size is a key practical lever for balancing annotation efficiency, computational cost, and model performance in DAL.

name: Performance of BADGE in Medical Image Segmentation
description: This cluster focuses on the empirical evaluation of the BADGE deep active learning strategy, particularly for medical image segmentation tasks such as cardiac MRI on the ACDC dataset. Comparisons against alternative acquisition strategies (e.g., Core-Set variants, Random, Confidence, Entropy, Margin) and fully supervised baselines highlight that BADGE often attains the best or second-best performance under constrained labeling budgets. Overall, the topic illustrates how BADGE is benchmarked as a strong DAL acquisition function in medical image analysis settings.

name: Distance Metrics in Core-Set Deep Active Learning
description: This cluster focuses on how the choice of distance or similarity metric within Core-Set-style deep active learning affects query selection and downstream performance, particularly in medical image analysis. Core-Set is instantiated with Euclidean (L2) distance and cosine similarity, yielding Core-Set-L2 and Core-Set-Cosine variants that keep the acquisition strategy fixed while changing only the embedding-space geometry. Their performance is compared against each other, against BADGE, and against fully supervised baselines over increasing labeling budgets, using metrics such as accuracy, AUC, Dice score, and Mean Average Surface Distance. The results consistently show that the distance metric strongly influences which unlabeled samples are selected as representative or diverse, and thus how close DAL methods can approach fully supervised performance under limited annotation budgets. The studies highlight that careful design of similarity measures is a key lever for improving core-set-based and related DAL acquisition functions.

name: Partial-Structure Queries and Partial Feedback in Active Learning
description: This topic covers active learning settings where only parts of a structured output or label space are annotated, reducing annotation burden while preserving informative supervision. In partial-structure active learning, complex outputs (e.g., token sequences, syntactic units, mention pairs) are decomposed into fine-grained units, and query strategies select which sub-structures to label, often requiring inference to obtain marginal probabilities over these components. Learning from such incomplete annotations demands models that can exploit structure: local discriminative models treat sub-structures independently, whereas global structured models use constraints and label interactions so that annotated parts decrease uncertainty in unannotated regions, enabling better query selection, efficient batch selection, and interactive correction. Semi-supervised techniques such as self-training or pseudo-labeling are used to fill in unannotated portions when full labels are ultimately needed. Relatedly, large-label classification can be reframed as structured prediction with partial feedback, where annotators answer yes/no questions about candidate labels or eliminate clearly incorrect classes, simplifying annotation while still guiding the active learner.

name: Submodular Information Measures for Targeted Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that employ submodular information measures, particularly submodular mutual information (SMI), as acquisition functions to guide sample selection. By defining SMI between a labeled reference set and unlabeled candidates via an underlying submodular function, these methods quantify set-level shared information, enabling simultaneous modeling of informativeness, diversity, and redundancy control. In object detection and classification, a reference set is often constructed from minority-class or target-class examples, and unlabeled samples are selected based on high SMI with this set to prioritize annotations that resemble underrepresented or clinically important classes. The submodular structure allows for efficient, near-optimal subset selection, generalizing representativeness-based querying to targeted, class-aware selection. Empirical results on medical imaging datasets such as X-rays, pathology, and dermoscopy demonstrate that SMI-based selection can substantially improve performance on minority classes under limited labeling budgets.

name: Annotation Burden in Medical Image Segmentation
description: Deep segmentation models for medical imaging require dense, pixel-wise labels, making the annotation process extremely time-consuming and labor-intensive for clinicians. This fine-grained labeling requirement is a central bottleneck for deploying high-quality segmentation systems in practice. In the context of deep active learning, this high annotation cost motivates strategies that selectively query only the most informative pixels, regions, or images for annotation, rather than labeling all data exhaustively. By exploiting active learning in medical image segmentation, researchers aim to reduce the overall pixel-level annotation burden while maintaining or improving segmentation performance.

name: One-shot Annotation in Deep Active Learning for Medical Imaging
description: One-shot annotation is a deep active learning setting where all samples to be labeled are selected in a single acquisition round, removing the need for repeated interactions with medical experts. It is motivated by practical constraints in medical image analysis, where physicians and radiologists are not continuously available and iterative annotation cycles can stall AL workflows. This setting focuses on maximizing the utility of a fixed, one-time labeling budget, requiring acquisition strategies that can identify a globally informative batch without feedback from later model updates. While it is related to cold-start active learning, one-shot annotation usually assumes a larger upfront annotation budget but strictly prohibits subsequent querying, which changes how sampling criteria and budget allocation are designed. As a result, one-shot strategies must carefully balance uncertainty, diversity, and coverage in a single selection to effectively bootstrap deep models for segmentation and other medical imaging tasks.

name: Annotation Budget Regimes in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on how task- and dataset-specific annotation budgets are configured to study deep active learning performance. It highlights the use of distinct high and low budget regimes (e.g., b = 1000 vs. b = 50 for classification, b = 10 slices for segmentation) to systematically evaluate AL methods. By setting low budgets relative to the large underlying datasets, the experiments create challenging data-scarce scenarios where label efficiency is most critical. Such controlled budget settings enable fair comparison of AL strategies across tasks and clarify how performance scales between low- and high-budget regimes.

name: Theoretical Foundations and Open Problems in Active Learning
description: This topic covers the theoretical underpinnings of active learning, including formal models of interaction between learner and oracle, query strategies, and conditions under which active learning can provably reduce label complexity. It emphasizes how learners select informative instances based on uncertainty or related criteria, and how these choices relate to performance guarantees. Within this framework, it highlights open research questions such as designing more effective query strategies, adapting active learners to evolving data streams, and defining robust evaluation protocols that reflect realistic deployment scenarios. These foundations and research directions are directly relevant for principled design and analysis of (deep) active learning systems, particularly in stream-based settings.

name: BADGE Gradient-Embedding Hybrid Active Learning
description: This topic covers BADGE (Batch Active learning by Diverse Gradient Embeddings), a deep active learning strategy that uses per-sample loss gradients as joint representations of uncertainty and diversity. BADGE constructs gradient embeddings—typically for the final-layer parameters—using pseudo-labels from the model’s most confident predictions, and then applies k-Means++ clustering in this gradient space to select a batch that is both high-magnitude (informative) and well-dispersed (diverse). The gradient magnitudes serve as an uncertainty proxy grounded in how much a labeled update would change the model, while the clustering step explicitly mitigates redundancy, enabling a single acquisition rule to balance uncertainty and diversity without extra hyperparameters. Empirically, BADGE achieves strong and often state-of-the-art label efficiency across datasets and tasks (including classification and segmentation), especially in low-budget regimes, though its performance can degrade under distribution shifts or in very high-budget settings. Comparative studies show consistent AUBC gains over pure diversity methods such as k-Means, and performance competitive with or superior to leading uncertainty-based strategies, highlighting the effectiveness of gradient-informed hybrid selection in deep active learning.

name: Overconfidence and Uncertainty Calibration in DAL
description: This topic concerns the tendency of deep neural networks to be over-confident in their predicted probabilities and the impact of this miscalibration on deep active learning. Simple probability-based uncertainty metrics derived from a single forward pass can assign extremely high confidence to incorrect or inherently ambiguous cases, distorting the underlying uncertainty structure of the data. Such miscalibrated softmax scores undermine uncertainty-based query selection, since samples may be chosen due to artifacts of overconfidence rather than genuine epistemic uncertainty. To enable reliable active learning, methods are needed that improve the calibration and quality of uncertainty estimates so that queried samples truly correspond to regions of high model uncertainty.

name: Benchmark Datasets and Metrics for Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers the design of benchmark suites and evaluation metrics tailored to deep active learning in image classification. name: Weakly Supervised CT Segmentation in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers the integration of weak annotation types—such as scribbles, bounding boxes, and extreme points—into deep active learning pipelines for CT image segmentation. Instead of full voxel-wise masks, cheaper sparse labels are used to supervise deep segmentation models for organs and tumors, substantially reducing annotation cost. In a DAL context, the learner can query informative regions or volumes where these weak labels are most beneficial, thereby maximizing label efficiency under a limited annotation budget. The datasets involved include MSD lung, colon, and KiTS19 kidney CT scans with varying numbers of annotated volumes, illustrating how DAL frameworks exploit weak supervision at scale for clinically relevant structures.

name: Deep Active Learning for Prostate Segmentation
description: This topic concerns the use of deep active learning for prostate gland segmentation in MRI, with a focus on realistic clinical datasets such as Fed-Prostate. The segmentation task is organ-level delineation of the prostate in volumetric scans to support diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up. Within a federated or multi-site setting, active learning must operate under data privacy constraints, requiring decentralized model training and query selection without centralizing raw patient data. Deep active learning methods are employed to minimize annotation cost while maintaining segmentation accuracy, by selectively querying the most informative prostate volumes or slices for expert labeling. These studies highlight how active learning strategies can be adapted to distributed medical imaging environments where labeled data are scarce and expensive.

name: Medical CT Segmentation Datasets for Deep Active Learning
description: This cluster summarizes CT-based (and related MRI) datasets used as benchmarks for deep active learning in medical image analysis, with a focus on organ and lesion segmentation. Datasets such as colon CT, KiTS19 kidney and tumor segmentation, and various in-house organ segmentation volumes illustrate the high annotation cost of 3D voxel-wise labels that motivates selective labeling strategies. Larger multi-organ resources, including AbdomenAtlas-8K and other liver, pancreas, spleen, and hippocampus segmentation datasets, provide diverse anatomical targets and label types for evaluating DAL methods. The OrganMNIST classification task offers a related, organ-level CT benchmark where image-wise querying can be explored. Several datasets explicitly support experiments on sampling granularity, contrasting acquisitions at the level of full volumes, fixed-size slice sets, or single images (e.g., CheXpert), thereby enabling the study of how query unit choice affects annotation effort, query design, and segmentation performance in deep active learning.

local_topics.title: Sampling granularity in medical image datasets

name: Farthest-First Traversal for Diversity-Based Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers the use of farthest-first traversal as a diversity-driven acquisition strategy in deep active learning. In pool-based settings, samples are iteratively selected such that each new query is maximally distant in feature space from already labeled or selected points, encouraging broad coverage of the data manifold rather than focusing solely on uncertainty. Implementations typically rely on L2 or cosine distance over deep feature embeddings and are often used to construct an initial labeled set or to complement uncertainty-based criteria. In medical image analysis, this strategy has been applied to breast ultrasound, liver CT, and chest X-ray segmentation, with extensions that incorporate contextual diversity and GNN-augmented features to better capture structural relations between images. Overall, farthest-first traversal operationalizes diversity sampling as a core mechanism to improve annotation efficiency in deep active learning pipelines.

name: Deep Active Learning for Colonoscopy Imaging
description: This topic covers the use of deep active learning and related deep models for classifying colonoscopy and gastrointestinal endoscopic images. In Zhou et al. (2017), a relatively small, in-house colonoscopy dataset of 4,000 images is used to study colon image pattern classification under a limited annotation budget, illustrating how deep active learning can be applied in institution-specific medical imaging settings. Related gastrointestinal image classification datasets with around 7,800 colonoscopy images further demonstrate how deep models distinguish different tissue types and findings to support computer-aided diagnosis and screening. Together, these works highlight colonoscopy as a key application domain where active selection of informative images can reduce labeling effort while maintaining diagnostic performance.

name: Deep Active Learning for Colonoscopy Image Quality Assessment
description: This topic concerns using deep active learning to assess colonoscopy image or video frame quality as a supervised classification task. In-house colonoscopy datasets with tens of thousands or a few thousand images are used to distinguish between different quality levels, enabling automated filtering of low-quality frames. Deep models are trained to classify image quality while active learning aims to minimize the number of labeled images needed from these medical datasets. Such DAL-based quality assessment supports clinical workflows by prioritizing the annotation and analysis of the most informative frames and ensuring that downstream diagnostic models operate on reliable imagery.

name: Task-Independent Deep Active Learning Frameworks
description: This topic covers Deep Active Learning frameworks and architectures designed to be task-independent, so that the same AL machinery can be reused across diverse applications without extensive task-specific modification. Such approaches often embed query selection or uncertainty estimation components directly into deep network architectures, yielding unified models where feature extraction and sample selection are tightly integrated. Existing task-agnostic methods are still relatively few and are predominantly based on uncertainty-driven acquisition, which aligns naturally with deep neural predictors. The literature also highlights the need for deeper fusion of deep learning and active learning modules to improve portability and robustness across domains. Extending these task-independent frameworks with diversity-based or hybrid selection strategies is identified as an important but challenging future direction.

name: Automated Design of Deep Active Learning Methods
description: This topic covers automated approaches to designing Deep Active Learning (DAL) systems, where both query strategies and underlying deep architectures are discovered algorithmically rather than manually engineered. Methods in this area leverage meta-learning, neural architecture search, and other optimization or search frameworks to learn task- and dataset-specific acquisition functions and model configurations. By automating the choice and combination of AL components (e.g., uncertainty estimators, diversity criteria, and network architectures), these approaches aim to improve label efficiency and robustness under limited annotation budgets. They also address challenges such as model uncertainty by adaptively tailoring DAL pipelines to the data, reducing reliance on expert-crafted heuristics and enabling more scalable deployment of DAL in practice.

name: Handling Outliers in Uncertainty-Based Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on the interplay between uncertainty estimation, outlier detection, and performance prediction in deep active learning. Uncertainty-based query strategies often select samples that the model finds most difficult, but without considering intrinsic sample characteristics this can lead to systematically choosing outliers that harm training. Such mis-selected instances waste labeling budget and can degrade model performance instead of improving it. Integrating outlier detection and performance prediction mechanisms into the AL loop can provide additional signals to distinguish informative ambiguous samples from harmful anomalies, leading to more efficient and robust instance querying.

name: Class-Balanced Sampling in Medical Deep Active Learning
description: This topic addresses how redundancy and class imbalance in medical images affect sampling strategies in deep active learning. High intra-class similarity means that many images from the same anatomical region or condition are visually and semantically redundant, so naive informativeness-based acquisition may repeatedly select similar samples. At the same time, healthy cases vastly outnumber diseased ones, producing skewed label distributions that standard selection strategies typically do not correct. Deep active learning methods therefore need class-balance-aware acquisition functions or sampling schemes that explicitly counteract label skew while avoiding redundant queries. This is crucial to maintain performance on rare but clinically important classes under limited annotation budgets.

name: Challenges and Future Directions for Deep Active Learning in Medical Imaging
description: This topic addresses open challenges and prospective advances of deep active learning in medical image analysis. It emphasizes domain-specific constraints such as clinical reliability, safety, and regulatory considerations that complicate the deployment of DAL-driven annotation workflows in healthcare. Scalability and integration into real clinical pipelines are highlighted as key obstacles, including handling large datasets, diverse imaging modalities, and realistic annotation budgets. The topic also notes the need for better evaluation protocols and benchmarks tailored to medical imaging, and underscores that DAL in this domain remains a developing area with substantial academic and translational potential.

local_topics.title: Applications and future challenges of AL in medicine

name: Evidential Deep Learning for Uncertainty-based Acquisition
description: This topic covers the use of Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) to produce Dirichlet-distributed outputs that jointly encode class predictions and calibrated uncertainty for deep active learning. By modeling evidence parameters rather than point probabilities, EDL enables principled estimation of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty via measures such as mutual information and expected entropy, which are then used directly as acquisition scores in active learning loops. In medical image analysis, this uncertainty-aware modeling helps prioritize ambiguous or low-quality cases, such as atypical lesions, for annotation. For object detection, specialized evidence heads are used to adaptively scale Dirichlet parameters and compute box-level epistemic uncertainty, which is then aggregated to image- or sample-level scores, enabling fine-grained selection of informative images under a labeling budget.

name: Federated Deep Active Learning with Evidential Uncertainty
description: This topic focuses on deep active learning in federated settings where data remain distributed across clients, particularly for medical image analysis. A shared global model and client-specific local models are trained within an evidential deep learning (EDL) framework to jointly exploit aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. Aleatoric uncertainties from both global and local models, together with epistemic uncertainty from the global model, are used to drive query selection under privacy constraints. In addition, epistemic uncertainty is leveraged to quantify domain shift between global and client domains and to calibrate aleatoric uncertainties, enabling image-wise active domain adaptation. These uncertainty-aware strategies aim to reduce annotation costs while handling heterogeneous client data distributions in federated deep active learning.

name: Future Research Directions in Deep Active Learning
description: Future research in deep active learning focuses on improving query selection strategies, optimizing training procedures tightly coupled with querying, and developing task- and dataset-agnostic methods. Key open problems include establishing a stronger theoretical foundation for why and when specific acquisition functions work, and how they interact with deep model dynamics under limited label budgets. Scalability and robustness are central challenges, particularly for handling large unlabeled pools, distribution shifts, and noisy or adversarial labels in human-in-the-loop settings. Another important direction is better designing the human interaction loop—e.g., annotator guidance, feedback integration, and cost-aware querying—to maximize labeling efficiency. Finally, integrating DeepAL with self-supervised, semi-supervised, and continual learning paradigms is expected to yield more efficient, reliable, and broadly applicable active learning systems.

name: Label-Free Gradient-Based Acquisition in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on deep active learning strategies that compute gradient-based informativeness scores without access to true labels. Instead of using ground-truth annotations, gradients are obtained from supervised losses with pseudo-labels or from unsupervised objectives such as entropy, allowing uncertainty estimation directly on unlabeled data. A central idea is to use the norm of these label-free gradients as an acquisition score, with theoretical results indicating that larger gradient norms correspond to tighter upper bounds on test loss. In practice, this is implemented through expected empirical loss and entropy-based objectives that only depend on predicted class probabilities, enabling efficient sample selection in domains like cryo-electron tomography subtomogram classification. These methods extend gradient-based active learning (e.g., BADGE-style approaches) to settings where labels are entirely absent at query time, improving performance over competing selection strategies.

name: Gradient-Based Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers gradient-based uncertainty measures where a sample’s gradient with respect to model parameters quantifies its influence on learning and thus its informativeness for active querying. In deep active learning, especially for medical image analysis, larger gradient norms indicate samples that would induce larger parameter updates and are therefore treated as more uncertain and valuable for annotation. These methods are explicitly decoupled from predictive probabilities, making them less vulnerable to over-confident posterior estimates that can mislead probability-based acquisition functions. Several concrete metrics are used in this paradigm, including raw gradient norms, Fisher information approximations, and influence-function-based scores, which underpin multiple gradient-driven querying strategies.

name: Fisher Information and Gradient-Based Acquisition
description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that use gradients and Fisher Information (FI) to define acquisition functions. FI, computed from gradients or Hessians of the loss with respect to model parameters, quantifies how strongly candidate samples can influence parameter uncertainty and convergence, and selection objectives may minimize the trace of the inverse FI for the labeled subset relative to the pool. In practice, samples that induce large parameter gradients or high FI are treated as more informative and prioritized for annotation, directly tying query selection to the model’s local loss landscape rather than just output probabilities. Related methods extend this idea with influence scores measuring the impact of individual samples on the training loss, or with submodular coverage objectives that use gradient-based metrics to build diverse yet informative query sets. These approaches are particularly relevant in deep neural networks, but their exact FI computation can be expensive, motivating approximations to make FI- and gradient-based DAL scalable.

name: Concept Drift in Stream-Based Active Learning
description: This topic addresses how different types and rates of concept drift affect active learning in data streams and how models must adapt. Drift is characterized by how quickly the data-generating distribution changes, influencing when and how often active learners should update their models. Abrupt, gradual, and incremental drifts, as well as recurring concepts, each pose distinct challenges for detecting changes and maintaining reliable query criteria. Because drift alters which instances are most informative, active learning strategies for streams must integrate drift detection and adaptation to preserve the effectiveness of their selection mechanisms over time.

name: Taxonomy of Deep Active Learning Query Strategies
description: Deep active learning methods are commonly organized by how they select unlabeled samples for annotation, leading to a taxonomy of uncertainty-based, representativeness/diversity-based, and combined (hybrid) querying strategies. Uncertainty-based approaches prioritize instances where the model is least confident, while representativeness and diversity-based methods aim to cover the data distribution and avoid redundancy in the queried set. Hybrid strategies explicitly integrate both uncertainty and diversity, for example via weighted-sum optimization or multi-objective formulations. This taxonomy also links conceptual criteria (e.g., representativeness, diversity) to specific algorithmic families such as clustering, point processes, and other structured selection mechanisms, providing a structural map from high-level DAL principles to concrete algorithms.

name: Comparing Sampling Strategies in Remote Sensing AL
description: This cluster covers comparative studies of active learning sampling strategies for supervised remote sensing image classification, focusing on how different query mechanisms affect accuracy as a function of labeled pixels. Random sampling (RS) and margin sampling (MS) are contrasted with more sophisticated uncertainty-based strategies such as MCLU and its variants (e.g., MCLU-ABE / MCLU-ABD), typically paired with an SVM classifier. The methods are evaluated under matched experimental setups, plotting overall accuracy against the number of labeled pixels to assess label efficiency. The comparisons highlight how informed acquisition functions can yield higher performance than RS and standard SVM baselines for the same annotation budget, illustrating the benefits of uncertainty-driven query selection in pool-based active learning.

name: Annotation Costs in Medical Imaging for Deep Active Learning
description: Medical image analysis faces extremely high annotation costs due to the need for dense, fine-grained labels on large volumetric datasets, such as voxel-wise segmentation masks. Even as datasets like BraTS have grown from a few dozen to over a thousand patients, the resulting hundreds of thousands of annotated slices highlight the substantial expert effort required. This persistent gap between data volume and feasible manual annotation makes exhaustive labeling economically and logistically challenging. In the context of deep active learning, these constraints motivate the design of query strategies that minimize expert workload by selecting only the most informative medical images or regions for annotation under a limited labeling budget.

name: Practical Selection of Active Learning Heuristics
description: This topic addresses how the choice of active learning selection heuristics should be guided by practical, problem-specific constraints rather than by marginal performance differences or the underlying model type alone. When non–margin-based strategies are used, multiple heuristics often yield similar accuracy, so considerations such as available computation time, allowable number of active learning iterations, and acceptable algorithmic complexity become primary. The discussion further stresses that batch size per iteration and user requirements in realistic workflows (e.g., remote sensing applications) should drive heuristic selection. These insights are directly applicable to deep active learning, where acquisition functions can be computationally heavy and must therefore be chosen with both efficiency and performance in mind.

name: Self-Supervised Pretext Loss for Deep Active Learning
description: This topic concerns deep active learning strategies that leverage self-supervised pretext tasks to guide sample selection. Self-supervised learning first trains models on unlabeled data using pretext objectives such as rotation prediction, contrastive learning, or masked modeling to obtain informative representations. The loss values from these pretext tasks are then repurposed as acquisition signals within the active learning loop, either as standalone criteria or in combination with standard uncertainty measures. A key finding is the empirical correlation between pretext-task loss and downstream task loss, enabling dynamic sampling strategies that prioritize high-loss samples early and low-loss samples later in training. Among different pretext tasks, rotation prediction has shown particularly strong performance as an informativeness proxy in this combined self-supervised and active learning setting.

name: Deep Active Learning for Histopathology Gland Analysis
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods applied to histopathology, with a focus on patch-based classification and gland segmentation in colon and prostate tissue. Studies on the GlaS dataset formulate tasks at the patch level to capture fine-grained gland structures and reduce the need for exhaustive whole-slide annotations. Within an active learning framework, only subsets of patches are queried (e.g., small batch sizes, varying labeled proportions such as 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 50%), reflecting the high cost and effort of expert pathology labeling. These approaches extend active learning from diagnostic image-level classification to detailed structural segmentation, aiming to improve performance while tightly controlling the annotation budget. Similar strategies are discussed for prostate histopathology, where informative tissue patches are selectively labeled to support cancer detection and grading.

name: Deep Active Learning for Entity-Centric NLP
description: This topic covers the use of deep active learning to build efficient models for entity-centric NLP tasks, particularly named entity recognition (NER) and entity resolution (ER), under limited labeling budgets. Deep models are trained on both general and domain-specific corpora, including news, biomedical text, and scientific literature, where annotated entities are expensive to obtain. Query strategies focus on selecting the most informative sentences or spans for annotation, often leveraging sequence-level uncertainty and diversity to maximize information gain per labeled example. In ER, deep active learning is further combined with transfer learning to adapt models from high-resource to low-resource domains, improving cross-database entity matching when labeled pairs are scarce. Overall, these methods aim to reduce annotation cost while preserving or improving performance across multiple ontologies and domains.

name: Multi-round Annotation in Deep Active Learning
description: Deep active learning experiments are often organized into multiple annotation rounds, where each round queries a batch of unlabeled samples and updates the model with the newly obtained labels. The process typically assumes a fixed total number of rounds T, with each t-th round operating on the current model state and remaining unlabeled pool. This iterative setup enables gradual refinement of model performance while explicitly controlling and monitoring the labeling cost across cycles. By evaluating performance after each round, researchers can analyze how the accumulation of labeled data influences learning dynamics and the efficiency of different query strategies under a fixed annotation budget.

name: Disagreement-Based and Committee Active Learning
description: This topic covers disagreement-based query strategies, particularly query-by-committee (QBC), where a committee of models is used to identify instances on which predictions most disagree. Disagreement is quantified via measures such as vote entropy, variation ratio, or KL-divergence between predictive distributions, and these scores define the acquisition criterion. Committees may be composed of heterogeneous models, or arise from Bayesian treatments of a single model’s parameters, with dropout in neural networks serving as a practical deep Bayesian approximation for uncertainty estimation. The methods extend naturally to batch-mode selection, where multiple samples are chosen jointly based on committee disagreement, although training k committee members can be computationally expensive for deep models and classifier diversity is not always guaranteed. Overall, these strategies target regions of the hypothesis space that remain poorly constrained by current labeled data, making them a core family of query methods for (deep) active learning in both pool-based and streaming settings.

name: Committee Disagreement and Entropy-Based Querying
description: This topic covers committee- and ensemble-based query strategies in deep active learning that select samples by measuring prediction disagreement. Methods such as vote entropy and entropy over committee outputs quantify how diverse the predicted labels are, with higher entropy indicating greater uncertainty and expected informativeness. For dense prediction and segmentation tasks, selection can be done at the pixel or patch level, prioritizing regions where models disagree most. More advanced measures like entropy-weighted Dice distance combine predictive entropy with segmentation overlap to capture both uncertainty and structural inconsistency, focusing annotation on the most challenging medical images. These approaches directly operationalize the active learning objective of querying the most uncertain and informative instances under limited annotation budgets.

name: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Active Learning in NLP
description: This topic focuses on active learning settings where annotation must be allocated across multiple domains, languages, or tasks, often in natural language processing. Instead of running separate active learning processes per target, a single shared model and joint selection strategy are used so that queried examples benefit several domains or tasks simultaneously. Central questions include how to design acquisition functions that consider all targets jointly, how to exploit shared representations, and how to balance improvements across heterogeneous but related targets. A key concern is how to optimally allocate a limited labeling budget across multiple domains or languages to avoid over-focusing on high-resource settings while still enabling effective transfer.

name: Membership Query Synthesis and Generative Active Learning
description: This topic covers membership query synthesis, an active learning setting in which the learner is free to query labels for any point in the input space, including synthetically generated instances not present in a fixed unlabeled pool. In deep active learning, this often manifests as generative active learning, where models create or transform data (e.g., adversarial or boundary-centered examples) to probe informative regions of the feature space under a label budget and possible performance-based stopping criteria. While the approach offers maximal flexibility and can be tailored with domain-specific transformations in vision, NLP, and speech, it faces practical constraints: in high-dimensional domains like images or complex text, generated instances may be unnatural or uninterpretable for human annotators. Consequently, the design of synthetic query generation must balance informativeness with human interpretability and annotation feasibility in human-in-the-loop systems.

name: Hybrid Deep Active Learning Query Strategies
description: This topic covers hybrid and combined deep active learning strategies that integrate multiple querying criteria, most prominently uncertainty and diversity. Such methods formulate sample selection as a multi-objective optimization problem, often realized via weighted-sum objectives that trade off informativeness against representativeness, or via two-stage/multi-stage pipelines that apply different criteria sequentially. These strategies aim to construct large, diverse batches that both refine the decision boundary and cover the data distribution well. The cluster emphasizes that these combined approaches, including methods like CCAL, exploitation–exploration frameworks, WAAL, and BADGE variants, have become dominant in practical DAL due to their improved effectiveness over single-criterion querying.

name: Taxonomy of Active Learning Heuristic Families
description: This topic covers the main families of heuristics used to rank unlabeled instances for querying in active learning, which directly underpin acquisition strategies in Deep Active Learning. The survey distinguishes committee-based, large-margin-based, and posterior probability-based heuristics, each modeling classifier uncertainty in different ways to select informative samples from a pool. A fourth family, cluster-based heuristics, operates by refining a hierarchical clustering of the data until clusters become label-consistent, relying on an unsupervised data distribution model rather than a predictive classifier. This taxonomy provides a structured view of how different query strategies trade off exploration of the data space versus exploitation of current model uncertainty, and it informs the design and comparison of DAL acquisition functions. Although illustrated in remote sensing image classification, the families are generic and directly transferable to deep model settings.

name: Distribution Shift and Concept Drift in Active Learning Streams
description: This topic formalizes different types of distribution shifts in data streams using time-dependent probability distributions p_t(x), p_t(y|x), and p_t(y), providing the foundation for active learning in non-stationary environments. It distinguishes virtual drift (covariate shift), where only the input distribution p_t(x) changes while p_t(y|x) remains stable, from real concept drift, where the conditional distribution p_t(y|x) itself evolves and can severely degrade model performance. The text also emphasizes that in many real-world streaming scenarios, virtual and real concept drift co-occur, jointly altering both feature frequencies and label relationships and thus complicating model adaptation and labeling decisions. Additionally, it highlights label distribution shift, where only the marginal label distribution p_t(y) changes, affecting class priors and calibration over time. These probabilistic distinctions are crucial for designing stream-based active learning strategies that decide when to query labels and update deep models under evolving data distributions.

name: Learnable Sampling with Neural Selectors in DAL
description: This topic covers deep active learning approaches where the sampling strategy itself is parameterized and learned by a neural network. Instead of computing explicit informativeness scores followed by heuristic selection, a neural selector directly outputs which unlabeled samples should be queried, forming an end-to-end trainable selection policy. These methods move beyond hand-crafted uncertainty or diversity metrics by optimizing the selection mechanism from data or proxy supervision signals. Within the DAL pipeline, learnable sampling tightly couples representation learning and query selection, aiming to better exploit structure in the unlabeled pool under constrained annotation budgets.

name: Deep Active Learning for Sensor-Based Human Activity Recognition
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods for human activity recognition using sensor data from wearables, smartphones, and smart environments. DeepAL is used to select the most informative sensor segments or activity windows, typically based on uncertainty measures, to reduce the labeling burden on users and annotators. Approaches include context-aware annotator selection frameworks that adaptively choose which annotator to query, as well as resource-efficient deep ensembles and approximate Bayesian neural networks to quantify predictive uncertainty on-device. These methods target both generalized activity recognition on public datasets and personalized models that can incrementally adapt to individual users with minimal manual annotation, improving label efficiency in continuous, multimodal time-series settings.

name: Cover-Based Core-Set Selection in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers cover-based and core-set methods that formulate deep active learning as a k-center or set-cover problem in feature space. These approaches select a representative subset of unlabeled samples whose deep feature embeddings well cover the data manifold, minimizing redundancy and the maximum distance from any pool point to the selected set. Implementations often rely on L2 distances in learned embeddings, sometimes enhanced with contextual or semantic diversity metrics and graph convolutional models to better capture relationships between labeled and unlabeled data. Submodular formulations provide greedy algorithms with approximation guarantees for near-optimal coverage under labeling budget constraints, particularly in medical image analysis. Despite their effectiveness, core-set methods can be computationally expensive due to distance matrix construction and can over-select outliers when the labeled set is small.

name: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Cold-Start Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on using self-supervised pretraining to mitigate the cold-start problem in deep active learning, where only few or no labeled samples are initially available. Self-supervised models are trained on large unlabeled datasets to learn task-agnostic feature representations, which then provide strong initialization for downstream active learning workflows. These pretrained features enable more informed initial query selection compared to random or naive strategies, improving early-cycle performance under tight annotation budgets. Methods like ALPS explicitly formulate the cold-start setting and leverage self-supervised representations to drive the first acquisition steps, establishing self-supervision as a central paradigm for cold-start-aware DAL strategies.

name: Cold-Start Problem in Deep Active Learning
description: The cold-start problem in (deep) active learning arises when there is little or no labeled data available at the beginning of the process, so the model is too poorly trained to provide reliable uncertainty or informativeness estimates. In this phase, standard query strategies can make misleading sampling decisions and may even perform worse than random sampling because the underlying model is inaccurate. This issue is prominent in data-hungry deep models and in domains with expensive annotation, such as medical image analysis and data streams. Mitigation strategies include careful design of initial seed selection that differs from the later-stage query policy, as well as pretraining or self-supervised learning to bootstrap the model before active querying begins. Addressing cold-start is thus a critical design aspect for practical deep active learning systems, especially in low-label and streaming scenarios.

name: Benchmarking Deep Active Learning on Medical Imaging Datasets
description: This topic covers systematic benchmarking of deep active learning methods on medical imaging datasets. The surveyed work evaluates multiple representative AL algorithms across several datasets spanning different imaging modalities, organs, and tasks, including both image classification and segmentation. Careful experimental setups are described, with explicit dataset splits, network architectures, and training hyperparameters to enable fair comparison and reproducibility. The benchmarks address the scarcity of standardized performance evaluations in medical image analysis and release code to facilitate transparent comparison and further DAL research in this domain.

name: Generative Active Learning via Query Synthesis
description: This topic covers generative active learning, where a generative model is integrated into the active learning loop to synthesize informative samples for annotation. Instead of passively selecting instances from a fixed unlabeled pool, the learner actively guides the generator to explore the data manifold and produce candidate queries tailored to an acquisition strategy. This setting corresponds to membership query synthesis, allowing queries at arbitrary points rather than being restricted to existing data. It contrasts with traditional uses of generative models for mere data augmentation by explicitly optimizing synthetic sample generation for maximal informativeness under a label budget.

name: Prequential Evaluation in Streaming Active Learning
description: Prequential (test-then-train) evaluation is a standard protocol for assessing active learning methods in data streams, where instances arrive sequentially and must be processed online. At each time step, the model first predicts on the incoming instance, the active learning strategy then decides whether to query its label under a labeling budget, and the model is updated only when a label is acquired. This produces a time series of prediction errors that reflects how performance evolves over time in non-stationary environments. The approach is particularly suitable for streaming and drifting data, where static holdout sets are inadequate because they do not capture changing data distributions. In the context of online and stream-based active learning, prequential evaluation tightly couples prediction, query decisions, and budget consumption within a unified, temporally ordered framework.

name: Online Active Learning for Customer Interaction Streams
description: This topic covers the use of online (stream-based) active learning in customer-facing applications such as customer service and marketing. Models interact with streaming customer data and selectively query labels or additional information during or after each interaction to improve response or targeting quality. Selection policies identify the most informative interactions to label, balancing exploration of new behaviors with exploitation of known patterns. Over time, the system refines predictions for optimal responses, personalization strategies, and marketing actions using past labeled interactions. Performance is typically evaluated through business-relevant metrics such as conversion, engagement, and customer support accuracy.

name: Loss-Prediction-Based Acquisition in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that use learnable loss prediction to guide sample acquisition. An auxiliary network is trained to regress the target model’s loss (or error reduction) on inputs, using labeled data to match predicted and actual losses. At query time, unlabeled instances with the highest predicted loss are selected, under the assumption that these hard or mis-modeled samples will yield the greatest performance gains when annotated. This reframes acquisition as a supervised regression problem over losses, enabling adaptive, data-driven querying that can be relatively model-agnostic. Variants such as the Loss Prediction Loss (LPL) implement this idea by adding a small prediction head and optimizing it jointly with the main model.

name: Learning Loss Prediction for Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers active learning methods that train auxiliary neural modules to predict per-sample loss and use this prediction as an acquisition signal. In the LLAL framework, a loss prediction head is attached to a target network and takes features from multiple hidden layers to estimate the future loss of unlabeled samples. The model is trained with a joint objective combining the task loss and the loss-prediction loss, encouraging strong correlation between predicted and true losses. During querying, a top-K strategy selects the most informative samples based on the highest predicted loss, effectively turning loss prediction into a task-agnostic uncertainty measure. This approach has been shown to outperform or match standard active learning baselines across image classification, object detection, human pose estimation, and medical imaging applications such as lung nodule detection and COVID diagnosis.

name: Margin-Based Uncertainty with Diversity Constraints
description: This topic covers margin-based uncertainty sampling, where unlabeled instances close to the classifier's decision boundary (i.e., with small absolute decision function values or small posterior margins) are treated as the most informative for labeling. It explains how this large-margin heuristic operationalizes uncertainty by ranking samples according to the magnitude of a decision function or class-posterior gap. The topic further addresses a key limitation of pure margin sampling—its tendency to select highly redundant, similar points—and describes augmenting it with diversity constraints. These diversity-aware variants penalize or filter candidates that are too similar to already selected samples, combining uncertainty and representativeness in feature space. Although exemplified in supervised remote sensing image classification, the same margin-based and diversity-constrained principles directly inform acquisition strategies in deep active learning, where decision margins are computed from deep models' outputs.

name: Annotation Cost Modeling in Active Learning for NLP
description: This topic examines how to model and measure annotation cost in active learning for NLP, where labeling effort is highly heterogeneous. Costs can vary with sentence length, label complexity, span boundary decisions, and the need for agreement checks, and active learners typically query harder, more ambiguous instances that are especially expensive. Treating annotation as a uniform per-instance cost can therefore distort both evaluation and the apparent ranking of query strategies. The topic highlights time-based cost, measured in user studies, as the most realistic metric, and discusses regression-based cost models that predict annotation time or effort from input features. Such cost models can be integrated into the querying process to balance expected information gain against true labeling effort, leading to more cost-effective deep active learning workflows for NLP tasks.

name: Reinforcement Learning for Learnable Query Policies
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that cast sample or region selection as a sequential decision problem and learn query policies via reinforcement learning or imitation learning. Instead of hand-crafted acquisition functions, a policy network (agent) observes model state and candidate instances or patches, and learns to select those whose annotation maximizes long-term downstream performance within a limited label budget. In NLP, such learning-to-select policies may be trained on labeled data or with the task model acting as an imperfect annotator, though they can suffer from reliance on labeled supervision and unstable learning signals for complex semantics. In medical image analysis, reinforcement learning is used both for instance-level querying and for patch selection, guiding annotation effort toward the most informative regions. Overall, these approaches aim to produce adaptive, task-specific querying strategies that update during active learning rounds based on oracle feedback and evolving model performance.

name: Reinforcement Learning for Active Query Policies
description: This topic covers the use of reinforcement learning (RL) as a general decision-making framework for active learning, where querying strategies are modeled as policies optimized over time. RL-based approaches go beyond bandit-style formulations by exploiting richer state representations and feedback signals, allowing explicit modeling of label costs, information gains, and long-term performance. In pool-based settings, an RL agent can learn which instances to query to maximize cumulative reward, reflecting improved model accuracy under a limited annotation budget. For data streams and dynamic environments, online RL is proposed to continually adapt the sampling policy as the data distribution and task evolve. This directly targets Deep Active Learning scenarios where query decisions must balance exploration of uncertain instances and exploitation of current knowledge over trajectories.

name: Deep Generative Models for Active Learning in Medical Imaging
description: Deep generative models are increasingly used to synthesize realistic, clinically plausible medical images that approximate complex data distributions in modalities such as X-rays and other scans. Within deep active learning, these models enable membership query synthesis, where the learner can actively generate and query synthetic samples rather than only selecting from a fixed pool of real images. This integration aims to improve model performance under limited annotation budgets by targeting informative synthetic examples that complement scarce labeled data. In medical image analysis, such generative models form a foundation for AL frameworks that mix real and synthetic data, enhancing label efficiency while preserving clinical realism.

name: Deep Active Learning for Lung Segmentation on Chest X-rays
description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies for lung field segmentation on chest X-ray images using the Jaeger et al. dataset. The studies vary the labeling budget from roughly 30% to 50% of the available images in fine-grained increments (e.g., 2.5%), investigating how selective querying can minimize manual delineation while maintaining segmentation accuracy. Models begin from very small or even zero labeled sets and iteratively request labels for the most informative X-rays, reflecting a pool-based DAL setting. The focus is on quantifying the trade-off between annotation effort and segmentation performance under constrained label budgets, specifically for medical imaging segmentation tasks.

name: Label Scarcity and Annotation Cost in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on label scarcity and high annotation costs as the primary motivation for deep active learning, particularly in domains like medical imaging and data streams. In such settings, raw data are abundant but manual labeling by experts is slow, expensive, and often the main bottleneck for deploying accurate deep models. Deep active learning methods are designed to improve label efficiency by strategically selecting the most informative instances to query under a limited annotation budget. The topic also covers the challenge of evaluating active learning strategies when comprehensive ground-truth labels are unavailable, creating a discrepancy between controlled research protocols and realistic deployment scenarios. This raises methodological questions about how to design evaluation schemes that remain faithful to the core constraint of scarce labels while still enabling reliable performance comparison.

name: Deep Active Learning for ECG Classification
description: This topic covers the application of deep active learning to electrocardiogram (ECG) signal classification, particularly for arrhythmia and related cardiac condition diagnosis. Deep active learning frameworks select the most informative ECG segments or beats for cardiologist labeling, thereby reducing annotation costs in highly expert-driven medical settings. Methods may combine hand-crafted features, such as eigenvalue-based representations, with deep learning classifiers to better exploit the limited labeled data. Performance is typically evaluated as classification accuracy over multiple arrhythmia classes versus the number of labeled ECG segments, highlighting gains in label efficiency compared to passive learning.
