name: Threshold-Based Querying in Stream-Based Active Learning
description: This topic concerns threshold-based querying policies for online active learning on data streams, where labels are requested only for instances whose informativeness exceeds a predefined or dynamically adjusted threshold. Informativeness is typically measured via an instance selection criterion, such as the classifier’s margin, and the threshold controls how aggressively the learner queries over time. In margin-based approaches, unlabeled instances are queried if their absolute margin falls below a current threshold that is gradually tightened, for example by iteratively halving it until a sufficient number of misclassifications is observed among queried examples. Such error-driven adaptation allows the query budget to concentrate on regions of uncertainty that are actually associated with classification mistakes. In evolving data streams, these strategies can be combined with update rules (e.g., reflection-based updates of a linear classifier) that emphasize recent data, making the overall active learner responsive to concept drift while still limiting annotation costs.

name: Deep Active Learning for Person Re-Identification and Activity Recognition
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods tailored to activity recognition and person re-identification, where annotation of video frames, identities, and bounding boxes is particularly expensive. DeepAL frameworks focus labeling effort on difficult or ambiguous samples to achieve high recognition and re-identification accuracy with substantially fewer labeled examples and reduced computational resources compared to conventional deep learning. In video-based person re-identification, active learning is integrated into deep architectures so that the oracle is queried primarily for the most informative sequences or instances. Some approaches employ deep reinforcement learning, where an agent learns a selection policy that uses oracle feedback to preferentially sample highly uncertain or valuable data points, iteratively refining this policy over time. Performance is typically evaluated in terms of re-id accuracy and pedestrian detection quality as a function of the labeled budget on datasets such as PRID, MARS, BDD100K, DukeMTMC-VideoReID, CityPersons, and Caltech Pedestrian.

name: Standardized Pipelines and Frameworks for Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on resolving pipeline inconsistency in Deep Active Learning (DeepAL) by developing standardized, modular frameworks. Different DAL studies often combine deep models, acquisition functions, and training schedules in ad hoc ways, making results hard to reproduce and compare. Redesigned DeepAL pipelines aim to decouple components (model, query strategy, labeling loop, retraining schedule) through clear interfaces so they can be reused and recomposed across tasks and domains. Common framework initiatives explicitly target this standardization, providing unified implementations that bring consistency to experimental protocols and ease transfer to new applications. Such frameworks help establish more reliable benchmarks and facilitate systematic evaluation of DAL methods under comparable conditions.

name: Challenges in Integrating Deep and Active Learning
description: This topic addresses the specific difficulties that arise when combining pool-based active learning with modern deep neural networks. It highlights how high annotation costs and very large unlabeled pools stress traditional active learning assumptions, requiring adaptations of query strategies and acquisition functions to high-dimensional representation spaces. The cluster emphasizes challenges in estimating model uncertainty for deep models, dealing with insufficient labeled data, and maintaining consistency across the active learning pipeline. These issues motivate specialized Deep Active Learning methods, including uncertainty-aware query strategies, data expansion techniques, and unified frameworks designed to make deep active learning more robust and effective.

name: Single-pass and window-based sampling in stream active learning
description: This topic focuses on sampling strategies for stream-based deep active learning, contrasting single-pass online querying with window- or batch-based selection. Single-pass methods must decide immediately for each incoming instance whether to request a label, typically under strict time and memory constraints and without storing or revisiting past data. In contrast, window-based approaches buffer a fixed-size chunk of the stream and then perform best-out-of-window selection, choosing the top-k most informative instances for labeling given storage and computational limits. Window-based strategies are particularly suitable for high-volume streams without hard real-time constraints, enabling more informed acquisition decisions by comparing candidates within the buffer. Single-pass approaches are favored when latency or resource restrictions preclude maintaining multiple models or large buffers, offering a lightweight alternative to ensemble- and batch-based methods in online classification.

name: Deep Active Learning for Dermoscopic Skin Lesion Analysis
description: This cluster covers deep active learning methods applied to dermoscopy-based skin lesion analysis, including both image-level diagnosis and pixel-wise lesion segmentation. Multiple ISIC benchmarks (2016, 2017, 2018, 2020) and related datasets (e.g., Fed-ISIC, large dermoscopy cohorts) are used to study how performance scales under constrained annotation budgets, with labeled subsets ranging from a few dozen images up to 50% of the dataset. Experimental protocols systematically vary the initial labeled set size, query batch size, and labeled fractions (e.g., 0–10–30–50% or 40–60% in 2.5% steps) to quantify label-efficiency benefits of DAL for melanoma and other lesion-type discrimination. The works highlight challenges such as class imbalance, dense pixel-wise labeling costs, and large-scale dermatology data, and demonstrate that carefully designed acquisition strategies can substantially reduce required expert annotations for reliable skin lesion classification and segmentation. Some setups also consider federated or distributed scenarios (e.g., Fed-ISIC), further emphasizing DAL’s role in realistic clinical data settings.

name: ISIC 2020 Dataset for Deep Active Learning in Dermatology
description: This topic covers the ISIC 2020 dermoscopic image dataset as a benchmark for deep active learning in skin lesion classification. The dataset comprises over 33,000 images from more than 2,000 patients, with binary labels indicating benign or malignant lesions. Labels are derived from expert diagnosis, long-term follow-up, or histopathology, making them clinically meaningful but costly to obtain, which aligns well with active learning scenarios focused on reducing annotation effort. A severe class imbalance (tens of thousands of benign vs. only hundreds of malignant cases) poses additional challenges for acquisition strategies, which must balance uncertainty and rare-class discovery. Typical experimental setups split the data into training, validation, and test sets (e.g., 6:1:3), and are used to study how DAL methods handle clinical variability, patient-level diversity, and imbalanced risk-sensitive decision making.

name: Hybrid Informativeness–Representativeness Query Strategies
description: This topic covers active learning strategies that jointly exploit informativeness and representativeness when selecting data points for annotation, a design that directly transfers to Deep Active Learning. Rather than relying solely on uncertainty (which can over-sample outliers or noisy instances), these hybrid methods also assess how well candidate points reflect the overall structure and distribution of the unlabeled pool. Representativeness is used to mitigate sampling bias by encouraging coverage of dense regions and reducing redundancy among queried instances. In practice, these criteria are integrated to favor samples that are both challenging for the current model and broadly representative, leading to more efficient use of annotation budgets in deep models as well.

name: Slice- and Region-Based Sampling in Medical Deep Active Learning
description: This topic concerns how the choice of sampling unit in deep active learning for medical image analysis affects annotation efficiency and learning performance. Instead of querying labels at the whole-image or whole-volume level, many methods operate at finer granularity, such as 2D slices or local regions within 3D scans. In volumetric imaging (e.g., CT, MRI), neighboring slices exhibit strong semantic redundancy, which can be exploited by selectively querying only the most informative slices, thereby reducing annotation costs while preserving performance. Slice-based active learning strategies typically integrate uncertainty, representativeness, and diversity criteria over slices to identify which subparts of a volume deserve expert annotation, enabling more targeted use of limited labeling budgets. These design choices reflect DAL-specific concerns about how to structure queries in complex, high-dimensional medical data.

name: Deep Active Learning for Object and Defect Detection
description: This topic focuses on deep active learning methods tailored to object detection and industrial defect detection, where annotation of bounding boxes or defect regions is expensive. Detection models query the most informative images or regions using uncertainty-based criteria, sometimes computed in feature space, to select samples for manual labeling. In industrial defect detection, an average margin–based strategy is used to control the sampling ratio for each defect category, addressing class imbalance while still prioritizing uncertain instances. Applications span LiDAR-based 3D object detection in autonomous driving, surface defect inspection in manufacturing, and ecological and wildlife monitoring, all aiming to reach strong detection performance with substantially fewer labeled examples. Benchmarks such as VOC, KITTI, NEU-DET, and various wildlife datasets are used to evaluate how well these DAL strategies reduce annotation cost in detection tasks.

name: Application Domains of Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers how Deep Active Learning (DeepAL) is applied across a broad spectrum of domains and tasks. While DeepAL has been used for image recognition, object detection, visual question answering, and other computer vision problems, current research is still dominated by vision-centric applications. The survey also highlights successful uses of DeepAL in NLP, speech and audio processing, social network analysis, medical imaging, wildlife protection, industrial robotics, and disaster analysis, where query strategies and deep architectures are adapted to domain-specific data characteristics. It emphasizes that different task properties—such as data modality, output space, and label noise—shape the choice and performance of active learning strategies. Overall, the survey argues for a more systematic, application-oriented view of DeepAL, noting the lack of a unified classification framework and pointing to future directions in domain-specific method design and evaluation.

name: Deep Active Learning for Visual Recognition
description: This topic covers the application of deep active learning to visual data processing, where high-dimensional imagery makes label acquisition particularly costly. Image classification and recognition are treated as foundational tasks, providing the basis for extending DeepAL methods to more complex computer vision problems such as object detection and semantic segmentation. The focus is on designing query strategies that can identify the most informative unlabeled images in large visual pools, thereby achieving strong classification performance with minimal annotation effort. DeepAL in this domain explicitly addresses the challenges of scaling active learning to high-dimensional input spaces while tightly controlling labeling budgets.

name: Adversarial Representation Learning for Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that use adversarial representation learning to distinguish labeled from unlabeled data and guide query selection. Frameworks such as VAAL train a VAE to map both labeled and unlabeled samples into a latent space while an adversarial discriminator predicts whether latent codes originate from the labeled or unlabeled pool, effectively estimating an H-divergence–like discrepancy between the two distributions. Query strategies then select those points that the discriminator deems most likely to be unlabeled or distributionally distinct, improving diversity and mitigating issues like outlier sensitivity and distance concentration that affect uncertainty and density-based methods. Extensions like DiscAL and WAAL generalize this idea by using discriminators to capture representativeness and batch-level distributional differences, while TA-VAAL and ARAL integrate task-aware uncertainty (e.g., loss prediction) and synthetic samples from generative models to better exploit both global data structure and task-specific information under limited annotation budgets.

name: Budget-based benchmarking of deep active learning
description: This topic concerns the systematic evaluation of deep active learning strategies under different annotation budget regimes in medical image analysis tasks such as pathological tissue and skin lesion classification. Studies distinguish between low-budget settings (e.g., b = 50, with 50–300 labeled samples) and high-budget settings (e.g., b = 1000, with 1000–6000 labeled samples) to examine how performance evolves as more labels are acquired. Multiple query strategies—Random sampling, confidence-based, entropy and margin uncertainty, BALD, DBAL, and BADGE—are compared using metrics like accuracy and AUC, reported as mean ± standard deviation over active learning rounds. The experimental design highlights how uncertainty- and diversity-based acquisition functions behave under strict versus generous labeling budgets, enabling nuanced analysis of query efficiency and performance scaling specific to deep active learning.

name: Batch-Mode Deep Active Learning and Diversity
description: Batch-Mode Deep Active Learning (BMDAL) replaces sequential, one-by-one querying with batch-based selection to better match the training dynamics and computational costs of deep models. Instead of frequently retraining on nearly identical datasets, BMDAL scores candidate batches from the unlabeled pool via a batch acquisition function that depends on the current model trained on the labeled set, turning acquisition into a batch-level optimization problem. A central challenge is that selecting the most informative individual points can lead to highly redundant batches if correlations between samples are ignored. Consequently, modern BMDAL strategies aim to jointly maximize information content and within-batch diversity, either by explicitly enforcing diversity in input or representation space or by directly optimizing mutual information over whole batches. These designs seek globally effective query sets that provide large information gains while avoiding overlap and redundancy.

The benchmarks include knee and brain MRI datasets from the fastMRI initiative, associated with works such as Bakker et al. (2020) at NeurIPS. name: Deep Active Learning with Self-Supervised Pretraining
description: This topic examines how self-supervised pre-trained models are integrated into deep active learning pipelines, particularly in medical image analysis. Powerful feature extractors trained on large-scale unlabeled data are used as backbones for active learning, providing richer representations that improve uncertainty and diversity estimation in query strategies. By starting from self-supervised encoders instead of training from scratch, active learning can achieve stronger performance with fewer labeled samples, enhancing label efficiency under strict annotation budgets. The studies highlight that even with randomly selected small labeled sets, fine-tuning self-supervised models yields strong baselines, and further active selection on top of these representations can amplify gains in downstream performance.

name: Wasserstein Adversarial Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers Wasserstein Adversarial Active Learning (WAAL), a discrepancy-based deep active learning method that models annotation as a distribution matching problem between labeled and unlabeled data. WAAL replaces traditional H-divergence with the Wasserstein distance to better preserve diversity while aligning the two distributions. It extends VAAL by adding a sample-selection module trained adversarially to minimize the Wasserstein distance, encouraging queries that are both highly uncertain and likely unlabeled. The method explicitly balances uncertainty and diversity in a hybrid query strategy and decomposes the procedure into neural network parameter optimization and query batch selection. Overall, WAAL exemplifies adversarial, distribution-based DAL where acquisition is driven by aligning data distributions under a principled optimal transport metric.

name: Data Processing Paradigms in Online Active Learning
description: This topic addresses how online active learning methods process data streams under strict single-pass or streaming constraints. It contrasts single-pass schemes, where each instance is seen once and must be immediately evaluated for querying, with approaches that temporarily accumulate instances to enable joint or batch querying decisions. These processing paradigms directly shape how acquisition strategies are implemented in streaming settings, including when and how informativeness is assessed. They also determine memory usage, computational efficiency, and latency, thereby constraining the design of practical query strategies for real-time or resource-limited environments.

name: Discrepancy-Based Sampling in Deep Active Learning
description: Discrepancy-based active learning selects unlabeled samples that maximize a distributional distance between the labeled and unlabeled sets, aiming to make the labeled pool more representative of the overall data distribution. The core idea is to iteratively query points from regions where the labeled distribution poorly covers the unlabeled data, thus reducing the discrepancy between the two. This requires defining and efficiently computing distances between high-dimensional probability distributions, a non-trivial problem in deep learning settings. Formal measures such as H-divergence are used to quantify this distributional gap and to rank unlabeled instances for annotation. By repeatedly querying the top-scoring samples under such discrepancy measures, the method aligns the labeled set with the full data distribution and can improve DAL performance under limited annotation budgets.

name: Discrepancy-Based Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that select samples by minimizing statistical discrepancies between labeled and unlabeled data or between model predictions. Methods instantiate this idea using distances such as Wasserstein distance, maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), cosine-based measures, H-divergence, and KL divergence to quantify how candidate samples differ from the current training distribution or ensemble predictions. Active learning is framed as a distribution alignment problem, where selected samples are those expected to most reduce these empirical gaps in feature or latent spaces. Several approaches embed data into a latent representation and apply Wasserstein distance, combined with latent space optimization and nearest-neighbor search, to guide sample acquisition. These discrepancy criteria are often integrated with uncertainty or diversity measures in hybrid selection schemes, particularly in medical image analysis settings.

name: Superpixel-Based Region Selection for Deep Active Segmentation
description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that operate at the superpixel level for medical image segmentation. Images are first pre-segmented into superpixels using color- and texture-based methods, and pixel-wise uncertainty is aggregated (e.g., by averaging) to define informativeness scores for each superpixel. Querying then targets compact, coherent regions instead of individual pixels, improving annotation efficiency while preserving spatial consistency. In interactive segmentation settings, acquisition functions such as expected prediction error are used to select the most informative foreground and background superpixels, directing expert effort to regions that most refine segmentation boundaries. These approaches instantiate region-based active learning tailored to dense prediction tasks, integrating uncertainty-based acquisition with structured image representation.

name: Batch-Mode Deep Active Learning and Diversity
description: Batch-mode active learning selects multiple unlabeled instances in each iteration instead of querying a single point, which is especially important for deep models where retraining is computationally expensive. In deep learning scenarios with high-dimensional data, such as images or complex NLP tasks, retraining after a single newly labeled instance often yields negligible performance gains relative to its cost, making larger batches more efficient. This shifts the design objective toward constructing batches that are not only highly informative but also diverse, reducing redundancy so that each queried example contributes distinct information. Batch selection therefore balances informativeness, representativeness, and intra-batch diversity to better exploit limited annotation budgets in deep active learning setups.

name: Batch Construction Strategies in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers how deep active learning methods convert sample scores (e.g., uncertainty or representativeness) into concrete query batches. A common approach is simple top-k selection, where the most informative samples according to a scoring function are chosen at each iteration to control the annotation budget. Several works introduce explicit class-balance constraints on the queried set to counter dataset imbalance, which is especially critical in medical imaging tasks. Other strategies employ hybrid or fusion schemes that combine multiple criteria or multi-round selection to refine the batch, and some frameworks even use reinforcement learning to learn the sampling policy directly. Together, these mechanisms define the batch-level query policy that operationalizes scoring modules within each active learning cycle.

Overall, the focus is on correcting known pathologies of pure informativeness-based querying while preserving its benefits in deep active learning workflows.

name: Informativeness-Based Query Strategies in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers query strategies that rank unlabeled instances by an informativeness score and select those with the highest expected benefit for annotation. Informativeness is formalized as how much a labeled instance is expected to improve the model, for example via expected error reduction, model change, or performance gains on a target metric. In deep active learning, such strategies typically operate on model outputs or internal representations to quantify informativeness through uncertainty measures and representativeness of the data distribution. They often refine or extend basic uncertainty sampling by integrating task-specific criteria or combining multiple metrics, thereby better aligning selection with real performance improvements under limited labeling budgets. A key characteristic is that each instance is scored independently, without explicitly modeling relations among unlabeled samples.

name: BatchBALD for Batch-wise Mutual Information Acquisition
description: BatchBALD generalizes the BALD acquisition function from single-instance to batch active learning by computing the joint mutual information between a batch of unlabeled samples and the model parameters. Instead of scoring each candidate independently, it treats the batch as a joint random variable over inputs and labels, allowing it to explicitly model correlations between queried points. This joint mutual information formulation reduces redundancy among highly uncertain samples and naturally balances uncertainty with diversity within each selected batch. As a result, BatchBALD provides more informative and complementary batches for labeling, improving label efficiency in deep active learning compared to independent BALD or purely uncertainty-based batch selection.

name: Crowdsourcing for Cost-Efficient Active Learning
description: This topic covers the integration of crowdsourcing with active learning to further reduce annotation costs while maintaining model performance. Active learning selects the most informative instances, which are then labeled by non-expert crowd workers, making large-scale annotation more affordable. However, the use of crowds introduces noisy and potentially inconsistent labels, so methods for label quality control, aggregation, and worker reliability estimation become crucial. The combination also motivates cost-aware query selection strategies that account for both informativeness and expected annotation cost and quality. These issues are central when deploying active learning pipelines in realistic, large-scale settings such as NLP tasks.

name: Informativeness Metrics and Sampling in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers the core methodological components of deep active learning: evaluating sample informativeness and designing sampling strategies. Informativeness metrics quantify how valuable it would be to annotate each unlabeled instance, typically in terms of expected model improvement or uncertainty. Sampling strategies use these scores to select a subset of data points to be labeled under a constrained annotation budget. In deep active learning pipelines, especially in medical image analysis, these mechanisms jointly determine how efficiently the system can query data to maximize performance gains per labeled sample. The focus is on integrating such criteria with deep models to guide query selection rather than random or heuristically chosen labeling.

name: Top-k Sampling Strategies in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers the widespread use of top-k sampling to convert informativeness scores into concrete query batches in deep active learning. Unlabeled samples are ranked according to an acquisition function (e.g., uncertainty, entropy, H-divergence, estimated loss), and the k highest-scoring instances are selected for annotation under a given labeling budget. This simple ranking-and-cutoff scheme serves as the de facto standard for batch-mode querying, especially in medical image analysis applications. While effective and easy to implement, it typically ignores additional structural constraints such as diversity, class balance, or redundancy control, relying solely on the informativeness metric to drive label efficiency.

name: Adversarial-Based Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that estimate uncertainty via adversarial robustness, treating the required perturbation strength to cross a decision boundary as a proxy for a sample’s uncertainty. By generating visually imperceptible adversarial examples and measuring how easily an input can be pushed across the model’s decision boundary, these methods rank unlabeled data such that points closer to the boundary (requiring smaller perturbations) are selected as most informative. Selection is typically implemented by ordering unlabeled samples by their adversarial distance and querying labels for the Top-k, directly coupling adversarial example generation with pool-based query strategies. In medical image analysis, such adversarial-based uncertainty is used both to target inherently uncertain, boundary-near cases and to improve model robustness, though its adoption remains limited. The literature also points to future extensions, including federated learning scenarios where adversarially informed uncertainty sampling must be balanced with communication and robustness constraints.

name: Active Domain Adaptation for Medical Imaging
description: This topic covers active domain adaptation in medical image analysis, where models are adapted from a labeled source domain to a shifted, sparsely labeled target domain while selectively querying new labels. By combining domain adaptation with active learning, the approach aims to handle distribution shifts between scanners, institutions, or imaging modalities under a constrained annotation budget. Region-wise and image-wise active domain adaptation strategies determine at what spatial granularity and for which target samples labels should be requested to maximize performance gains per queried annotation. Overall, the focus is on minimizing labeling effort while ensuring robust cross-domain generalization in medical imaging tasks.

name: Deep Active Learning with Weak Annotations
description: This topic studies how deep active learning can leverage weak forms of supervision, such as image-level or bounding-box labels, instead of full pixel-wise masks, to reduce annotation costs. It contrasts traditional region-based active learning, which still demands dense labeling within selected regions, with approaches that deliberately simplify the annotator’s task. In instance segmentation, annotators provide only object class labels and bounding boxes, and the model learns to segment instances without explicit mask supervision. The core idea is to combine query strategies of active learning with weak or partial labels to maintain competitive performance while significantly lowering annotation complexity. This direction is especially emphasized for medical image analysis, where dense annotations are costly and expert time is limited.

name: Representativeness and Density-Based Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers representativeness-based deep active learning, where the goal is to select a subset of unlabeled samples that collectively approximate the full data distribution. Methods are taxonomized into clustering-based, cover-based, discrepancy-based, and density-based approaches, using tools such as set cover, submodular optimization, similarity measures, H-divergence, Wasserstein distance, and MMD to operationalize representativeness. Density-based active learning explicitly estimates data density in feature space and prioritizes high-likelihood samples, often combined with clustering to reduce redundancy and improve diversity. In contrast, cover-based methods seek to geometrically cover the dataset and may over-select outliers in low-budget regimes, making density-based criteria more suitable when annotation budgets are very limited. These ideas are instantiated in deep AL query strategies and in medical imaging workflows, such as selecting representative 2D slices from 3D volumes to minimize annotation while preserving semantic diversity.

name: Initialization of Model and Labeled Pool in Deep Active Learning
description: Deep active learning pipelines typically begin with constructing an initial labeled pool to obtain a reasonably trained starting model before any query strategy is applied. A small random subset of data is selected and annotated to form this seed set, which is then used to train the initial deep model f_θ0 so that uncertainty or acquisition scores are meaningful and not driven by random initialization noise. The size of this initial pool is often tied to the annotation budget or a predefined fraction of the dataset, providing a common and fair starting point for comparing different active learning methods. Random selection is usually controlled via fixed random seeds to ensure experimental reproducibility across runs and methods. This careful initialization stabilizes subsequent active learning dynamics and makes comparisons between query strategies more reliable.

name: Region-Based Query Units in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that query labels at sub-image granularity, using regions, patches, slices, superpixels, or points instead of whole images. By redefining the labeling unit to localized regions, these approaches focus the annotation budget on the most informative parts of medical images, which is especially beneficial for dense prediction tasks such as segmentation, lesion detection, and volumetric analysis. Region-based strategies often sample only a fraction of patches or superpixels within selected images, sometimes in multi-scale setups (e.g., slice- and pixel-level, pixel- and point-level), aligning annotation effort with clinical workflows. Some methods further leverage latent space optimization and nearest-neighbour search to select representative or uncertain slices or regions, integrating region granularity directly into the acquisition function. Overall, region-based deep active learning improves label efficiency by targeting uncertain or complex local structures rather than exhaustively annotating full images or volumes.

name: Active Domain Adaptation in Deep Active Learning
description: Active Domain Adaptation (ADA) integrates deep active learning with domain adaptation by selectively querying labels for target-domain samples to mitigate distribution shift under a limited annotation budget. Methods prioritize target examples that are both uncertain for the current model and representative of the target distribution, aiming to close the gap to fully supervised target training with minimal labels. In medical image analysis, ADA is commonly instantiated at the image-wise level, where entire target images are selected for annotation based on their expected contribution to domain alignment and task performance. Region-wise ADA refines this further by querying labels for sub-image units such as patches or superpixels, which is especially beneficial for dense prediction tasks like segmentation. By operating at different granularities of selection, ADA offers a principled way to allocate labeling effort where it most improves cross-domain generalization.

name: Performance-Based Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers active learning strategies that estimate uncertainty through predicted task performance rather than directly from output probabilities. Methods use surrogate metrics (e.g., loss, Dice score, IoU, temporal output discrepancy, or loss rank) and learnable performance estimators to approximate how well a model would perform on unlabeled samples if they were labeled. These estimated performance scores are then converted into query criteria, typically prioritizing samples predicted to yield low performance as more informative for annotation. This paradigm contrasts with classical probabilistic uncertainty (e.g., entropy or margin) by tightly coupling the acquisition function to task-specific outcome metrics, which is particularly useful in domains like medical image segmentation. The approach enables DAL systems to align sample selection with downstream evaluation objectives even when true labels are unavailable.

name: Mismatch Between Classical Active Learning and Deep Learning Pipelines
description: This topic addresses the fundamental mismatch between traditional active learning assumptions and the requirements of deep learning models. Classic active learning typically operates with very small labeled sets and one-by-one query strategies, which conflicts with deep networks’ need for large labeled datasets and mini-batch training. Traditional AL methods also assume a fixed feature representation and focus on querying in a static feature space, whereas deep learning jointly learns feature representations and classifiers, tightly coupling representation learning and prediction. As a result, naïvely wrapping deep models in conventional AL loops or splitting supervision and querying into separate stages can cause divergence between learning and querying objectives and lead to suboptimal performance. These challenges motivate unified deep active learning frameworks that integrate model training and query selection in a coherent process.

name: Generative Models for Synthetic Querying and Augmentation in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on integrating generative models into deep active learning pipelines to synthesize informative samples and augment limited labeled datasets. GANs and related generative networks are used to create additional training images, especially in medical imaging, to increase diversity, balance class distributions, and enrich the pool between query iterations without proportional labeling cost. Beyond passive augmentation, generative models support membership query synthesis, explicitly generating instances in regions of high model uncertainty or disagreement. Approaches with VAEs and Bayesian data augmentation model the uncertainty of generated data itself, allowing the learner to target contentious areas of the hypothesis space while accounting for the reliability of synthetic samples. Collectively, these methods aim to improve label efficiency and robustness of deep active learners by coupling acquisition strategies with learned generative priors over the input space.

name: Adversarial and Generative Query Synthesis in DAL
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that use adversarial representations and generative models to synthesize or identify highly informative queries. Adversarial perturbation–based approaches such as AdvDeepFool locate samples near decision boundaries, exposing model weaknesses and targeting boundary regions for labeling and data augmentation. Generative Adversarial Active Learning (GAAL) employs GANs to synthesize candidate queries, aiming for samples near the classifier’s decision boundary, though naïve boundary-focused generation can produce semantically meaningless or hard‑to‑label instances. Bayesian Generative Active Deep Learning (BGADL) refines this idea by combining Bayesian acquisition (e.g., BALD), VAE/ACGAN generators, and disagreement-based targeting of regions with high epistemic uncertainty, so that synthetic data are as informative as pool‑selected points. Overall, these methods integrate robustness and generative modeling into the active learning loop to improve label efficiency while carefully managing the trade‑off between informativeness and human labelability.

name: Adversarial Attack–Based Query Strategies in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers Deep Active Learning methods that use adversarial attacks, particularly DeepFool, to drive sample selection. These approaches estimate each unlabeled sample’s distance to the decision boundary via the minimal adversarial perturbation required to change the model’s prediction, and interpret small perturbations as high uncertainty. Query strategies such as DFAL and AdvDeepFool select points with the smallest perturbations, effectively operationalizing boundary-based uncertainty sampling in a deep setting. Variants may use other attacks like the Basic Iterative Method, but share the core idea of ranking samples by adversarial distance. While these methods can speed up convergence of deep models like CNNs, they may reduce batch diversity because they concentrate queries near the current decision boundary rather than covering the broader data distribution.

name: Bayesian Deep Active Learning (DBAL)
description: Bayesian Deep Active Learning uses Bayesian treatments of deep neural networks to obtain principled uncertainty estimates for query selection. Instead of relying on overconfident softmax scores, it employs approximate Bayesian inference methods such as Monte Carlo dropout, deep ensembles, or Bayesian convolutional neural networks to approximate posterior distributions over model parameters. These posterior-based estimates emphasize epistemic uncertainty, allowing acquisition functions like BALD and related mutual-information criteria to target regions where the model lacks knowledge. By providing more reliable uncertainty for high-dimensional data and mini-batch querying, DBAL addresses key challenges in combining deep learning with uncertainty-driven active learning strategies.

description: This topic concerns heuristic deep active learning (HDAL) frameworks that couple convolutional neural networks with active learning query strategies for biometric and related recognition tasks. Building on CEAL-style architectures, these methods integrate deep feature learning and query model training in a single loop, using the same deep network as both feature extractor and classifier. Informative samples are selected for annotation via model uncertainty or heuristic criteria, enabling high recognition accuracy under limited labeling budgets. The approaches demonstrate the applicability of deep active learning beyond generic image classification to domains such as face recognition and verification code recognition, where annotation costs and domain-specific variations make efficient sampling particularly valuable.

name: Taxonomy of Deep Active Learning Sampling Strategies
description: This topic covers a structured taxonomy of sampling strategies in deep active learning, with particular emphasis on medical imaging applications. It extends beyond traditional informativeness-based querying to explicitly categorize approaches such as diversity sampling, class-balanced sampling, hybrid sampling, and learnable sampling. Diversity sampling aims to reduce redundancy by selecting varied samples that better cover the data manifold, while class-balanced sampling counters skewed label distributions by enforcing or approximating class balance during query selection. Hybrid strategies combine multiple criteria (e.g., uncertainty and diversity) to improve selection robustness, and learnable strategies employ neural networks to adaptively learn selection policies from data. Together, this taxonomy provides a comprehensive framework for designing, analyzing, and comparing deep active learning methods under realistic labeling constraints.

name: Data Stream Dynamics in Online Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on how assumptions about data stream dynamics affect the design and performance of online active learning methods. It distinguishes stationary streams, where the data-generating distribution remains stable, from drifting streams, where gradual or abrupt concept drift changes informativeness scales, may invalidate existing models, and requires additional labeled data. It also considers evolving streams, where new concepts or classes can appear, imposing stronger requirements on model updating and query selection strategies. Correctly identifying whether a stream is stationary, drifting, or evolving is crucial for choosing appropriate acquisition strategies, scheduling model replacement or adaptation, and maintaining the effectiveness of active learning over time.

name: Deep Active Learning for Medical Image Reconstruction
description: This topic covers the use of deep active learning to improve and accelerate medical image reconstruction, particularly for modalities with long acquisition times such as MRI and CT. Instead of passively using all available measurements, active learning is used to selectively choose which observations, slices, or measurement configurations to acquire or label so as to maximally benefit the reconstruction network. By doing so, these methods aim to reduce the number of measurements while maintaining or improving reconstruction quality, thereby shortening scan times and patient waiting periods. MRI reconstruction, including applications like knee imaging with datasets such as fastMRI, is highlighted as a key clinical use case in which deep active learning helps train networks on undersampled data and prioritize the most informative samples for model updates. Overall, the focus is on integrating acquisition decisions and labeling effort into the learning loop to optimize reconstruction performance under resource constraints.

name: Online Model Updating in Stream-based Active Learning
description: This topic concerns active learning in data streams where the model is updated online as queried instances are labeled. A subset of incoming stream instances is selected for annotation, and their labels are immediately incorporated into the classifier, enabling real-time adaptation of the decision boundary. The setting typically assumes stationary data streams so that incremental updates remain valid over long periods without expensive retraining from scratch. Immediate feedback from queried labels allows the active learner to continuously refine its selection strategy and explore new regions of the input space using the most up-to-date model state. This online updating mechanism is a core component of stream-based active learning systems that must operate under latency and budget constraints while tracking evolving data distributions.

name: Active Learning in Stationary and Drifting Data Streams
description: This topic addresses how active learning operates in data stream settings under both stationary and non-stationary (drifting) distributions. In stationary streams, the relative stability of the generative process allows stream-based active learners to focus on selective labeling and incremental model refinement without extensive drift detection mechanisms. In contrast, non-stationary streams require adaptive models that can track distributional shifts and update decision boundaries or parameters while querying labels efficiently over time. Work in this area predominantly studies online classification models that incrementally update with newly acquired labeled examples, aiming to maintain predictive performance under both stable and drifting concepts while respecting a limited annotation budget.

name: Cost-Sensitive and Proactive Annotation in Active Learning
description: This topic covers cost-sensitive active learning strategies that explicitly incorporate annotation cost into the query selection process. Methods prioritize instances based on a utility-per-cost or return-on-investment (ROI) criterion, sometimes with per-instance cost caps or combined utility–cost ranking, to reduce total labeling expenditure under a fixed budget. In more realistic multi-annotator settings, proactive learning jointly selects both the instance and the oracle, modeling annotator expertise, reliability, refusal, and error rates. For crowd-based and sequence labeling tasks, these approaches may collect multiple labels per instance and apply consolidation frameworks that account for noise–cost trade-offs. In Deep Active Learning, the same principles guide which high-impact examples to query and from which annotators, making better use of limited annotation budgets when training deep models.

name: Online Active Learning for Data Streams
description: This topic covers active learning in streaming or online settings, where instances arrive sequentially and the learner must decide on-the-fly whether to query their labels. The survey emphasizes query strategies tailored to data streams, focusing on selecting the most informative points under constraints such as non-stationarity, label budget, and real-time processing. Online classification is identified as the dominant task, with methods using either single classifiers or ensembles to handle stationary, drifting, and evolving distributions while actively querying labels. In contrast, online active regression—selectively querying continuous-valued targets in streams—is far less explored, creating a notable research gap. The topic also includes online semi-supervised formulations that combine labeled and unlabeled streaming data, highlighting how active querying is adapted across different predictive paradigms in the streaming context.

name: Data Expansion Techniques in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers strategies to expand the effective labeled dataset in deep active learning, reconciling the small labeled set assumption of active learning with deep models’ need for large training corpora. Instead of training solely on explicitly annotated samples, these approaches exploit the abundant unlabeled pool through data augmentation, semi-supervised learning, pseudo-labeling, and generative methods. The objective is to amplify the utility of each queried label, improving model performance without proportionally increasing annotation cost. Within the DeepAL setting, such techniques are tightly coupled with the querying process, aiming to mitigate label scarcity while maintaining label quality and label-efficiency.

name: Cost-Effective Deep Active Learning with Pseudo-Labels (CEAL)
description: This topic covers the CEAL framework, which integrates uncertainty-based active learning with pseudo-labeling to reduce annotation costs in deep active learning. At each iteration, a CNN evaluates unlabeled samples, forwarding the most uncertain instances to a human oracle while automatically assigning pseudo-labels to high-confidence predictions. Both oracle-labeled and pseudo-labeled data are then used jointly to fine-tune the network in a closed-loop process, effectively enlarging the labeled training set without proportional increases in manual labeling. The approach explicitly trades off label quality and annotation cost, aiming to limit noise from incorrect pseudo-labels while exploiting confident predictions. CEAL has been particularly influential in deep active learning for image classification, including medical image analysis, where labeling is expensive.

name: Online Active Learning for Non-Stationary Data Streams
description: This topic covers online active learning in streaming settings where unlabeled instances arrive sequentially and cannot be stored in a pool for batch selection. At each time step, the learner must immediately decide whether to query the label of the current instance, operating under labeling cost and global budget constraints. The setting is particularly important for high-velocity, real-time applications and evolving environments, where models must be updated continuously as new labeled examples become available. Methods must also cope with various forms of distribution shift and concept drift, often coupling query policies with drift detectors to maintain performance over time. For deep active learning, these ideas translate into designing streaming query strategies and budget-aware policies that can efficiently update deep models under non-stationary conditions.

name: Practical Challenges in Stream-based Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on the practical obstacles encountered when deploying stream-based active learning systems in real-world settings. Methods must operate in real time on continuously arriving, potentially unbounded data streams while querying labels under strict annotation budgets and latency constraints. Key challenges include the high cost and limited availability of labels, noisy or delayed annotations, and the need to coordinate effectively with human annotators. Furthermore, systems must cope with changing data distributions and application-specific requirements in domains such as healthcare, autonomous driving, and industrial monitoring. These constraints directly affect the design of active querying strategies, the management of labeling costs, and the overall robustness of deployed active learning pipelines.

name: Imbalance-Aware Query Strategies in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep and traditional active learning methods that explicitly address class imbalance during data selection and annotation. Instead of passively inheriting skewed label distributions, the acquisition function is modified to prioritize underrepresented or rare classes, both in NLP and in medical image analysis. Such class-balance aware querying helps construct more balanced training sets and improves performance on minority classes, including rare but clinically critical conditions. The perspective also reframes active learning as a tool for dataset curation, not just model training, by steering annotation budgets toward difficult or infrequent phenomena. Across applications, these strategies integrate imbalance considerations directly into the selection criterion for new labels, rather than relying solely on post-hoc reweighting or resampling.

name: Pool-Based Deep Active Learning Framework
description: This topic covers the standard pool-based active learning (AL) setting, where a fixed, unlabeled pool serves as the source from which informative instances are iteratively queried for annotation. The core loop starts from an initial labeled set and an unlabeled pool, trains a model, applies a query strategy over the pool to select one or more samples, obtains labels from an oracle (e.g., domain experts such as medical doctors), and updates the labeled set and model until a stopping criterion or annotation budget is reached. Pool-based AL contrasts with stream-based and membership-query settings and is the dominant framework in deep active learning, especially in data-rich domains like NLP, medical imaging, and image classification. The framework often assumes a static pool and uses batch or single-instance querying governed by a parameter k, balancing label efficiency against the computational cost of retraining deep models. Within DAL, this scenario defines the experimental setup in which acquisition functions, uncertainty measures, and diversity strategies are evaluated under realistic labeling-budget constraints.

name: Iterative Pool-based Deep Active Learning Workflow
description: This topic covers the standard pool-based deep active learning workflow, in which a deep model is initialized or pre-trained on an initial labeled set and then iteratively improved by querying labels for selected unlabeled samples. At each iteration, the current model is used to score an unlabeled pool via an acquisition function or query strategy, and the most informative instances are selected and sent to an oracle for labeling. The labeled and unlabeled sets are updated accordingly, and the deep model is retrained on the expanded labeled set, often using the model’s feature extraction capabilities to guide selection. The process continues until a labeling budget is exhausted or predefined stopping criteria or performance targets are met. The framework is typically decomposed into query strategy design and deep model training, with additional attention to generalization and stopping strategies, and while commonly applied to classification, it naturally extends to other domains such as image segmentation.

name: Multiple-Inference Uncertainty Estimation in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that estimate uncertainty by performing multiple stochastic inferences per sample and aggregating the resulting predictions. Techniques such as Monte Carlo dropout, model ensembles, and test-time/data augmentation introduce variability either in model parameters or in the input to generate diverse outputs. Disagreement or dispersion among these outputs is then quantified using metrics like entropy, margin-based scores, BALD, variance, variance ratio, KL divergence, and gradient-based measures. These richer uncertainty signals are used as acquisition functions to select informative samples for annotation, particularly in safety-critical medical imaging applications where over-confident but wrong predictions must be mitigated. The topic highlights how multi-inference schemes systematically organize and enhance uncertainty-based querying strategies in deep active learning pipelines.

name: MC Dropout Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers the use of Monte Carlo (MC) dropout to obtain multiple stochastic inferences from deep models for uncertainty-based active learning. By keeping dropout active at test time and running many forward passes, practitioners estimate epistemic uncertainty via measures such as variance, entropy, and BALD, and use these scores to select informative samples. In medical image analysis, this mechanism is exploited to prioritize expensive annotations for tasks like skin lesion analysis, brain cell type classification, and endoscopy imaging. Methods such as DBAL further refine this idea by combining MC dropout with entropy-based acquisition, averaging predictive probabilities across passes before computing entropy to better capture uncertainty. Overall, MC dropout serves as a practical Bayesian-style tool that integrates naturally with deep active learning pipelines where robust uncertainty estimates are critical.

description: This topic covers entropy-based acquisition functions for deep active learning, where predictive entropy over class probabilities is used to quantify model uncertainty. description: This topic covers uncertainty-based query strategies used as standard baselines in deep active learning. Methods such as Least Confidence, Margin, Entropy, BALD, DBAL, VarRatio, MeanSTD, and their dropout-based variants select samples from an unlabeled pool by exploiting the model’s predictive distributions to target highly uncertain or informative instances. Random sampling serves as a non-informed reference to quantify the benefit of uncertainty-driven selection. The strategies are evaluated under varying annotation budgets (e.g., 1000–6000 labeled samples) using metrics such as mean accuracy, standard deviation, AUBC, and final accuracy across multiple datasets, including medical image analysis and MNIST. Performance gaps to full-data training highlight issues like redundancy and distribution shift, motivating exploration of more sophisticated DAL methods.

name: BALD Information-Theoretic Acquisition in Deep Active Learning
description: Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement (BALD) defines an information-theoretic acquisition function that selects unlabeled samples by maximizing the mutual information between model predictions and model parameters. In deep active learning, BALD targets epistemic uncertainty, distinguishing it from simpler predictive entropy or margin-based measures, and is often approximated via Bayesian deep models such as MC Dropout. This acquisition function explicitly links query selection to expected reduction in posterior parameter uncertainty, formalized as α_BALD(x, M) for each candidate input. BALD is a core uncertainty-based strategy and is frequently contrasted with other information-theoretic measures like entropy and margin in DAL surveys. In batch-mode DAL, BALD is often naively extended by repeatedly applying the one-by-one acquisition rule to select the top-K highest-scoring samples, effectively summing per-sample mutual information terms while ignoring interactions within the batch.

name: Deep Active Learning for Visual and Medical Image Classification
description: This topic covers the application of deep active learning to image classification problems, with a strong emphasis on medical image analysis. Convolutional neural networks are trained in a pool-based AL setting, where the most informative unlabeled images (e.g., specific tissue types such as stroma, tumors, mucosa, and other structures) are selectively queried for expert annotation to reduce labeling costs while maintaining diagnostic performance. Similar strategies are applied to standard visual recognition benchmarks (e.g., MNIST, CIFAR-10, CACD, Caltech-256, and face/video datasets) to study how different query criteria impact accuracy versus the number of labeled samples. In biomedical and related domains such as plankton classification and automatic cell counting, uncertainty- or informativeness-based sampling is used to prioritize expensive expert labels, highlighting the value of DAL in high-stakes, annotation-intensive settings.

name: Ensemble-Based Uncertainty and Diversity Sampling
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that use ensembles to drive query selection via both uncertainty and diversity criteria. Ensemble variance, measured as disagreement across model predictions, is used as a robust uncertainty estimator to identify highly informative unlabeled instances. Diversity is promoted through cover-based criteria and similarity measures (e.g., cosine similarity) to avoid redundant queries and better explore the input space. These ideas are applied in both pool-based and streaming/online scenarios, where ensemble variance is treated as a global criterion over time rather than on isolated data chunks. Multi-round or cyclical selection strategies iteratively refine the labeled set by combining these uncertainty and diversity signals across successive active learning iterations.

name: Motivation and Scope of Deep Active Learning
description: Deep Active Learning (DAL) combines deep neural networks’ representation learning capabilities with active learning’s selective querying to reduce annotation costs in data-hungry settings. It is motivated by the limitations of classic active learning on high-dimensional data and the high labeling demands of modern over-parameterized deep models. By leveraging deep learning to handle complex, high-dimensional inputs and active learning to prioritize the most informative samples, DAL aims to achieve strong performance with substantially fewer labeled examples. This paradigm is particularly attractive in domains where labels are expensive and require domain expertise, and it has been applied to tasks such as named entity recognition, semantic parsing, object detection, image segmentation, and counting. The field has also led to unified DAL frameworks that systematize these ideas and support practical deployment.

name: Consistency Regularization in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers how consistency regularization is integrated into deep active learning to better exploit large pools of unlabeled data. By enforcing that model predictions remain stable under input perturbations or weak/strong augmentations, consistency regularization provides an unsupervised or semi-supervised loss that improves robustness and reduces overfitting. Within an AL–SSL framework, confidently and consistently predicted unlabeled samples are used as additional training signals, while active learning focuses expert labeling on more ambiguous or uncertain instances. Pseudo-labeling is often combined with consistency losses, where confident predictions on weakly augmented images are treated as labels and the model is trained to match them across stronger augmentations. This synergy increases label efficiency, which is especially valuable in domains like medical imaging where annotations are costly.

name: Deep Active Learning for Noisy Label Correction
description: This topic covers deep active learning strategies that explicitly target correction of noisy annotations in medical imaging datasets, particularly chest X-rays. Methods such as active label cleaning rank samples based on estimated label reliability, correctness, and labeling difficulty to prioritize instances with potentially incorrect or uncertain labels. By integrating noise detection and relabeling into the query strategy, these approaches jointly improve label quality and model performance under a limited expert annotation budget. Compared to random selection, they achieve better performance with fewer additional labels by focusing annotation efforts on the most suspect or impactful samples.

name: Deep Active Learning for Annotation Cost Reduction
description: This topic focuses on using active learning to alleviate the labeling bottleneck created by expensive and time‑consuming annotation, especially for large deep learning models in domains such as NLP, medical imaging, and remote sensing. Deep active learning frameworks iteratively select the most informative unlabeled samples from a pool or stream, query an oracle (typically a human expert), and retrain the model, aiming to match or approach the performance of fully supervised training with far fewer labels. Query strategies are designed to balance labeling cost and model quality by exploiting differences in the value of individual samples for updating the model. In medical image analysis and segmentation, where expert annotations by radiologists or pathologists are particularly scarce and costly, DAL is emphasized as a core component of practical deep learning workflows. Across domains, the central objective is to maximize performance gains per labeled instance, thereby reducing annotation budgets while maintaining or improving model accuracy.

name: Deep Active Learning for Interactive Segmentation
description: This topic covers the integration of deep active learning with interactive segmentation in medical image analysis, where clinicians iteratively refine model-generated segmentations. Instead of allowing completely free placement of user annotations (clicks, scribbles, bounding boxes), active learning is used to propose the most informative pixels or regions for interaction, tailoring the acquisition strategy to dense, pixel-level labeling tasks. By focusing expert input on high-uncertainty or high-impact areas, the active learning loop reduces annotation difficulty and cost while improving adaptation to domain shifts and unseen regions of interest. The model thus becomes a proactive assistant during annotation, suggesting and updating segmentations based on expert corrections within a DAL-driven feedback cycle.

name: Integrating Deep Active Learning with Label-Efficient Paradigms
description: This topic covers frameworks that combine deep active learning with other label-efficient learning paradigms to further reduce annotation requirements. Methods integrate active querying with semi-supervised and self-supervised learning to exploit large pools of unlabeled data while selectively labeling only the most informative samples. Other approaches leverage transfer learning and domain adaptation to reuse knowledge from related domains, and region-based annotation schemes that query subregions (e.g., image patches) instead of full instances to save labeling effort. Generative models are also used for data augmentation or synthetic sample generation, complementing active selection. Overall, these synergistic designs target data-scarce, high-cost annotation settings such as medical imaging and NLP, where combining acquisition strategies with alternative supervision forms is particularly beneficial.

name: Uncertainty-Based Query Strategies in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on deep active learning strategies that rank unlabeled instances by how uncertain a model is about their predicted labels. Core approaches use single-model uncertainty scores such as least confidence, margin, and entropy, often computed from the softmax output of deep networks. More advanced DAL methods derive uncertainty from gradients, adversarial perturbations probing decision boundaries, or performance-estimation surrogates (e.g., Dice-based quality predictors for segmentation) to approximate per-sample expected improvement. In both pool-based and stream-based settings, these uncertainty scores drive which samples are queried under a limited annotation budget, but can introduce sampling bias if the most uncertain points are not representative of the overall data distribution. Consequently, recent work increasingly combines uncertainty with diversity criteria to form hybrid selection strategies that better balance informativeness and coverage.

name: Hybrid Uncertainty–Diversity Query Strategies in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers hybrid query strategies that jointly exploit uncertainty and diversity criteria in deep active learning. Instead of relying solely on uncertainty, which can lead to many redundant queries around the same decision boundary region, these methods explicitly encourage selection of informative yet non-redundant samples. They often implement a joint acquisition function or a staged pipeline, for example first filtering candidates by high uncertainty and then subselecting a diverse subset, or the reverse. By balancing informativeness with representativeness of the unlabeled data distribution, these hybrid strategies mitigate sampling bias from pure uncertainty sampling and avoid wasting labeling budget on low-information but diverse points. Overall, they reflect a broader move from single-criterion to multi-criterion query design in DeepAL.

name: Pseudo-Labeling in Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers the integration of pseudo-labeling into deep active learning pipelines, especially for medical image analysis. In these approaches, the model assigns labels to unlabeled samples when its predictions are sufficiently confident, expanding the effective labeled set without additional expert effort. Active learning then prioritizes truly ambiguous or diverse cases for manual annotation, while pseudo-labeled data provide broader coverage of the unlabeled pool. This AL–SSL synergy aims to reduce annotation cost, mitigate label scarcity, and improve representation learning by jointly exploiting queried labels and reliably pseudo-labeled examples. Across implementations, pseudo-labeling is embedded directly within the active learning loop, iteratively refining the model as both human and pseudo labels accumulate.

name: Deep Active Learning with Semi- and Self-Supervision
description: This topic focuses on integrating deep active learning with semi-supervised and self-supervised learning to better exploit the large pool of unlabeled medical images between query rounds. In these frameworks, active learning selects the most informative samples for expert annotation, while semi-supervised methods such as pseudo-labeling and consistency regularization leverage the remaining unlabeled data to further improve performance. Self-supervised learning is used to pretrain or refine representations from unlabeled images, which can enhance the effectiveness of subsequent active selection. The combined approaches aim to maximize label efficiency and reduce the burden of expert annotation, particularly in medical image segmentation and analysis tasks where labels are expensive and scarce.

name: Integrating Semi-/Self-Supervised Learning with Deep Active Learning
description: This topic covers hybrid methods that combine deep active learning with semi-supervised or self-supervised learning to better exploit large pools or streams of unlabeled data. Beyond querying labels for a small subset of instances, these approaches use pseudo-labels, self-training, EM-based estimation, and consistency regularization so that unlabeled examples can contribute to representation learning and model refinement between active learning queries. In pool-based DAL, jointly training on actively labeled data and model-generated labels alters the informativeness of remaining unlabeled samples and thus interacts with the acquisition strategy. In stream-based settings, incoming unlabeled instances may first be used for semi-supervised updates, while only a carefully chosen subset is queried, effectively viewing active learning as a special case of semi-supervised learning where the system controls which labels to acquire. Overall, these hybrids aim to increase data efficiency and generalization across AL cycles, especially under tight annotation budgets.

name: Uncertainty and Gradient-Based Query Strategies in DAL
description: Deep active learning often selects queries by estimating how informative unlabeled instances are for a neural model. Uncertainty-based methods use model outputs, such as entropy, least-confidence, or margin scores, to prioritize examples where a deep classifier or Transformer is least certain. Extensions consider local prediction instability, measuring how outputs change under nearest-neighbor replacements, adversarial perturbations, or data augmentation to detect points near decision boundaries. Gradient-based approaches, such as Expected Gradient Length (EGL), instead rank instances by the expected norm of the loss gradient with respect to model parameters or embeddings, approximating how strongly each label would update the network. These families of strategies are widely applied in deep NLP tasks, including sequence labeling, speech recognition, and text classification, and form a core component of modern DAL systems.

name: Deep Learning Paradigms in Active Learning Loops
description: Deep active learning integrates neural architectures and modern training paradigms directly into the query–train loop. Pretrained language models and other deep encoders provide rich representations that can improve both uncertainty estimation and diversity-aware selection in high-dimensional spaces. Transfer learning and semi-supervised techniques, such as fine-tuning, consistency training, or pseudo-labeling, allow DAL to exploit large pools of unlabeled data alongside scarce annotations. The interaction between query strategies and deep training dynamics—such as overfitting, representation drift, and batch acquisition effects—becomes a key design consideration. Surveyed work analyzes how these advanced learning techniques change the effectiveness, stability, and sample efficiency of active learning in NLP and related domains.
