name: Error-Driven and Ambiguity-Based Querying
description: Error-driven strategies directly target instances that are currently mispredicted, ambiguous, or high-loss for the task model. A common approach is to train auxiliary models that predict instance-wise loss, correctness, or the need for expert querying, effectively turning performance prediction into a query utility. Inspired by data maps, some methods focus on examples with intermediate average correctness over training, which are neither trivial nor hopeless. In machine translation, error-prone instances can be identified via round-trip consistency checks (back-translation) or quality estimation models, which approximate human judgments. These predictors allow deep active learning systems to prioritize examples where correcting the model is likely to yield tangible performance gains.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

name: Representativeness via Density and Discrepancy
description: Representativeness-based active learning aims to select labeled examples that reflect the broader unlabeled data distribution rather than rare outliers. Density-based methods prefer instances lying in dense regions, using proxies such as n-gram statistics, word-count features, or similarity-based density in an embedding space, often approximated with k-nearest neighbor similarity for scalability. Complementary discriminative approaches emphasize coverage of novel or underrepresented patterns by selecting unlabeled instances that differ most from the already labeled set. These can rely on feature-based signals like unseen n-grams or out-of-vocabulary terms, similarity scores that penalize proximity to labeled data, or classifiers/adversarial models trained to distinguish labeled from unlabeled points. In domain adaptation and distribution shift settings, domain separators play a similar role by steering selection toward regions where the labeled coverage is weakest.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

name: Batch Diversity via Greedy and Clustering Methods
description: Batch-mode active learning must avoid redundant queries by enforcing diversity among selected instances. Greedy iterative selection builds a batch step by step, each time choosing items that are both high-utility and dissimilar from those already chosen, and can approximate principled criteria such as coresets or determinantal point processes. Clustering-based approaches instead partition the unlabeled pool and pick one or more representatives from different clusters to ensure coverage of distinct regions of the space. Similarity for both greedy and clustering methods can be defined using raw input features, learned representations, model-based similarity scores, gradient information, or embeddings derived from masked language model surprisal. These strategies help deep active learning scale to large pools while avoiding wasted annotation effort on near-duplicate examples.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

name: Hybrid Query Strategies for Deep Active Learning
description: Hybrid query strategies combine informativeness with representativeness and diversity to better balance exploration and exploitation. Static hybrids merge multiple criteria—such as uncertainty and density—into a single score using fixed weighted sums or multiplicative combinations that remain constant throughout training. Integrated hybrids more tightly fuse signals, for example by performing uncertainty-weighted clustering, encoding both uncertainty and diversity in gradient-based similarity, or using determinantal point processes that factorize item quality and mutual diversity in a unified probabilistic model. Multi-step hybrids apply criteria in sequence, such as filtering by uncertainty and then clustering, or choosing the most uncertain sample within each cluster to ensure coverage. Dynamic hybrids go further by changing the mixture of strategies over time, as in methods like DUAL and GraDUAL that shift from density-focused selection in early stages to uncertainty-focused selection once the model becomes more reliable.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

local_topics.title: Static hybrid combinations of query criteria

name: Active Learning for Structured Prediction
description: Structured prediction tasks in NLP, such as sequence labeling and parsing, produce interdependent outputs that complicate query design and annotation workflows. A key decision is whether to query full output structures or only selected sub-structures, which directly affects how utilities, uncertainties, and labeling costs are defined. For full-structure querying, uncertainty-based utilities like entropy must operate over exponentially large output spaces, and are approximated using dynamic-programming formulations for sequence or tree entropy, or via top-k approximations that treat a k-best list as a proxy for the full distribution. Disagreement-based strategies similarly face challenges: exact whole-structure agreement is often too strict, so partial-disagreement metrics and task-specific scores (e.g., F1 over sequence labels) are employed, along with length normalization to mitigate biases toward longer instances. More generally, utilities can be constructed by aggregating token- or factor-level scores—through sums, averages, frequency-weighted sums, or focusing on the least probable sub-structures—enabling practical deep active learning in complex structured output spaces.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

name: Structured query granularity and grouped annotation
description: This topic studies querying at coarser structural units rather than at the smallest token level in deep active learning pipelines. Methods select sub-sequences, dependency edges, neighborhood pools, or whole phrases and sentences to better match how annotators read and reason about text. Coarser granularity reduces context switching and cognitive load, since annotators label meaningful chunks instead of scattered isolated items. It also mitigates the missed-class effect, where rare or difficult classes may be overlooked when sampling too locally. Grouped querying strategies, such as first selecting uncertain sentences and then uncertain tokens within them or querying spatially or semantically neighboring instances, further streamline the annotation workflow.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

name: Interactive annotation and computer-assisted labeling
description: This topic focuses on tighter interaction between models and annotators to reduce labeling cost in deep active learning. Computer-assisted annotation provides pre-annotations or top-k predictions that humans correct, turning labeling into a post-editing task rather than annotation from scratch. Interactive systems continuously update their predictions in response to user corrections, as in interactive machine translation where each keystroke or corrected segment triggers model adaptation. Active learning is integrated to select the most informative segments for display, maximizing the impact of human effort. Crowdsourcing can complement these techniques by distributing pre-annotated or interactively chosen instances across many non-expert annotators.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

name: Efficient active learning with proxy models
description: This topic addresses reducing wait time and computational cost in deep active learning loops while preserving query quality. Query-time speedups include sub-sampling large unlabeled pools, caching invariant computations, and approximating densities or nearest neighbors with fast k-NN-style methods. On the training side, practitioners often favor full retraining over naive incremental warm-starting for neural models, but may use lightweight surrogate models during querying and reserve heavier models for final training. Distilled or proxy networks approximate larger models and can perform uncertainty estimation and selection much faster, periodically synchronized via knowledge distillation and sometimes augmented with pseudo-labeling or sub-sampling. Additional efficiencies come from batch-mode active learning and parallel architectures that decouple and continuously run annotation, training, and scoring processes.

local_topics.title: Reducing wait time in active learning loops

name: Transfer and pretraining strategies for active learning
description: This topic investigates how transfer learning and pretraining can reduce annotation requirements in deep active learning. Large pre-trained language models provide strong initial representations, so active learning starts from a high-capacity encoder that needs fewer task-specific labels to reach good performance. Continual and transductive training adapt models to new domains or specific unlabeled target sets during the active learning process, allowing query strategies and models to exploit information from related domains. Cross-domain and cross-lingual setups leverage labeled or unlabeled data from other distributions or languages to guide selection in low-resource targets. Meta-learning and related techniques can also initialize models or query policies themselves so they adapt quickly from the small, actively acquired datasets.

name: Weak supervision and data augmentation in AL
description: This topic explores combining weak supervision and data augmentation with deep active learning to reduce reliance on expensive human labels. Weak supervision sources such as heuristics, programmatic labeling rules, gazetteers, execution results, or structural signals provide noisy but cheap labels that complement human annotations. Active learning policies can choose which instances should be sent to humans versus weak labelers, or which examples are most useful for refining labeling rules in semantic parsing, entity recognition, and other structured prediction tasks. Data augmentation further expands training sets via techniques like back-translation, mixup for sequence labeling, and phrase-to-sentence transformations for machine translation. Query synthesis extends this idea by generating new synthetic instances for annotation rather than sampling from an existing pool, which has shown particular promise for simpler text classification scenarios.

name: Datasets for Active Learning Stopping Criteria
description: The choice of dataset used to compute stopping metrics in active learning strongly influences the stability and reliability of stopping decisions. Using the same training pool can bias or destabilize estimates, motivating the use of a separate monitoring set. Because many stopping criteria rely on model outputs rather than gold labels, this auxiliary dataset can be unlabeled and relatively large to reduce variance. However, larger monitoring sets increase evaluation time and system latency, which is especially critical for deep models retrained frequently during active learning. Designing stopping datasets therefore requires balancing statistical stability, computational cost, and responsiveness to model changes.

name: Integrating Curriculum Learning with Active Learning
description: Curriculum learning can be combined with active learning to control not only which examples are queried, but also the order in which they are presented to the model. Instead of selecting purely by uncertainty or informativeness, the system can enforce a pedagogical progression from simpler to more complex instances. This integration aims to stabilize training dynamics, improve sample efficiency, and mitigate catastrophic forgetting in deep models. Designing such curricula requires criteria that jointly capture example difficulty, informativeness, and diversity over the active learning loop. The resulting frameworks can adapt the curriculum as the model improves, continually reshaping both query selection and presentation order.

name: System Efficiency and Deployment Constraints in Active Learning
description: Practical deployment of active learning hinges on computational efficiency and low annotator wait time. Deep models must often be retrained or at least incrementally updated after each batch of queried labels, turning training cost and inference speed into critical bottlenecks. Long delays between query selection and availability of updated predictions can degrade annotator experience and make interactive labeling workflows infeasible. Real-world deployments are typically non-repeatable, so choices of model architecture, query strategy, and hyperparameters must be robust under tight resource constraints. Addressing these efficiency and latency challenges is essential for moving active learning from simulated studies into reliable industrial systems.

name: Active Learning for Complex NLP Tasks and Cross-Domain Transfer
description: Most active learning research focuses on relatively simple classification tasks, leaving complex NLP problems such as text generation, natural language inference, and question answering underexplored. These tasks involve structured, high-dimensional outputs and nuanced inputs, which complicate both uncertainty estimation and annotation workflows. At the same time, many query strategies and heuristics developed in domains like computer vision may be transferable to these NLP settings with appropriate adaptation. Leveraging cross-domain insights can help design query criteria, acquisition functions, and model architectures better suited for complex language tasks. Systematic studies are needed to understand how methods from other modalities perform and must be modified when applied to sequence-to-sequence and reasoning-heavy NLP problems.

local_topics.title: Applying AL to complex NLP tasks

name: Active Learning with Rich and Auxiliary Supervision
description: Active learning can target more than just primary task labels, extending to auxiliary supervision such as feature annotations, rationales, explanations, evaluations, or symbolic rules. By selectively querying informative instances for these richer annotation types, systems can build interpretable models, improve sample efficiency, or learn better intermediate representations. For deep models, annotated rationales and explanations can guide attention mechanisms or constrain latent spaces, while rule-like supervision can regularize decision boundaries. Designing acquisition functions that account for the cost and utility of different supervision types is a central challenge. This broader view positions active learning as a general framework for interactive supervision, not just label acquisition.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning for natural language processing

name: Compact Informative Training Sets in Active Learning
description: In deep active learning, training sets should be kept as small as possible while still being highly informative. Rather than sampling pixels uniformly, the labeled set is constructed to concentrate on discriminative regions, especially around class boundaries. This requirement is crucial in very high spatial or spectral resolution settings, where the feature space is large and complex but labeled data are scarce. Designing compact, boundary-focused training sets motivates many active learning criteria that seek samples with maximal expected impact on the decision function.

local_topics.title: Requirements for compact, informative training sets

name: Pool-Based Active Learning Setup and Iterative Loop
description: Pool-based active learning assumes an initial labeled set L = {(x_i, y_i)} with class labels y_i ∈ {1,…,N} and feature vectors x_i in a d-dimensional space ℝ^d, together with a large unlabeled pool U = {x_j}. Since |U| ≫ |L|, the learner repeatedly selects a small subset of candidates from U to be labeled by an oracle. After each annotation step, the classifier is retrained or updated using the expanded labeled set. This defines an iterative cycle of sample selection, labeling, and model refinement that is standard in deep active learning and remote sensing applications. The notation and loop structure provide the foundation on which specific query strategies and models are built.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

name: Uncertainty-Based Query Scoring with SVM Margins
description: In uncertainty-driven deep active learning, each unlabeled candidate in the pool is scored by a heuristic that estimates its potential usefulness for improving the model. For SVM-based learners, the decision function f(x) expressed in terms of kernels, dual coefficients, and support vectors provides a natural confidence measure: the absolute value |f(x)| reflects the distance to the separating hyperplane, with smaller margins indicating higher uncertainty. Candidates are ranked by such scores so that the algorithm queries labels for the most uncertain or informative samples, explicitly targeting regions where the model currently has low confidence. This process can be interpreted as directly aiming to reduce classification uncertainty and sharpen decision boundaries. Margin-based strategies, often referred to as margin sampling, most ambiguous, binary-level uncertainty, or SVMSIMPLE, all implement this same core idea. Visualizations with toy multi-class examples further illustrate how objectives such as Margin Sampling (MS) and MCLU identify areas of maximal ambiguity near SVM decision hyperplanes.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

name: Committee-Based Active Learning via Bagging and Multi-View Features
description: Committee-based active learning constructs a set of diverse classifiers whose disagreements guide sample selection. One way to build such a committee is bagging, where multiple training sets are produced by sampling with replacement from the labeled data and each bootstrap set trains a separate model, ensuring diversity because each classifier only sees part of the labeled pool. For high-dimensional remote sensing data, an additional source of diversity comes from multi-view learning, where the original feature space is partitioned into disjoint subsets and an independent classifier is trained on each view. In hyperspectral imagery, these views can be derived from block-diagonal structures in the covariance matrix, with each block defining a feature subset. The committee’s multiple predictions for each unlabeled pixel enable disagreement- or entropy-based query heuristics, which underpin selection rules such as those used in advanced multi-view disagreement (AMD) strategies.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

name: Uncertainty–diversity heuristic families in active learning
description: This topic covers families of pool-based active learning heuristics that combine uncertainty and diversity, with a focus on margin-based methods such as Breaking Ties (BT), MCLU, and its MCLU-ABD extension. Multiclass uncertainty is quantified from the classifier’s output scores or margins, while diversity is enforced through similarity measures (e.g., kernel or angle-based) so that selected samples both challenge the current decision boundary and are not redundant. A trade-off parameter balances these two components in a single objective, generalizing classic margin and Maximal Angled Orthant (MAO) ideas to arbitrary feature spaces. The comparison of heuristic families emphasizes that no single strategy is universally best; performance depends on data geometry, class overlap, and model capacity. Information-theoretic criteria such as KL-divergence can be more informative but often require training many models per iteration, highlighting a practical trade-off between selection quality and computational cost that also matters for deep active learning.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

name: Probability calibration for active learning
description: This topic addresses how margin-based classifiers are converted into probabilistic predictors so they can be used with probability-driven active learning criteria. Methods such as Platt scaling fit a sigmoid to raw decision scores, yielding approximate per-class posterior probabilities even for models like SVMs that are not inherently probabilistic. Although these calibrated quantities are not exact Bayesian posteriors, they provide a practical basis for heuristics like entropy sampling, Breaking Ties, or expected error reduction. The same calibration principles extend to deep networks, where calibrated probabilities or logits are crucial for reliable uncertainty estimates in deep active learning. Proper calibration therefore acts as a bridge between deterministic decision functions and probabilistic acquisition functions.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

name: Experimental protocols for active learning evaluation
description: This topic describes how to design and report experimental protocols for evaluating active learning algorithms over time. Labeled examples are added to the training set in fixed-size batches across multiple iterations, with separate configurations for different models or datasets to ensure fair comparison. Protocols specify the total number of iterations, batch sizes, stopping criteria, and any committee settings for query-by-committee methods, as well as how much of the available labeled data is used for initialization. Performance is typically tracked as a learning curve of accuracy (or another metric) versus labeling effort, allowing different heuristics to be compared on data efficiency. Clear, reproducible protocols are essential for assessing and benchmarking deep active learning strategies in realistic scenarios.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

name: Margin-Based Uncertainty Sampling with SVMs
description: Margin-based heuristics such as Margin Sampling (MS) and related criteria like MCLU select points according to their distance to the SVM decision boundary, avoiding the need for fragile probability calibration. Empirical results show that these methods outperform probability-driven strategies like nEQB and BT when training data are scarce, because posterior estimates (e.g., via Platt scaling) are unreliable in the low-sample regime. By relying directly on the decision function values, margin-based active learning achieves more stable and informative query rankings. This insight transfers naturally to deep active learning, where margin-like scores derived from logits or softmax outputs are often more robust than fully calibrated probabilities early in training.

name: Active Learning with LDA and Class Statistics
description: In Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), active sampling can substantially improve the estimation of class means and covariances, leading to a better discriminant subspace. Random sampling tends to include more outliers and mislabeled or uninformative points, which can distort Fisher’s ratio and yield a suboptimal linear combination of features. By selectively querying informative pixels, heuristic-driven active learning refines both per-class statistics and the resulting decision boundaries, improving classification accuracy. However, when uncertainty estimates depend heavily on poorly estimated statistics—either in LDA or in bagging-based committees built from small bags—confidence scores and disagreements can be misleading. Designing active learning strategies that acknowledge the unreliability of early-stage class statistics is therefore crucial, including in deep generative or feature-space models that mimic LDA-like assumptions.

name: Diversity and Structure-Aware Sampling for Hyperspectral Data
description: For hyperspectral image classification, augmenting uncertainty sampling with diversity criteria such as spectral diversity (e.g., MCLU-ABD) helps reduce redundancy among queried pixels. These methods typically provide small but consistent gains in accuracy with limited additional computational cost, and rarely degrade performance relative to uncertainty-only selection. Structure-aware strategies, including kernel k-means within MCLU-ECBD or distance-to-support-vector heuristics like cSV, explicitly model relationships in feature space to better capture complex data manifolds. Multi-view approaches such as AMD and ECBD-ABD further exploit complementary structure in different spectral representations, making them particularly well suited to high-dimensional hyperspectral data. Together, these ideas inform deep active learning designs that combine uncertainty, diversity, and manifold structure to construct more representative labeled sets.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

name: Advantages of Active Sampling over Random Labeling
description: In supervised remote sensing image classification, active learning heuristics consistently outperform random pixel selection once sufficient iterations of querying and retraining have occurred. For a fixed labeling budget, strategies that target informative or representative pixels achieve higher overall accuracy than random sampling, demonstrating the value of informed query policies. Using metrics such as overall accuracy across a range of labeled-set sizes provides a clear quantitative basis for comparing active selection methods like MCLU, MCLU-ABD, and standard SVM training against random baselines. This evaluation paradigm is directly applicable to deep active learning, where gains are likewise measured in terms of accuracy or related metrics per unit of annotation effort.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

name: Active Learning in Semi-Supervised Remote Sensing
description: This topic studies how to actively select unlabeled pixels to improve semi-supervised classification of remote sensing imagery. The goal is to query the most informative samples so that limited labeling effort yields maximal improvement in classifier performance. It focuses on the interaction between labeled and unlabeled data, where active learning policies guide which pixels receive ground-truth annotations. The setting is particularly relevant when using deep or other complex models that benefit from carefully curated labels rather than large, randomly sampled training sets.

sources.article_title: A survey of active learning algorithms for supervised remote sensing image classification

name: Spatial and Context-Aware Active Learning Heuristics
description: This topic addresses active learning strategies that explicitly exploit spatial structure and contextual information in images. Instead of treating each pixel or sample independently, query heuristics are adapted based on neighborhood relations, textures, and positional context. The aim is to design selection criteria that reason directly over spatial patterns and local image structure, not just over spectral or feature vectors. Such spatially adaptive heuristics can yield more informative queries and faster learning in spatially correlated data, such as remote sensing imagery. These ideas are particularly powerful when combined with deep models that already encode context but still rely on informative labeled points.

name: Active Learning for Cross-Domain Model Adaptation
description: This topic explores how active learning can support adaptation of classifiers across different domains, scenes, or sensor conditions. A model trained in a source domain is transferred to a target domain, and the learner selectively queries labels on target samples to correct for domain shift. The objective is to reduce annotation cost in the target domain while still achieving high performance, making model deployment more scalable. This is especially relevant for deep models in remote sensing, where data distributions can vary drastically across geographic regions or acquisition setups.

name: Online Active Learning with Moving Sensors
description: This topic focuses on active learning in scenarios where moving sensors acquire data sequentially, such as along satellite or aerial trajectories. In this setting, batch-based querying is unnecessary or inefficient, and the learner must decide in near real time whether and where to request labels. Emphasis is placed on very low-computation heuristics, such as breaking ties or simple KL-based criteria, that can be updated rapidly as new data arrive. The challenge is to balance computational constraints with informativeness of queries, particularly when deep models are used in resource-limited or onboard environments.

name: Noise-Robust Uncertainty-Based Active Learning
description: This topic examines the behavior and limitations of uncertainty-driven active learning heuristics under high noise conditions, such as in SAR imagery. Since these methods rely on model uncertainty at the sample level, strong noise can corrupt probability estimates and lead to misleading query choices. The core challenge is to design selection strategies whose uncertainty measures remain reliable in the presence of noise or to augment them with robustness mechanisms. Developing noise-aware or denoising-integrated active learning schemes is an open research area, particularly for deep models trained on low-SNR remote sensing data.

name: Expert Annotation Challenges in Medical Imaging
description: Medical image annotation often requires pathologists and radiologists to inspect large, high-resolution images across multiple magnifications, making the process slow and cognitively demanding. Crowdsourcing is generally unsuitable for such data because accurate labels depend on specialized clinical expertise and are constrained by strict privacy requirements. As a result, annotation must rely on well-compensated experts who may spend tens of minutes per case for tasks like slide assessment or tumor segmentation. To reduce bias, multiple annotators or repeated labeling rounds are frequently used, introducing intra- and inter-observer variability that further increases cost and complexity. These factors create a strong motivation for deep active learning methods that minimize the number of expert-labeled samples needed.

name: Active Learning Problem Settings and Data Access
description: Canonical active learning is typically categorized into membership query synthesis, stream-based selective sampling, and pool-based active learning, each defined by different assumptions on how unlabeled data are accessed. In membership query synthesis, the learner can generate synthetic instances to be labeled by an oracle. In stream-based settings, samples arrive sequentially and must be accepted or discarded for labeling on the fly, often under memory or compute constraints such as on edge devices. In pool-based settings, a large static pool of unlabeled data is available, and the learner iteratively selects the most informative subset for labeling. These settings provide the foundational framework for formulating and comparing deep active learning strategies in medical image analysis.

name: Informativeness-Based Sample Selection in Deep AL
description: Deep active learning typically relies on an informativeness function that scores each unlabeled sample according to its expected utility for improving the current model. Given a model state and an unlabeled pool, this function produces a value for each candidate, capturing notions such as uncertainty, diversity, or expected loss reduction. A sampling strategy then uses these scores to choose a batch of highly informative samples to query from the oracle. By iteratively retraining on newly labeled batches, this process concentrates expert effort on cases that most effectively enhance model performance under limited annotation budgets.

name: Batch-Mode Pool-Based Deep Active Learning and Gaps
description: In deep active learning, batch-mode selection is commonly adopted because retraining large neural networks after each individual annotation is computationally impractical and a single labeled example rarely yields a noticeable performance gain. Most medical imaging applications therefore assume a pool-based setting, where the learner repeatedly selects batches of informative samples from a large unlabeled dataset. Existing surveys have documented this batch-mode, pool-based paradigm but have struggled to keep pace with the rapid methodological progress in deep active learning. Important open issues include limited synthesis of how active learning interacts with other label-efficient techniques, such as semi-supervised or self-supervised learning, and a lack of systematic evaluations on diverse medical imaging benchmarks. These gaps highlight the need for more comprehensive and experimentally grounded surveys of batch-mode deep active learning in clinical domains.

description: Prior surveys have examined active learning from multiple perspectives, including its role as a label-efficient paradigm in medical image analysis and its application to tasks such as segmentation under imperfect annotations. General active learning surveys in machine learning and computer vision have provided foundational introductions and taxonomies of model-driven and data-driven query strategies. More recent overviews address deep active learning in computer vision and natural language processing, offering systematic comparisons and re-implementations of influential methods. Together, these works establish the broader context and methodological baselines against which specialized surveys on deep active learning for medical imaging are positioned.

name: Dataset Partitions, Budgets, and Oracle Updates
description: Deep active learning typically maintains three dataset partitions at each iteration: an unlabeled pool, a queried subset, and a labeled training set. A sampling strategy ranks unlabeled examples by an informativeness score computed from the current model, and an annotation budget constrains how many of these can be selected per round. The queried subset is sent to a human oracle (e.g., medical experts) to obtain ground-truth labels. Newly labeled samples are added to the labeled set and removed from the unlabeled pool, ensuring that no example is queried twice. This formalization supports both multi-round (iterative) and one-shot active learning schemes by making the budget, query set, and update rules explicit.

name: Supervised Deep Model Training in AL Loops
description: In deep active learning, the model is typically retrained or fine-tuned in a fully supervised manner after each annotation round. The current labeled set defines an empirical risk minimization objective, such as minimizing a task-specific loss over all labeled input–label pairs. Updated parameters are then used to recompute uncertainty or other acquisition scores on the remaining unlabeled pool. The quality and stability of this supervised training step critically affect subsequent query decisions and overall sample efficiency.

name: Prediction-Probability Uncertainty Metrics for Querying
description: Classical uncertainty-based query strategies rely on the model’s predictive probability distribution over classes. Common metrics include Least Confidence, which uses one minus the maximum predicted class probability, and Entropy, which aggregates uncertainty across all classes. Margin sampling measures the difference between the top-1 and top-2 predicted probabilities, while mean variance of class probabilities captures dispersion in the prediction vector. These scores quantify how peaked or diffuse the prediction distribution is and serve as basic acquisition functions for selecting informative unlabeled examples in deep active learning.

name: Hybrid and Learnable Deep AL Sampling
description: Hybrid sampling strategies combine multiple acquisition signals, such as uncertainty, representativeness, and class balance, into a single query rule. This fusion aims to avoid the weaknesses of any single heuristic and better cover the data distribution while still focusing on ambiguous samples. Learnable sampling approaches go further by parameterizing the query policy itself, often with neural networks or reinforcement learning. These policies are optimized end-to-end to maximize downstream performance or label efficiency, adapting the acquisition behavior to task- and dataset-specific characteristics.

name: Annotation-Efficient and Cost-Aware Medical DAL
description: Annotation-efficient strategies in medical deep active learning explicitly model the high cost of expert labeling. Techniques such as slice-based annotation for volumetric scans and one-shot or minimal-example labeling seek to reduce the amount of clinician time per training signal. Cost models may weight samples by expected annotation effort, integrating label cost directly into the acquisition function. By aligning query strategies with realistic clinical workflows and constraints, cost-aware DAL methods strive to maximize performance gains per unit of expert effort.

name: Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning for Medical Imaging
description: Uncertainty estimation is central to deep active learning in medical imaging, where data are highly variable and expert annotations are costly. By quantifying predictive uncertainty, models can identify ambiguous cases, artifacts, or out-of-distribution patterns that are most informative to label. Conceptually, uncertainty is often decomposed into aleatoric (data-intrinsic noise) and epistemic (model ignorance) components, but in practice most methods operate on overall predictive uncertainty. Aleatoric uncertainty captures irreducible factors such as motion or metal artifacts, while epistemic uncertainty can be reduced by acquiring more labeled data. Active learning strategies typically target samples with high predictive (often mainly epistemic) uncertainty to improve generalization and safety in clinical deployment.

name: Taxonomy of Uncertainty-Based Deep Active Learning Methods
description: Uncertainty-based deep active learning methods can be organized into a taxonomy that clarifies the diverse ways uncertainty is quantified and exploited. Multiple inference approaches estimate uncertainty from repeated stochastic predictions, such as Monte Carlo dropout, model ensembles, and data or model disagreement. Gradient-based methods use gradient norms, Fisher Information, or influence functions to link parameter sensitivity to sample informativeness. Performance-estimation approaches build surrogate or learned predictors of downstream performance to guide querying. Uncertainty-aware models such as evidential networks or mixture density networks output richer uncertainty estimates, while adversarial-based methods probe the model with adversarial examples or adversarial training to expose fragile or uncertain regions of the input space.

name: Committee and Disagreement-Based Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
description: Committee and disagreement-based strategies estimate uncertainty by comparing predictions from multiple models, input views, or feature-space prototypes. Classical Query-by-Committee schemes train several segmentation networks or heterogeneous models and select samples with maximal disagreement, quantified via prediction variance, KL divergence, or vote entropy. Model-ensemble approaches, including independent ensembles, snapshot ensembles, and Stein variational ensembles, trade computational cost for stronger uncertainty estimates and often improve performance in medical image segmentation. Data-disagreement methods avoid many models by perturbing inputs or viewpoints and measuring predictive inconsistency across augmentations, enabling fine-grained image- and region-level selection. Extensions leverage class activation maps and geometric distances (e.g., Dice, Hausdorff) or prototype-based feature interpolations to capture spatial and representation-level disagreement, further refining which unlabeled cases introduce genuinely novel information.

name: Gradient-Based Deep Active Learning for Medical Imaging
description: Gradient-based deep active learning methods quantify sample informativeness through the sensitivity of model parameters to each training example. Early work applies expected gradient length in medical image classification, selecting fundus images whose gradients have large expected norms, thereby prioritizing samples likely to induce substantial model updates. More advanced approaches project segmentation loss gradients onto a learned data manifold, typically obtained from a variational autoencoder trained on MRI scans, to focus on realistic, clinically plausible directions of change. By ranking unlabeled images according to manifold-aligned gradient components, these methods emphasize cases that most effectively reshape the decision boundary within the true data distribution. Such techniques have demonstrated improved efficiency in annotating complex tasks like brain tumor and whole-brain MRI segmentation.

name: Fisher Information and Gradient Embedding Approximations
description: This topic covers approximations that make Fisher information (FI)-based active learning feasible in deep neural networks. Instead of computing the full parameter-wise FI matrix, layer-wise and last-layer approximations use averaged or final-layer gradients to drastically reduce computational and memory costs. These approximations connect naturally to gradient-embedding methods such as BADGE, where last-layer gradients encode both uncertainty and diversity. Such FI-inspired gradient embeddings have been successfully applied to dense prediction tasks like medical image segmentation, preserving much of FI’s informativeness while avoiding full quadratic complexity. The result is a practical class of FI-based acquisition functions scalable to modern deep architectures.

name: Surrogate Performance Metrics from Prediction Consistency
description: This topic focuses on surrogate metrics that approximate true task performance by exploiting prediction agreement and output discrepancies. Examples include computing intersection over union (IoU) across multiple Monte Carlo dropout predictions and correlating it with true Dice scores, as well as averaging Dice between intermediate and final outputs under deep supervision. Cyclic Output Discrepancy (COD) extends this idea temporally by measuring the norm of changes in network outputs between successive annotation or training rounds. Under limited training, sample loss can be bounded by COD, making it a useful proxy for both loss and evaluation metrics. These label-free surrogates enable active learning systems to prioritize samples likely to have high true error without requiring ground-truth annotations for scoring.

sources.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

name: Learnable Loss Ranking with Diversity and Disagreement
description: This topic addresses active learning strategies that learn to predict or rank sample losses and combine them with diversity and disagreement signals. Instead of regressing exact loss values, ranking-based approaches train models to order samples by relative uncertainty, which better aligns with the needs of acquisition functions. For example, RankCGAN-inspired modules replace loss regressors in LLAL-style frameworks, directly optimizing for correct uncertainty ordering and improving selection quality. In practical applications such as COVID-19 diagnosis and polyp detection under federated active learning, predicted loss is fused with model disagreement and diversity measures to select informative yet diverse samples across distributed clients. This composite design improves coverage of the data space while still targeting highly uncertain examples.

sources.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

name: Probabilistic and Evidential Deep Models for Active Learning
description: This topic covers deep models that inherently represent predictive uncertainty through probabilistic or evidential outputs. Examples include variational autoencoders and probabilistic U-Nets, which produce full predictive distributions instead of point estimates, reducing overconfidence and providing calibrated uncertainty with a single forward pass. Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) further models uncertainty by treating network outputs as evidence parameters of distributions such as Dirichlet or decomposed Beta distributions in multi-label settings, enabling class-wise aleatoric uncertainty estimation. These evidential representations can be exploited in multi-label medical image classification and in active domain adaptation, where samples with high data and distributional uncertainty are prioritized. Overall, probabilistic and evidential models form a principled backbone for uncertainty-driven deep active learning, especially under distribution shift.

sources.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

name: Influence Function-Based Sample Selection in Deep AL
description: This topic discusses the use of influence functions to guide sample selection in deep active learning. Influence functions estimate how upweighting a candidate sample would perturb model parameters and, consequently, the loss on a validation or labeled set, using gradients and the inverse Hessian of the empirical risk. For unlabeled data, the missing ground-truth is handled by approximating the required gradients with respect to an expected empirical loss. This yields an acquisition criterion grounded in classical robust statistics but adapted to deep models, particularly in medical imaging. By directly targeting samples expected to most improve performance when labeled, influence-function-based selection provides a theoretically motivated alternative to purely heuristic uncertainty measures.

name: Adversarial and Disagreement-Based Uncertainty Sampling
description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that quantify uncertainty via adversarial perturbations and classifier disagreement. Adversarial examples are crafted by maximizing the Kullback–Leibler divergence between predictions on original and perturbed inputs under a bounded norm, so samples with large induced distributional shifts are deemed most informative. In parallel, multi-classifier schemes alternate between updating classifier heads to increase prediction disagreement and updating a shared feature extractor to reduce this discrepancy, thereby exposing ambiguous regions of the input space. Samples that maximize adversarial sensitivity or inter-classifier disagreement are prioritized for annotation, encouraging exploration near complex decision boundaries. These strategies exploit adversarial objectives both to probe model robustness and to define richer uncertainty metrics than raw confidence alone.

name: Bias from Pure Uncertainty-Based Querying
description: This topic analyzes how uncertainty-only query strategies can introduce dataset bias in deep active learning. Because such methods preferentially select samples near the current decision boundary, the labeled set can become heavily skewed toward this narrow region in feature space. This distribution misalignment between queried and overall data may harm generalization and lead to overfitting boundary noise or outliers. Moreover, focusing solely on model confidence neglects visual content and inter-sample relationships, which can exacerbate outlier selection. These limitations motivate informativeness measures that integrate uncertainty with diversity, representativeness, and structural relationships among samples.

name: Feature-Space Representativeness and ROI Verification
description: This topic addresses how feature representations and task design shape deep active learning for medical images. High-dimensional medical images encode complex anatomical and pathological cues, so representativeness-based querying is typically performed in a learned feature space that compresses yet preserves clinically relevant structure. In connectomics and segmentation settings, prediction masks are first generated and the annotation task is reformulated as verifying the correctness of regions of interest rather than drawing full labels from scratch. By concentrating human effort on potentially erroneous or uncertain ROIs, these methods substantially reduce annotation cost while maintaining accuracy. Together, feature-space reasoning and verification-style labeling enable more efficient and clinically practical active learning workflows.

name: Clustering-Based Deep Active Learning for Segmentation
description: This topic focuses on clustering-driven query strategies for deep active learning in medical image segmentation. A basic framework clusters image embeddings and selects cluster centroids for annotation, exploiting the natural grouping of similar images in feature space to obtain diverse, representative labeled sets. Building on this, coarse-to-fine clustering schemes first form broad groups of patches and then refine clusters inside each group to pinpoint especially informative nuclei or tissue regions. More advanced designs learn separate feature spaces for segmentation masks and raw images using variational autoencoders, enabling mask-level clustering of object shapes followed by image-level clustering within mask groups. Such hierarchical and multi-stream clustering better captures both structural and appearance-based similarities, guiding selection of diverse and uncertain regions or images for labeling.

name: Cover-Based and Submodular Representativeness in Active Learning
description: Cover-based active learning formalizes representativeness as a covering problem in feature space, where selected samples act as centers that should cover the remaining data. Set cover enforces complete coverage but can lead to large effective radii and outlier selection, while maximum cover relaxes this constraint to prioritize covering as much of the data as possible with fewer, more central points. Early segmentation-focused methods such as SA first query highly uncertain samples and then greedily add points that maximize a continuous maximum-cover objective defined via cosine similarities. Medical imaging extensions modify feature extraction, similarity functions, and clustering strategies (e.g., RA, ProbCover, self-supervised features, SIFT-based templates) but still rely on cover-style objectives to balance representativeness and diversity. These objectives are naturally modeled as monotone submodular set functions, enabling efficient greedy algorithms with near-optimality guarantees for selecting informative and well-distributed samples.

name: Distribution Discrepancy Measures for Deep Active Learning
description: Discrepancy-based active learning methods quantify the distance between labeled and unlabeled distributions to guide sample selection, often using similarity measures such as average cosine similarity between feature embeddings. Graph-based approaches, including GCN variants, model relationships among samples and query unlabeled nodes that are weakly connected to the labeled set, while prototype-based methods construct class or feature prototypes and select samples far from these prototypes. Optimal transport formulations minimize Wasserstein distance between labeled and unlabeled sets, sometimes using mixed-integer programming or continuous candidate optimization in feature space to obtain globally diverse, well-spread labeled subsets. Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) offers a kernel-based integral probability metric to compare distributions via their mean embeddings, and is widely used in active domain adaptation to pick target samples that are both representative and diverse. These techniques fit into broader taxonomies of discrepancy measures, where Wasserstein and MMD belong to the family of integral probability metrics, with MMD also linked to H-divergence–style perspectives.

sources.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

name: Adversarial Latent-Space Discrepancy for Active Learning
description: Adversarial discrepancy-based active learning, exemplified by VAAL-style methods, learns a shared latent representation via a VAE and trains a discriminator to distinguish labeled from unlabeled samples, querying those that appear most unlabeled in latent space. Multimodal extensions reconstruct multiple medical image modalities from a single latent code to enforce cross-modal consistency in tasks like brain tumor segmentation and chest X-ray classification. Other variants soften or replace the adversarial signal, for example by injecting prediction uncertainty, combining VAE and task-network features, or adding auxiliary discriminators that distinguish real from reconstructed features so that selected samples are both uncertain and representative. Hybrids further augment the discriminator input with learning-loss predictions or other supervision signals, enriching the criteria used to prioritize unlabeled samples. Collectively, these methods leverage learned latent discrepancies rather than explicit distance metrics to drive deep active learning across diverse vision and medical imaging tasks.

sources.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

name: Density-Based Deep Active Learning Methods
description: Density-based deep active learning estimates the data distribution in feature space and favors samples that are both representative and novel. In medical image segmentation, InfoVAE can be used to model densities over labeled and unlabeled MRI scans, replacing the KL divergence with an MMD regularizer and using the encoder’s posterior as a density metric. Samples that have high density in the unlabeled pool but low density relative to the labeled set are prioritized, balancing coverage of common patterns with exploration of underrepresented regions. Other variants operate either on fixed feature representations or in an end-to-end fashion, jointly learning embeddings and cluster assignments through a learnable k-means module. Compared with NP-hard coverage-based selection, density estimation provides a more computationally tractable way to exploit dataset structure for querying informative batches.

name: Diversity Sampling Strategies in Deep Active Learning
description: Diversity sampling in deep active learning aims to select batches that cover many distinct regions of the data space so that the labeling budget is not wasted on redundant examples. Core strategies include clustering, farthest-first traversal, and determinantal point processes, which are often combined with uncertainty or other informativeness scores. In medical imaging, simple random partitioning of the unlabeled pool into stochastic batches, followed by batch-level uncertainty scoring, has been shown to act as an effective diversity mechanism under extremely low annotation budgets. More principled methods formulate batch selection using Fisher-information-based semidefinite programs or greedy approximations that maximize information gain while controlling redundancy. Hashing and locality-sensitive bucketing approaches further scale diversity sampling by compressing images into compact codes and drawing queries uniformly across hash buckets. Empirically, such diversity-aware strategies can also mitigate class imbalance, as demonstrated in imbalanced COVID-19 image classification tasks where heterogeneous batches improve minority-class coverage.

name: Imbalance-Aware Strategies in Deep Active Learning
description: Imbalance-aware deep active learning methods explicitly steer querying toward minority or rare classes to counter long-tailed data distributions. Approaches include tail-aware sampling using deep generative models (e.g., VAEs with copula-based tail probability estimation) to prioritize samples from low-density regions that likely correspond to minority classes. Other strategies use simple classifier-based rules, such as triggering annotation when the predicted minority-class probability exceeds a fixed threshold, or estimating per-sample error probabilities via Bayesian decompositions over VAE features to guide selection. Optimization-based batch selection further balances uncertainty-driven sampling with targeted inclusion of confident minority-class examples to maintain class balance over time. In dense prediction tasks like medical image segmentation, region- or patch-level active learning can be made class-balanced by biasing region selection toward areas containing small or rare anatomical structures, ensuring that limited annotation effort covers critical but underrepresented regions.

sources.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

name: Hybrid and Metric-Fusion Querying in Deep Active Learning
description: Hybrid deep active learning methods combine multiple informativeness criteria—such as uncertainty, representativeness, and diversity—rather than relying on a single metric. A common design is multi-round or staged sampling, where one metric first filters a candidate subset and a second refines the final query batch, enabling coarse-to-fine selection. Many strategies explicitly couple representativeness with uncertainty, for example by enforcing diversity among highly uncertain points or dynamically shifting labeling budget from typical, representative data toward high-uncertainty refinement as the model improves. Metric-fusion approaches instead aggregate several scores into a single composite value, or integrate multiple rankings, to produce a unified query priority. Adaptive, ranked batch-mode methods extend this idea by updating how metrics are weighted or combined across rounds, better capturing evolving notions of informativeness during training, especially in data-intensive domains like medical image analysis.

sources.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

name: Reinforcement and Meta-Learned Query Policies
description: Sample selection in deep active learning can be cast as a reinforcement learning problem where a neural selector acts as an agent interacting with a dataset environment. The agent repeatedly chooses a subset of samples for annotation and receives rewards reflecting their impact on downstream model performance. Actor-critic architectures and probabilistic policy networks trained with policy-gradient methods such as REINFORCE are used to learn these query policies end-to-end. Beyond standard RL, few-shot and meta-learning formulations train selectors that generalize across tasks or datasets, enabling rapid adaptation of sampling strategies with limited labeled data. Together, these approaches replace hand-crafted query heuristics with data-driven neural policies optimized directly for performance gains.

sources.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

name: Hybrid Semi-Supervised Deep Active Learning
description: Deep active learning pipelines can be made more data-efficient by jointly exploiting both labeled and unlabeled samples instead of leaving most of the unlabeled pool idle. Hybrid methods combine active learning with semi-supervised learning, using consistency-based regularization techniques such as MeanTeacher, VAT, and related variants to learn from unlabeled images. Pseudo-labels generated by deep models are further refined, for example with dense conditional random fields, to enforce spatial and appearance consistency in segmentation tasks. In medical image analysis, these hybrids have been applied to problems like chest X-ray classification and other radiological tasks, often outperforming pure active learning or pure semi-supervised baselines. This perspective reframes the unlabeled pool as a training asset, not just a reservoir of query candidates.

sources.article_title: A comprehensive survey on deep active learning and its applications in medical image analysis

name: Uncertainty and Curriculum-Based Sample Selection
description: Deep active learning for medical imaging often relies on uncertainty and difficulty-aware criteria to decide which samples to annotate or pseudo-label. Techniques such as Monte Carlo dropout estimate prediction uncertainty via multiple stochastic forward passes, guiding selection of images for expert annotation versus automatic pseudo-labeling. Curriculum-based strategies explicitly categorize samples into hard and easy cases, always querying labels for hard examples while treating easy ones more flexibly. Training loss on easy samples is then used as a proxy for label reliability: low-loss examples are kept as trustworthy pseudo-labels, while high-loss ones are treated as noisy and discarded. These mechanisms jointly tailor the annotation effort to the most informative and reliable data points, improving model performance under limited labeling budgets.

name: Uncertainty Estimation and Acquisition in DAL
description: This topic covers how deep active learning methods quantify and exploit predictive uncertainty to select informative samples. It includes single-model, single-pass strategies that use measures such as entropy, margin, least confidence, Best-versus-Second-Best (BvSB), and probability of misclassification to rank unlabeled data. Multiple-inference approaches, including MC Dropout, model ensembles, and committee-based disagreement (e.g., BALD, variance across predictions), approximate predictive distributions to better capture epistemic uncertainty. The topic also encompasses gradient-based uncertainty (e.g., Fisher Information, influence functions) and performance-estimation-based measures that predict loss or segmentation quality as surrogates for uncertainty. Together, these techniques provide a taxonomy of acquisition functions for estimating and leveraging epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty in deep active learning, particularly for medical imaging tasks.

name: Diversity and Hybrid Uncertainty–Diversity Criteria
description: This topic focuses on acquisition strategies that emphasize diversity and coverage of the data manifold, often beyond simple distance-based measures. Contextual and coverage-based criteria aim to select sets of samples that collectively span different semantic regions and appearance patterns in feature space, which is especially important in complex medical images. Methods in this category treat acquisition as a set-level optimization problem, favoring batches that improve global coverage rather than only picking individually uncertain points. Hybrid fusion strategies further combine uncertainty signals (e.g., entropy, MC Dropout variance, model disagreement) with diversity or clustering-based distances into unified scoring functions. These composite approaches seek to balance informativeness and representativeness, improving label efficiency and robustness of deep active learners.

name: Consistency-Based Semi-Supervised Active Learning
description: This topic addresses active learning methods that exploit consistency regularization to measure sample informativeness within semi-supervised frameworks. Unlabeled images are passed through the model multiple times with stochastic perturbations, such as data augmentation or dropout, and a consistency loss is computed based on the variance or disagreement among the predictions. Samples that exhibit low consistency (high output variance) are treated as more informative and prioritized for annotation. At the same time, high-consistency unlabeled data can be leveraged for training via consistency regularization, improving feature learning without labels. The joint use of consistency for both semi-supervised training and acquisition leads to more sample-efficient and stable deep active learning pipelines.

name: Adversarial Training and Querying in DAL
description: This topic covers active learning methods that integrate adversarial robustness concepts into both training and querying. Some approaches generate adversarial examples around current decision boundaries and use their difficulty, measured via metrics like KL divergence or Bhattacharyya distance, to prioritize queries. Others combine adversarial training with classical uncertainty or margin-based selection, encouraging the model to focus on boundary and hard-to-classify cases that better expose its weaknesses. These strategies aim to simultaneously enhance model robustness and label efficiency, particularly in safety-critical medical imaging scenarios. By aligning adversarial perturbations with active selection, they explicitly target samples that are both informative and robustness-critical.

name: Task-Specific and Radiomic Selection Metrics
description: This topic examines domain- and task-specific criteria used as acquisition signals in deep active learning for medical imaging. For segmentation and localization, methods may exploit performance proxies such as Dice score, IoU, Hausdorff distance, or temporal output discrepancy estimated on unlabeled data. Other approaches use radiomic descriptors, deep saliency features, saliency maps, or higher-order statistics like kurtosis to characterize lesion and organ appearance. These medically informed features allow the active learner to focus queries on anatomically or clinically critical errors rather than only on generic predictive uncertainty. By aligning selection metrics with clinical objectives and imaging characteristics, such strategies better adapt deep active learning to real-world medical workflows.

name: Hybrid Multi-Round Acquisition Strategies
description: Hybrid strategies in deep active learning combine multiple acquisition criteria, such as uncertainty, representativeness, consistency, and pseudo-label reliability, either within a round or across successive rounds. Methods may allocate equal quotas to different criteria or adaptively change the mixture over time based on the model’s state. This multi-round hybridization aims to mitigate the weaknesses of any single criterion while exploiting their complementary strengths. By iteratively alternating or blending strategies, the acquisition process can better track evolving decision boundaries and data coverage. Consistency-based components and pseudo-label quality often play a role in these pipelines, further stabilizing selection in noisy, label-scarce regimes.

name: Semi-Supervised and Self-Supervised Guided Querying
description: This topic covers integrating semi-supervised and self-supervised learning signals directly into the deep active learning loop. Pseudo-labeling extends supervision to unlabeled data between acquisition steps, and the resulting pseudo-label confidence or stability can be used as a selection score, often via Top-k rules. Self-supervised learning (SSL) contributes additional signals, such as the loss of a pretext task, where higher loss indicates harder or underrepresented samples that may merit annotation. These methods aim to exploit the full unlabeled pool, simultaneously improving the representation quality and guiding which samples to query. By unifying SSL losses, pseudo-label quality, and consistency metrics, they reduce annotation requirements while preserving or improving downstream performance.

name: Uncertainty and Disagreement-Based Acquisition
description: Uncertainty-driven deep active learning can rely on both single-model heuristics and multi-inference disagreement metrics. Single-model approaches compute scores from output probabilities, such as Best-versus-Second-Best margins or distances of predicted probabilities to decision thresholds, providing lightweight measures of ambiguity without ensemble overhead. Multi-inference methods evaluate each sample multiple times, using techniques like stochastic forward passes, test-time augmentation, or Monte Carlo dropout, and then quantify disagreement via entropy, variance, or cross-entropy between predictions. Samples with the greatest disagreement or highest heuristic uncertainty are prioritized for labeling, as they are expected to yield the largest information gain. This family of methods forms a core baseline for many deep active learning pipelines.

name: Diversity and Structure-Aware Sample Selection
description: Diversity- and representation-based strategies select samples that are dissimilar from the labeled set to improve coverage of the feature space. Cosine similarity between feature embeddings is commonly used to measure angular distance; samples with low similarity to labeled examples are favored to promote exploration of underrepresented regions. Structure-aware extensions build graphs over image or feature representations and incorporate domain cues such as saliency maps, which highlight diagnostically important regions. Graph-based algorithms then perform Top-k selection of the most informative nodes, balancing local saliency with global structural relationships. These methods complement uncertainty-based criteria by emphasizing coverage and structural relevance rather than only prediction ambiguity.

name: Performance-Aware Curriculum and Noise-Robust Querying
description: Performance-aware deep active learning explicitly estimates sample-wise task quality and difficulty to guide querying and training order. In medical image segmentation, surrogate models can predict metrics like the Dice score without access to ground-truth labels, allowing the system to prioritize samples with low expected performance for annotation. Curriculum learning strategies further order samples from easy to hard, stabilizing optimization and enabling the model to first master simpler cases. In parallel, noisy or mislabeled samples are detected and down-weighted or filtered, preventing unreliable annotations from degrading the learned decision boundary. Together, these ideas yield a curriculum- and quality-driven acquisition process that focuses labeling effort where it most improves true task performance while being robust to label noise.

name: Discrepancy, Uncertainty, and Adversarial Selection
description: This topic covers active learning acquisition functions that score unlabeled samples using discrepancy in semantic feature space, predictive uncertainty, and adversarial instability. Semantic and distinctive scores quantify how much a sample deviates from already labeled data or cluster structure, helping highlight atypical or informative points. These scores are often fused with model-disagreement signals from ensembles or multi-view predictors to prioritize samples whose predictions are inconsistent. Additional selectors enforce class balance and target instances whose predictions are unstable under adversarial perturbations, explicitly coupling robustness considerations with the active learning criterion.

name: Confidence-Based Routing in Semi-Supervised AL
description: This topic describes confidence-based routing mechanisms that link semi-supervised learning with an active learning loop. During training, samples with prediction confidence above a threshold are handled by semi-supervised objectives, while low-confidence samples are diverted to the active learner for expert annotation. This strategy focuses labeling effort on the most ambiguous instances while still exploiting abundant unlabeled data through semi-supervised learning, leading to more efficient use of annotation budgets.

name: Pretraining and Self-Supervision for Cold-Start AL
description: This topic focuses on using pretraining and representation learning to address the cold-start problem in medical image active learning. Large collections of raw, unlabeled images are first exploited via self-supervised or contrastive learning to learn domain-specific embeddings, or via supervised pretraining on datasets such as ImageNet. Active learning then operates in this representation space using strategies such as clustering-based selection with methods like BIRCH or k-means, graph-based greedy subset selection for coverage and diversity, and contrastive-loss magnitudes as informativeness scores. Some approaches further combine entropy and disagreement across image patches or augmentations, sometimes adding randomness to balance exploration and exploitation when choosing the initial labeled pool. Overall, these methods seek to construct a small but highly informative seed set that mitigates class imbalance, improves anomaly detection, and maximizes performance gains per queried medical image.

name: Contrastive Learning for Deep Active Learning
description: Contrastive objectives can be tightly integrated into deep active learning to make better use of limited or weak supervision. One line of work uses one-bit oracle feedback that only indicates whether a prediction is correct, and then applies contrastive learning to pull representations of correctly predicted samples closer while pushing incorrect ones away from their predicted class representations. This reduces annotation complexity in terms of bits while still improving model performance over standard active learning baselines. A complementary line addresses class distribution mismatch in the unlabeled pool by carefully defining negative samples in a contrastive loss to repel out-of-distribution or mismatched-class examples. In this way, contrastive active learning both filters away irrelevant samples and accentuates informative in-distribution instances for querying, with theoretical and empirical evidence of improved efficiency.

name: Region-Based and Cost-Aware Medical Image AL
description: Deep active learning for medical imaging often operates at the level of patches or regions to avoid redundant full-image annotations. Large, easy-to-segment structures contribute little marginal value when densely labeled, whereas small or hard-to-segment organs benefit greatly from targeted annotation, motivating spatially selective querying. Region-selection strategies can jointly optimize uncertainty and estimated annotation cost, preferring patches that are both informative and relatively cheap or fast to label. To better capture spatial context, per-patch confidences can be aggregated over neighborhoods to form region-level uncertainty maps, and the queried regions can use adaptive, non-square shapes that conform to tissue structures. Some methods further regularize training by applying latent-space mixup between labeled and unlabeled patches, improving generalization under limited expert annotations while still leveraging uncertainty-driven selection.

name: Generative Models for Annotation-Efficient AL
description: Generative models can be used within deep active learning to improve label efficiency by synthesizing informative data. Conditional generative models, for example those that map segmentation masks or other structured inputs to realistic medical images, allow controlled synthesis of anatomically plausible samples. Label-conditioned generators go further by taking the desired class label as input, ensuring that all generated examples come with automatically known labels. Such synthetic data can act as advanced data augmentation, effectively expanding the labeled dataset without additional manual annotation effort. When combined with active learning, generative models can be steered to produce diverse or uncertain samples that complement queried real data, accelerating performance gains under tight annotation budgets.

name: Generative Models for Synthetic Query Generation in DAL
description: Deep active learning can use generative models such as VAEs and GANs to synthesize informative samples for annotation. Approaches combine uncertainty measures (e.g., BALD or Monte Carlo Dropout) with conditional or bidirectional GANs and VAEs to generate samples in regions of high model uncertainty, as in chest X-ray classification and other medical imaging tasks. Low-data generative schemes like conditional SinGAN can be trained from a single image–mask pair to produce task-specific segmentation examples when labeled data are extremely scarce. Other methods score synthetic samples for label preservation and redundancy to select only label-consistent, non-overlapping queries from the generative model’s latent space. Early work revealed that low-fidelity or class-ambiguous GAN samples severely limit expert annotation, motivating strategies such as physics-based simulation to automatically label synthetic data at scale.

name: Implicit Semantic Data Augmentation for Active Learning
description: Implicit semantic data augmentation (ISDA) can be integrated into deep active learning by perturbing unlabeled samples in feature space rather than in pixel space. For each unlabeled point, multiple semantic augmentations are generated and the diversity among their predictions is used as a signal of informativeness. Samples whose augmentations yield highly diverse outputs are prioritized for annotation, since they likely lie near complex or uncertain decision boundaries. The model is trained jointly on original data and their ISDA-based augmentations, improving robustness and label efficiency. This framework leverages semantic perturbations to better explore informative regions of the feature space during the active learning cycle.

name: Uncertainty, Representativeness, and Domainness in Active Domain Adaptation
description: In active domain adaptation, query strategies must simultaneously consider predictive uncertainty and how representative each sample is of the target-domain distribution. Representativeness is often captured via domainness or targetness scores that quantify how strongly a sample belongs to the target domain rather than the source. Effective strategies therefore select target samples that are both highly uncertain and highly target-like, ensuring that labeled data correct model mistakes where they matter most for cross-domain performance. Balancing these criteria helps allocate limited annotation budget to target-domain examples that maximally reduce the adaptation gap. This makes active querying a principled complement to standard domain adaptation techniques.

name: Adversarial and Disagreement-Based Sampling for ADA
description: This topic covers active domain adaptation strategies that exploit adversarial objectives and predictive disagreement to choose informative target samples. One line of work combines a domain discriminator with a task model to estimate both label uncertainty and domain dissimilarity, using importance sampling so that uncertain and highly target-specific images are preferentially annotated. Another line focuses on segmentation, where a UDA-pretrained model with pseudo-labels is equipped with two prediction heads whose disagreement highlights poorly learned regions. By querying images or regions that maximize adversarial mismatch or head-level disagreement, these methods simultaneously improve task accuracy and reduce source–target domain gaps with limited annotation.
