name: Research Maturity and Conflicting Evidence in DeepAL
description: Deep active learning (DeepAL) is still in an early research phase compared to traditional deep learning and classical active learning, with relatively few widely accepted benchmark methods or standardized practices. This immaturity contributes to conflicting empirical findings about the effectiveness of different querying strategies, such as diversity-based, uncertainty-based, and random sampling. Some studies report that diversity-based methods consistently outperform uncertainty-based approaches and even random sampling, while later work disputes these conclusions. These inconsistencies suggest that results are highly sensitive to choices of dataset, model architecture, training pipeline, and evaluation protocol. As a result, the field requires more rigorous, standardized experimental practices before strong general claims about strategy superiority can be made.

description: Surveys of deep active learning organize existing work into taxonomies of application domains and benchmark datasets. These taxonomies typically group studies by task type, such as image classification, object detection, natural language processing, medical diagnosis, or remote sensing. They also document the datasets used, labeling regimes, and annotation costs, giving a structured view of where DeepAL has been practically deployed. Such categorization helps researchers identify understudied domains, choose representative benchmarks, and compare methods under similar conditions. name: Instability of Random Sampling Baselines in DeepAL
description: Random sampling baselines in deep active learning often exhibit surprisingly high variability across different studies, even when nominally using the same datasets and architectures. Reported accuracies for the same labeled fraction of data, such as 20% of CIFAR-10 or 40% of CIFAR-100 with a given backbone, can differ by many percentage points. This instability arises from differences in training schedules, regularization, data preprocessing, implementation details, and random seeds. As a consequence, it becomes difficult to judge whether a proposed DeepAL method truly improves over a well-tuned random baseline. Robust evaluation therefore requires stronger and more carefully controlled baselines, multiple runs, and transparent reporting of all experimental choices.

name: Ablation and Transfer Evaluation in DeepAL
description: Ablation studies are critical in deep active learning for disentangling which components of a proposed method are actually responsible for performance gains. By selectively removing or modifying elements such as the query strategy, representation learning module, or training schedule, researchers can identify the minimal ingredients needed for improvement. Transfer experiments, where the same active learning strategy is evaluated across different datasets, label budgets, or model architectures, test the robustness and generality of the approach. Together, ablation and transfer evaluations provide stronger evidence that observed gains are not artifacts of a single experimental setup. They thus support more principled design and fair comparison of DeepAL algorithms.

name: Hybrid Training with Unlabeled and Generated Data
description: Modern deep active learning increasingly couples query selection with hybrid training schemes that exploit labeled, unlabeled, and synthetically generated data. Semi-supervised and self-supervised objectives allow models to learn useful representations from large unlabeled pools while labels are acquired selectively. Generative models such as GANs or VAEs can augment scarce labeled data with synthetic samples that cover underrepresented regions of the input space. Integrating these components throughout the active learning cycle often yields larger performance gains than changing the query strategy alone, by fully leveraging all available data sources.

name: Integrated Methodological Advances in Deep Active Learning
description: Deep active learning research combines several complementary directions, including sophisticated query strategies, task-agnostic evaluation, and computational efficiency. Query optimization balances uncertainty, diversity, and representativeness while keeping selection methods tractable for large deep models. Work on general, non-specific application scenarios stresses methods that transfer across heterogeneous tasks rather than being tuned to a single domain. At the same time, results caution against over-aggressively shrinking labeled subsets in highly diverse datasets, where excessive sparsity can erode performance gains. Integrated approaches that jointly consider strategy design, training pipelines, and label-budget realism are key to maturing the field beyond its current early stage.

name: Pool-Based and Stream-Based Active Learning Foundations
description: Pool-based active learning assumes a fixed pool of unlabeled instances from which the learner repeatedly selects samples to query, fitting well with static datasets but poorly matching dynamic environments. Stream-based (online) active learning instead receives instances sequentially and must decide on arrival whether to request a label, under strict time and budget constraints. This shift changes the problem from batch subset selection to real-time sequential decision-making about labels. The literature also uses overlapping terminology such as stream-based active learning, online active learning, and (sequential) selective sampling, sometimes reserving the latter for querying decisions made during prediction. A clear understanding of both settings and their terminology is essential for formulating appropriate objectives and designing algorithms for real-world streaming scenarios.

name: Deployment Scenarios for Stream-Based Active Learning
description: Stream-based active learning can operate in diverse deployment scenarios, including fully supervised streams, partially labeled streams, and environments where labels are extremely scarce. These scenarios differ in how often labels can be queried, whether some labels arrive passively, and what latency is acceptable between observation and model update. Many real-world streams also exhibit concept drift, requiring algorithms to detect and adapt to changing data distributions while respecting labeling budgets. Explicitly characterizing the scenario helps determine feasible querying strategies, model update rules, and assumptions about stationarity and feedback. Scenario-aware design is therefore central to building robust deep active learning systems for data streams.

name: Taxonomy of Online Active Learning Methods for Data Streams
description: Online active learning methods for data streams can be organized by several dimensions, including the query strategy, the underlying model class, and how they handle drift and label budgets. Query strategies commonly include uncertainty-based, representativeness- or density-based, diversity-promoting, and hybrid or adaptive schemes. Methods may rely on single models, such as incremental neural networks, or ensembles that maintain and update multiple learners to increase robustness. Another axis distinguishes approaches by how explicitly they manage limited labeling budgets, for example through fixed quotas, dynamic budget allocation, or cost-sensitive querying. A clear taxonomy enables systematic comparison of algorithms, identification of underexplored design combinations, and structuring of the state-of-the-art landscape.

name: Evaluation Protocols and Metrics for Stream-Based Active Learning
description: Evaluating stream-based active learning requires protocols that reflect sequential data arrival, evolving distributions, and constrained access to labels. Performance is typically monitored over time using prequential or interleaved test-then-train evaluation, capturing how quickly and how well the model adapts. Metrics include predictive accuracy or loss under streaming evaluation, label efficiency (performance per queried label), and explicit measures of labeling cost. Additional considerations include robustness and recovery under concept drift, latency of adaptation, and computational resource usage such as memory and time per instance. Carefully designed evaluation setups are essential for fair comparison of algorithms and for understanding trade-offs between accuracy, responsiveness, and annotation cost in deep active learning for streams.

name: Research Landscape and Future Directions in Online Active Learning
description: The research landscape of online active learning spans multiple methodological families, including uncertainty-based querying, density- and diversity-aware strategies, drift-aware selection, and combinations with semi-supervised and self-supervised learning. Existing work is fragmented, and prior surveys have often emphasized either pool-based active learning or generic data-stream learning where all labels are assumed available, leaving a gap for truly label-efficient streaming methods. Synthesizing current approaches reveals common design patterns, such as budget-aware decision rules and adaptive thresholds, as well as recurring weaknesses in drift handling, theoretical guarantees, and scalability to deep models. Future research directions include more principled drift-aware querying, tighter integration with representation learning, improved benchmarks and evaluation standards, and methods that can reason about long-term label cost. Addressing these gaps is key to deploying online deep active learning in realistic, high-volume streaming environments.

name: Motivation and Settings for Active Learning
description: Active learning is motivated by situations where labeling data is expensive, slow, or requires scarce expert resources, making it infeasible to annotate all available samples. Under a labeling budget, the learner must query only a subset of instances while still achieving high predictive performance. Common operational settings include pool-based active learning, stream-based or online scenarios, and membership query synthesis, which differ in how unlabeled data are presented and how queries can be formed. Understanding these macro scenarios clarifies the interaction with the oracle, the timing of decisions, and practical constraints such as traceability requirements in high-volume manufacturing or other real-time applications. This perspective helps practitioners choose and evaluate algorithms under conditions that resemble their target deployment environment.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Uncertainty and Information-Theoretic Acquisition Functions
description: Uncertainty-based acquisition in pool-based active learning ranks unlabeled instances by how unsure the model is about their labels, targeting points expected to be most informative. This uncertainty is converted into acquisition scores using functions such as predictive entropy, margin or least-confidence scores, and variation ratio. Information-theoretic criteria like mutual information between labels and model parameters aim to approximate the expected reduction in future uncertainty after querying a label. In deep active learning, these quantities are often estimated from Bayesian neural networks, ensembles, or Monte Carlo dropout to capture predictive distributions. Carefully designed acquisition functions connect model uncertainty to label-query decisions, often yielding faster performance gains per labeled example.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Diversity, Density, and Hybrid Selection Strategies
description: Diversity- and density-based strategies aim to select labeled points that are both representative of the data distribution and non-redundant with respect to each other. Density is often captured using distance metrics, clustering, or graph-based constructions so that queries cover high-probability regions of the input space. Diversity encourages the batch of selected points to be spread across the space or across clusters, reducing wasted labels on near-duplicates. Graph-based semi-supervised methods, such as label propagation, can highlight influential nodes or regions where labels are poorly propagated, guiding more targeted queries. Many deep active learning methods adopt hybrid strategies that combine uncertainty with diversity and density, seeking instances that are simultaneously informative, representative, and complementary within each batch.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Mutual information and variation ratio criteria

name: Batch Size and Query Frequency in Active Learning
description: In pool-based active learning, the batch size controls how many instances are labeled before retraining the model. Small batches allow the acquisition function to adapt frequently to newly observed labels, potentially leading to more precise querying at the cost of frequent, expensive retraining. Large batches are more practical for deep models, where each training run is costly, but they increase the risk of selecting redundant or less informative points. Choosing batch size therefore involves a trade-off between computational efficiency, label efficiency, and the stability of the learning process. This trade-off is problem-dependent and often tuned empirically based on model complexity, dataset size, and available computational resources.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Batch size selection in active learning

name: Unsupervised Deep Representations for Online Active Learning
description: Unsupervised and self-supervised deep models, such as autoencoders or pretrained feature extractors, can be trained on large pools of unlabeled or streaming data before or during active learning. These representations compress raw inputs into feature spaces where class structure and informative samples are easier to identify. In online deep active learning, the model incrementally refines these features as new unlabeled instances arrive, while querying labels only for carefully selected points. This improves both prediction quality and the effectiveness of acquisition functions under tight labeling budgets. The approach is especially valuable when labels are scarce but unlabeled data is abundant and continuously arriving.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Confirmation bias in active query strategies

name: Pseudo-Labeling and Confirmation Bias in Deep Active Learning
description: Pseudo-labeling methods, including self-training and co-training, augment a small labeled set by assigning labels to unlabeled examples using confident predictions from deep models. Integrating these techniques into the active learning loop can greatly increase data efficiency, but also introduces confirmation bias, where early model mistakes are reinforced through erroneous pseudo-labels. Similar bias can arise from query strategies that repeatedly select examples aligned with the current hypothesis, neglecting challenging or contradictory instances. Deep active learning systems must therefore manage confidence calibration, re-weight pseudo-labeled data, and design diversity-aware acquisition functions to mitigate confirmation bias. Careful validation and periodic re-evaluation of pseudo-labeled samples are crucial for robust performance.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Graph-Based Regularization and Structure-Aware Sampling
description: Graph-based semi-supervised methods construct a graph over all labeled and unlabeled instances and enforce smoothness of deep model predictions along the graph structure. A regularization term, often derived from a graph Laplacian, encourages similar predictions for neighboring nodes while allowing sharp changes across low-density regions. In deep active learning, this structure can guide acquisition by prioritizing points near graph-based decision boundaries, in sparse regions, or far from existing labeled nodes. For streaming data, the graph and its embeddings must be updated incrementally, balancing computational cost with representational fidelity. This tight coupling of structural regularization and query selection helps exploit manifold geometry in high-dimensional data.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Online Deep Active Learning for Streaming Text Classification
description: In streaming NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis or spam detection, text instances arrive continuously and models must adapt in real time. Deep classifiers, for example based on transformers or recurrent networks, can be updated incrementally when selected instances are sent for annotation. Online active learning policies decide on the fly which incoming messages or documents to label, trading off uncertainty, diversity, and annotation cost. The system must handle evolving language patterns and topic drifts while keeping the labeling budget constrained. This setting emphasizes low-latency acquisition functions and efficient incremental training procedures for deep text models.

name: Sequential Decision-Making in Streaming Deep Active Learning
description: In domains like video streaming platforms and adaptive clinical trials, data arrive as a sequence of interactions or patients rather than as a fixed pool. Deep active learning must therefore operate in an online, sequential decision-making regime, where each arriving instance is either queried, ignored, or acted upon immediately. The acquisition policy balances information gain against user or patient burden, ethical or regulatory constraints, and strict timing or recruitment requirements. This often leads to formulations that blend deep active learning with contextual bandits or reinforcement learning. Designing such policies requires careful consideration of delayed outcomes, non-stationarity, and the cost of suboptimal decisions during deployment.

name: Smoothing-Based Probabilistic Sampling in Online AL
description: This topic covers smoothing-based formulations of sampling probabilities for online active learning in data streams. The sampling probability is modeled as a function of an informativeness score, typically of the form P_t = δ / (δ + s_t), where δ ≥ 1 is a smoothing parameter that regulates how aggressively labels are requested. By constraining δ and choosing appropriate scores (e.g., margins or transformed margins), the same functional form can reproduce different sampling distributions such as b-sampling or logistic sampling. This unified view clarifies how smoothing controls the trade-off between querying highly informative but frequent examples and limiting labeling cost. It is particularly relevant when integrating uncertainty-based sampling into deep or complex models that must operate under strict annotation budgets.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Specialized Active Sampling for Intrusion Detection
description: This topic focuses on online active learning strategies for real-time intrusion detection under evolving cyberattacks. In streaming network settings, attack patterns induce continual concept drift, making naive random sampling ineffective for maintaining high detection performance. Specialized query strategies selectively request labels for the most informative or suspicious traffic, adapting to non-stationary data distributions while respecting tight annotation budgets. These strategies contrast with uniform random sampling by explicitly modeling informativeness and drift, enabling faster adaptation to emerging attacks. The setting illustrates how domain constraints, such as latency and evolving adversaries, shape the design of active learning policies in practice.

name: Online Active Learning Frameworks with Drift Adaptation
description: This topic presents a general framework for online active learning in streaming environments with potential concept drift. The framework decomposes algorithms into key components: instance scoring, querying decisions, and model updates, all operating incrementally as data arrive. It interfaces with drift detection modules that monitor changes in the underlying distribution and trigger adaptation, such as resetting, reweighting, or modifying the active sampling policy. Within this framework, specific mechanisms include mistake-driven perceptron-style updates applied only to queried and misclassified examples, minimax gradient-based selection to be robust under label noise, and variance-aware soft-margin sampling that combines margin magnitude with uncertainty estimates. Together, these elements provide a flexible template for designing and analyzing online (deep) active learning methods under non-stationarity.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Confidence- and Cost-Aware Streaming Active Learning
description: This topic examines how model confidence and class-dependent costs shape sampling strategies in streaming active learning. Margin-based querying assumes that prediction scores are reliable proxies for uncertainty, which may fail when the underlying model is poorly calibrated or still evolving. To address this, sampling policies explicitly account for model confidence, adjusting query decisions when the learner itself is uncertain or unstable. In parallel, cost-sensitive loss formulations reweight errors for different classes to better handle class imbalance or varying application risks, emphasizing minority or safety-critical classes. Combining confidence awareness with cost sensitivity yields active learners that both respect real-world misclassification costs and avoid over-trusting unreliable model predictions.

name: Cold-Start Active Learning for Imbalanced Multiclass ELMs
description: This topic addresses cold-start challenges in imbalanced multiclass classification using extreme learning machines (ELMs) under an active learning regime. When some classes are severely under-represented, early model estimates for those classes are poor, which is especially problematic during initial deployment. The proposed approach extends an existing active learning framework to the multiclass setting and designs a sampling strategy that jointly considers instance uncertainty and diversity. Pairwise diversity measures are used to reduce redundant queries and to better cover rare classes, mitigating the impact of imbalance during the cold-start phase. The ideas generalize to other deep or shallow models facing similar multiclass, imbalanced, and label-scarce streaming scenarios.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Differentially Private Online SVM Active Learning
description: This topic studies an online margin-based active learning algorithm for SVMs under differential privacy constraints. The informativeness of each incoming instance is modeled as a decreasing function of its distance to the current SVM hyperplane, so that points near the margin are most likely to be queried. In the non-private setting, the algorithm uses a deterministic margin-band rule that queries labels only for points within a fixed distance of the decision boundary. To satisfy differential privacy, this deterministic rule is replaced by a randomized querying strategy whose probability mass is concentrated near the margin but perturbed by carefully calibrated noise. The approach aims to preserve the label efficiency of classic margin-based active learning while providing rigorous privacy guarantees for the labeled data stream.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Online Active Learning with Reject Option
description: This topic considers online active learning for classifiers equipped with a reject option, allowing the learner to abstain from prediction on highly ambiguous instances. The model uses a non-convex double ramp loss, which has a linear region that is informative for updating parameters and outer regions that correspond to confident predictions or rejections. During streaming operation, the algorithm queries the label of an instance only when the current prediction score falls within the linear band of the double ramp loss. The width and position of this band, controlled by a parameter ρ, determine which examples are rejected, which are predicted, and which are queried for labels. This design explicitly trades off misclassification cost, rejection cost, and labeling cost in sequential decision-making.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Bayesian Streaming Active Learning via Adaptive Submodularity
description: This topic presents a Bayesian framework for active learning on data streams based on policy-adaptive submodularity. The framework models the expected utility of labeling decisions as an adaptive submodular function, capturing diminishing returns as more labels are acquired. It distinguishes between a stream setting, where decisions can be deferred within a time window, and a secretary setting, where the learner must decide immediately whether to query each arriving instance. By updating the utility function with newly observed labels, the method adapts to the evolving data distribution and information state over time. The approach is general enough to encompass active classification, active clustering, and active feature selection under streaming and budget constraints, while retaining near-optimality guarantees from adaptive submodular maximization.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Disagreement-Based Online Active Learning and Guarantees
description: This topic develops a disagreement-based framework for online active learning over a hypothesis class with finite VC dimension under Tsybakov noise conditions. The learner maintains a version space of hypotheses consistent with observed labeled data and defines a disagreement region where members of this space predict different labels. Labels are queried only for instances falling inside this region, while outside it the learner predicts using an arbitrary hypothesis from the version space. After each iteration, the version space is pruned by removing hypotheses whose empirical error exceeds that of the current best classifier by more than a data-dependent threshold, thereby shrinking the disagreement region over time. The performance of the resulting policy is analyzed in terms of label complexity and regret, aiming to minimize the expected number of label queries subject to a bound on excess classification errors relative to an optimal hypothesis.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Surrogate-Loss Active Learning with Pseudo-Labels
description: This topic covers online active learning frameworks that allow the learner to either query true labels or assign pseudo-labels while optimizing a surrogate loss. At each time step, instances are added to a mixed set containing both truly labeled and pseudo-labeled examples, and empirical risk is computed over this combined set. This integrates active and semi-supervised learning, enabling the model to leverage weak labels to reduce query rates. Pseudo-labels can be generated by propagating labels from k-nearest neighbors via a weighted majority vote, enriching the training signal when ground-truth labels are sparse or delayed. Such mechanisms aim to preserve model accuracy while tightly controlling labeling cost in streaming settings.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Distribution shifts in drifting data streams

name: Bayesian Active Learning for Human Activity Recognition
description: This topic addresses semi-supervised active learning for online human activity recognition from sensor streams. A pre-trained conditional restricted Boltzmann machine is used as a generic feature extractor, providing representations robust to varying sensor layouts. Instance selection follows a Bayesian principle that compares current parameter uncertainty with the expected risk conditioned on each possible label. The discrepancy between these quantities quantifies the value of acquiring the label for the current instance. A dynamically adaptive threshold then decides whether the expected risk reduction justifies querying, balancing recognition performance against labeling cost over time.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Online Active Multiple Kernel Learning with Ensemble Agreement
description: This topic focuses on active learning with multiple kernel functions in an online setting, often using random feature approximations for efficiency. An ensemble of kernel-based predictors is maintained, each updated locally, and then combined into a single predictor whose kernel weights are learned via exponential weighting to minimize regret over queried, labeled instances. The query strategy is confidence-based, relying on the agreement of the weighted kernel ensemble: when all kernels make similar predictions on an instance, the system treats it as high-confidence and skips querying. A tolerance threshold on this agreement controls the trade-off between label savings and prediction reliability. This framework adapts both instance selection and kernel weights jointly as data arrive in a stream.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Distribution shifts in drifting data streams

name: Drift-Aware Active Learning and Concept Drift Adaptation
description: This topic studies active learning in non-stationary data streams where the underlying distribution may drift over time. It distinguishes between covariate shift, which affects only the feature distribution, and true concept drift, which changes the conditional relationship between features and labels. Purely unsupervised drift detection can fail to recognize concept drift when the input distribution is stable, motivating the use of selectively queried labels to validate suspected changes. A drift-aware strategy maintains a primary classifier and spawns a secondary classifier when drift warnings arise, training the new model on queried labeled data during the warning phase. Upon confirmed drift, the new classifier replaces the old one, enabling smoother transitions and focusing label queries on regions most indicative of changing concepts.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Distribution shifts in drifting data streams

name: Simulation-Based Label Forecasting for Delayed Feedback
description: This topic addresses active learning in streaming scenarios where queried labels are delayed. Instead of repeatedly querying similar instances from a region where labels are still pending, it simulates incoming labels using a bagging strategy that averages utility estimates over multiple hypothetical labelings. An alternative fuzzy-labeling scheme explicitly encodes label uncertainty by assigning soft labels rather than hard class decisions. These simulation mechanisms approximate the effect of future supervision, allowing the learner to avoid redundant queries and maintain progress while waiting for ground-truth labels.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Adaptive Uncertainty Criteria Under Imbalance and Drift
description: This topic focuses on advanced uncertainty-based querying strategies that adapt to class imbalance and temporal variation. A margin-based uncertainty measure (best-versus-second-best prediction) is controlled by per-class thresholds that depend on class-specific sample counts and a tunable parameter, so rare classes are more aggressively queried. The thresholds are further adjusted over time, for example via meta-learning on each data window, to balance label budget against responsiveness to evolving concepts. In addition, a discrepancy measure compares model uncertainty on an instance before and after its label is incorporated, and b-sampling prioritizes points expected to yield the largest uncertainty (and error) reduction. Together, these mechanisms create a family of active learning policies that tailor uncertainty criteria to class frequencies, temporal windows, and expected impact on model performance.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Concept-Drift-Aware Stream Active Learning with Hybrid Sampling
description: This topic covers stream-based active learning methods that explicitly detect and track concept drift while selecting informative labels. Incoming data are processed in fixed-length chunks whose adjacent distributions are compared to identify drifts, after which a multi-objective optimization selects instances that are both highly relevant to the emerging concept and mutually diverse, with diversity quantified via measures such as Pearson correlation. Instance selection often combines margin-based uncertainty sampling with random sampling so that the learner captures both changes near the current decision boundary and shifts occurring in previously unexplored regions. Density is modeled with a growing Gaussian mixture model that forms and splits clusters based on Mahalanobis distance, while a Bayesian logistic regressor with time-varying parameters tracks evolving class boundaries. An ensemble of dynamic classifiers is maintained with damped sliding-window weights, emphasizing recent models for abrupt drifts while retaining older ones to better handle gradual changes.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Bi-criteria GGMM-based active learning with drift handling

name: Clustering and Density-Peak Selection in Streaming Active Learning
description: This topic uses clustering structure to guide representative and informative querying in data streams. Each incoming data block is clustered, and points are chosen that are simultaneously informative for the current decision boundary and representative of their clusters, providing training data for more stable base classifiers. Density-peak clustering identifies high-density exemplars and uses an altitude-like measure to detect incomplete or weakly formed clusters in the evolving feature space. Labels are then requested from these underrepresented regions in subsequent iterations, improving coverage of emerging or poorly modeled areas. By targeting both cluster exemplars and incomplete clusters, the method balances representativeness and exploration in non-stationary streaming environments.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Density and Novelty-Based Streaming Query Strategies
description: This topic covers online active learning strategies that combine local density, classifier uncertainty, and novelty measures to select informative instances in data streams with concept drift and noise. One approach defines a local density score based on how often an observation appears as the nearest neighbor within a sliding cognition window, which is refreshed according to a memory-strength policy inspired by Ebbinghaus’s forgetting curve to handle gradual and abrupt drifts. Another approach uses a spherical potential measure, derived from kernel-based methods, to quantify the novelty of incoming samples and decide when to create new fuzzy rules. Labeling and structure-adaptation decisions are governed by thresholds on density, uncertainty, and spherical potential, aiming to remain label-efficient while maintaining a representative and adaptive model.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Conflict and Ignorance Criteria in Stream Learning
description: This topic focuses on conflict and ignorance as complementary criteria for single-pass active learning in evolving classifiers, including applications to visual inspection. Conflict quantifies how close an instance lies to the current decision boundary, indicating label ambiguity and motivating queries for boundary refinement. Ignorance measures the distance of a new sample from the labeled training set in feature space, highlighting unexplored regions where the model is poorly supported. In a visual quality-control setting, instances are processed once, and samples whose certainty (computed via conflict–ignorance for fuzzy models or best-versus-second-best margins for random forests) falls below a threshold are stored in a buffer for later labeling. The buffer size and certainty threshold jointly control the trade-off between rapid model updates and the frequency of human annotation.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Certainty-based querying in visual inspection streams

name: Active Learning for Evolving Regression in Data Streams
description: This topic addresses active learning for regression models that evolve over streaming data. A Bayesian probit framework with time-decay maintains an online posterior over classifier or regressor weights while downweighting older observations, enabling adaptation to concept drift and supporting query strategies such as entropy-based, function-value-based, and random sampling. For fuzzy and rule-based regressors, predictive uncertainty is quantified through locally adaptive error bars, and parameter uncertainty is assessed using alphabetic optimality criteria such as A-optimality, guiding which samples most reduce expected parameter variance. Latent-structure-based statistics like Hotelling T² and squared prediction error (SPE) further measure how strongly a new point violates the current latent subspace, indicating informative outliers for labeling. These ideas are implemented with models such as principal component regression, partial least squares, and Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy systems within sliding-window or single-pass streaming settings.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Hotelling T² and SPE for AL sampling

name: Adaptive Uncertainty Thresholds and Optimal Design in AL
description: This topic links adaptive query control in active learning with principles from optimal experimental design. In recurrent fuzzy classifiers, a variable uncertainty strategy adjusts the querying threshold over time, focusing labeling effort on rules with low support that are formed from few observations, thereby improving underrepresented regions of the input space. From an optimal design perspective, active learning is framed as choosing experiments or samples that maximize information gain for parameter estimation or prediction quality while minimizing the number of labeled runs. Classical optimality criteria from linear regression design provide a theoretical basis for these strategies, formalizing trade-offs between resource efficiency and model performance. Together, dynamic thresholds and design-based criteria address the what-to-learn question in a principled and data-efficient way.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Optimal experimental design and active learning

name: D-Optimality Criteria for Fuzzy Model Queries
description: This topic introduces D-optimality-based query strategies for evolving fuzzy models. The core idea is to reduce parameter uncertainty in the consequents of fuzzy rules by selecting samples that maximize the determinant of the information matrix, a classical D-optimal design criterion. Such samples are expected to yield the greatest reduction in the volume of the confidence ellipsoid for the parameters, improving estimation precision. Embedding D-optimality into online active learning allows fuzzy systems to grow and update using the most informative observations, rather than relying solely on heuristic uncertainty or error-based measures. This bridges optimal experimental design theory with practical stream-based active learning for fuzzy and rule-based models.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: D-optimality for fuzzy model parameter selection

name: Linear Regression Geometry for Optimal Design
description: A linear regression model y = Xβ + ε with Gaussian noise provides a convenient foundation for design-based active learning. The ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy depends on the information matrix XᵀX, or equivalently the moment matrix M = XᵀX / N. The eigenvalues and determinant of this matrix encode how informative the design is for estimating β, linking directly to classical A- and D-optimality criteria. Under Gaussian assumptions, β̂ is Normal with covariance σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹, inducing a confidence ellipsoid whose volume and axis lengths are governed by the spectrum of XᵀX. This geometric view connects parameter uncertainty to design quality and underlies many optimal-design-inspired active learning strategies.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Streaming Optimal Design for Sequential Labeling
description: Optimal experimental design can be adapted from offline batch settings to streaming scenarios where candidate points arrive sequentially. In this setting, the learner must decide online which observations to label in order to approximate A- or D-optimal designs under a fixed labeling budget. Extensions to heteroskedastic regression allocate labels to balance coefficient variances when noise depends on the covariates, generalizing A-optimality to non-constant error variance. Conditional D-optimality methods further refine selection by making the design marginally D-optimal relative to an existing labeled set and updating decisions as new points arrive. Together, these approaches provide principled sequential selection rules that align active querying with classical design optimality in dynamic data streams.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Norm-Thresholding and Robust Streaming Sampling
description: Norm-thresholding methods use the geometry of a whitened feature space to decide which streaming points to label. A passive warm-up phase collects an initial unlabeled set to estimate the data covariance, whiten both the design and warm-up features, and tune a norm threshold via kernel density estimation to achieve a target sampling rate. During active querying, points whose leverage or whitened norm lies within a prescribed range are selected, effectively targeting regions that are informative for reducing prediction variance. Introducing a double-threshold scheme bounds the sampling region, discarding very low-leverage points as uninformative and very high-leverage points as potential outliers. This annular selection region improves robustness, preventing optimal-design-inspired samplers from over-focusing on extreme observations while maintaining strong predictive performance.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Deep Active Learning for Streaming Decisions
description: Deep active learning in streaming settings studies how deep models decide when to query labels while processing data sequentially. One approach formulates the label-versus-predict choice as a reinforcement learning problem, where an LSTM-based policy observes the current state of the learner and chooses between requesting a label or issuing a prediction, trading off annotation cost against prediction errors. At the same time, many successful deep active learning methods for images rely on clustering or computing pairwise similarities in deep embedding space, which typically assumes multiple passes over a static dataset and substantial storage. These operations are often infeasible in single-pass, memory-constrained data streams, limiting the direct applicability of pool-based deep active learning methods. Research in this area seeks new architectures, objectives, and selection mechanisms that both exploit deep representations and respect strict streaming constraints.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Limits of deep AL in stream settings

name: Deep Feature Online Active Learning for Process Monitoring
description: Vision-based process monitoring can leverage deep feature extractors together with online active learning to reduce labeling costs on industrial image streams. A common approach is to use a pre-trained convolutional network such as ResNet-18 to obtain compact, expressive feature representations from each incoming frame. An online active learning module then evaluates these deep features to decide which images are most informative to annotate. This setup decouples heavy feature extraction from lightweight querying logic, making it suitable for high-throughput production environments. By selectively labeling only critical frames, the system maintains accurate process monitoring while significantly limiting manual annotation effort.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Active learning in compressor optimization loops

name: Gradient Embedding Diversity Sampling for Deep Streams
description: In deep streaming active learning, each incoming instance can be represented by the gradient of the loss with respect to the final network layer, using the model’s current prediction as a pseudo-label. These gradient vectors act as embeddings that capture how each example would update the model if it were labeled. A determinant-based selection rule, often implemented via a covariance matrix over gradient embeddings, chooses points that jointly maximize diversity and information gain. This results in querying examples that cover different directions in gradient space instead of repeatedly selecting similar uncertain instances. The approach is particularly well-suited to mini-batch or continual training regimes where deep models are updated incrementally.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Slice-Aware Active Label Budgeting for Streaming Object Detection
description: Streaming object detection in domains such as autonomous driving must contend with highly imbalanced conditions, including rare but safety-critical scenarios like fog, heavy rain, or nighttime. Slice-aware active learning addresses this by partitioning the data stream into slices corresponding to different conditions and tracking model performance per slice. Instead of allocating labels proportionally to slice frequency, the method dynamically directs more of the annotation budget to slices where the detector underperforms. This counters the tendency of passive or frequency-based sampling to neglect rare yet important environments. In deep detection pipelines, such slice-aware budgeting helps maintain robust performance across diverse conditions while keeping overall labeling costs under control.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

local_topics.title: Slice-aware budgeting in streaming object detection

name: Online Active Learning on Data Streams
description: This topic covers active learning when data arrive as a continuous stream and querying decisions must be made in real time. It emphasizes the common assumption that queried instances receive labels immediately, enabling rapid model adaptation and iterative selection. The dependence on real-time label availability shapes which algorithms are feasible in practice and how quickly models can react to evolving data distributions. It also highlights the need for practical annotation workflows and tools that can deliver timely labels and integrate seamlessly into streaming learning pipelines.

sources.article_title: Active learning for data streams: a survey

name: Query Strategies and Constraints in Online Active Learning
description: This topic focuses on strategies for selecting informative instances in online active learning, where data arrive sequentially and labeling budgets are limited. It includes mechanisms such as uncertainty sampling, diversity-based selection, query-by-committee, and reinforcement-learning-driven policies tailored to streaming data. The discussion also highlights that many dominant online classification approaches rely on ensembles or batch formation, which may be infeasible under tight memory, latency, or computational constraints. These limitations motivate the development of new, lightweight querying and modeling paradigms that better align with real-world streaming scenarios.

name: Batch-Mode Active Learning with Streamed Sampling
description: This topic addresses learning from data streams when instances are observed online but labels and model updates are deferred and processed in batches. Streamed sampling policies decide in real time which instances to store and later query, while respecting strict memory constraints. Once a batch is formed, the selected instances are labeled and used to update deep models in a standard batch-mode fashion. This hybrid design seeks to balance the responsiveness of streaming acquisition with the computational efficiency and stability of batch training.

name: Online Active Learning for Nonlinear Regression
description: This topic explores active learning methods for regression in online or streaming settings, with a particular emphasis on nonlinear models. It highlights the role of Bayesian optimization and related techniques that use probabilistic surrogate models to guide query selection. By balancing exploration and exploitation, these methods aim to efficiently improve function estimates while new data arrive over time. The focus is on extending beyond linear models and bandit formulations to richer nonlinear regression scenarios in dynamic environments.

name: Streaming Active Learning for Object Detection
description: This topic considers object detection as a structured prediction task within online active learning for data streams. It examines how to selectively label complex outputs such as bounding boxes under constraints on annotation cost and latency. Both single-model, fully online settings and scenarios with mini-batch processing are discussed. The goal is to extend data-stream active learning beyond classification and regression to more complex computer vision tasks while respecting streaming and resource constraints.
